1.1: Languages and cultures change and disappear all the time. We all know this. Sometimes they disappear because a culture is being oppressed. Sometimes it's an act of will. Sometimes it's a matter of historical contingency. Sometimes things simply change. Sometimes we just forget.
1.2: The materials and tools and techniques, the body of shared knowledge of the Western musical tradition, is not literally a language, but it's a codified body of practices that at this point is at least 2,000 years into its evolution. And it could disappear.
1.3: It might not look likely from our present vantage point, but if you think about how long it took for us to get here—to develop all the instruments, the scales, the keys, the rhythms, the whole body of materials upon which this art form depends— it was by no means an obvious development. It took place over an extremely lengthy span of time, and it required the input of countless musicians and performers. This is our great inheritance.
1.4: But it is possible that, of course, it won't last forever and that it could disappear not through an act of vandalism, not through being oppressed by anybody, but simply because we've forgotten. We haven't retained it. We haven't continued to transmit these skills.
1.5: The object of this course is to give you a grand tour through these tools, these traditions, these techniques, so that you'll have a broad understanding of what's involved in writing music.
1.6: Now, I gave a course earlier here at Peterson Academy on an Introduction to Musical Composition. One of the things I want to do from the outset is to differentiate between the two courses. So musical composition is a more applied course, you might say. It tells you in practical terms how you might go about making a piece, what the steps are, what some of the challenges are.
1.7: This course is a little bit different. In order to explain the particular nature of this course, I have to step back a little bit, and we have to talk about the term "music theory," to start with. The theory of music is kind of an unusual appellation, in a sense, because what we'regoing to talk about has got nothing in common with a scientific theorem. This is not exactly like that. Again, this is a body of past practices, which, of course, persist into the present.
1.8: But it's important to look at it that way in the sense that this is not prescriptive knowledge. It doesn't tell you what to do. It tells you what has been done. It's descriptive. It's not necessarily going to help you constitute a creative practice, but it's a matter of learning the grammar, the syntax, the building blocks of language in a way that allows musicians, performers, and audiences to communicate with each other.
1.9: Each one of us is both the inheritor and the guardian of this trove of knowledge, of this tradition, which depends on all of us for its continuation. If tomorrow we were to stop teaching the basics of harmony, if we were to stop teaching counterpoint, it's quite conceivable that this body of knowledge could come to an end. That's the spirit in which I approach this. This is a deeply valuable inheritance. It's important to look at this not as a collection of dry facts, but again, as an attempt to describe the phenomenon of music such that it can be transmitted.
1.10: We mentioned that languages, of course, change all the time, and that this course doesn't tell you what to do. But it's very useful for having an idea of what might lie at the center of this tradition. And a big part of that, a big part of what distinguishes the Western musical tradition, is two things.
1.11: The first is that a great deal of it has to do with notation. It has to do with writing down music, such that it can be reproduced in accordance with a written text in multiple different situations. There's a certain permanence of the musical idea this way. So that's one thing. It's largely a written tradition.
1.12: And the other thing is that Western music has tended to emphasize polyphony over other dimensions. That's something that I get into in more detail in my course on the History of Western Music. But I want to remind you of those two things because it's important in coming to terms with the particular nature of music theory as it's practiced in the West.
1.13: A lot of this is predicated on the practice of writing down music. Of course, we're all accustomed to the way that sheet music looks, the way that notation looks. We have some degree of familiarity. Even people who have never sat down at an instrument can recognize staff notation, a clef, and a note. We might think that this is completely obvious. How else could you do it?
1.14: But in fact, these systems, these symbols, these notations, took thousands of years to develop, and there's nothing obvious about it at all. If you think about what music notation attempts to do, it's attempting to take things that are by nature ephemeral— it's literally vibrations in the air—and attempts to give them a fixed form. That's actually very difficult to do. It took an immensely long time to sort out the various problems.
1.15: What we have today is by no means perfect. There are all kinds of things that are very difficult to convey through any written expression, any written form in music. But it's a broadly applicable and broadly useful language of symbols.
1.16: We're going to look at rhythm, how to notate it, how to understand rhythm. We're going to look at pitch, which involves intervals, both melodic and harmonic. We're going to look at the five-line staff, how to read it, what this whole language of symbols means. We're going to look at matters of harmony, and also just practical ear training exercises, so that each of us can hopefully become a better musician.
1.17: Remember that this gives you a very, very wide berth. You can do anything with this. There's absolutely no stylistic a priori in any of this material. The proof of that is that as you look at the music of the 20th century, it's extraordinarily broad. It encapsulates all kinds of different practices and styles, each of which has at least something to do with this body of knowledge.
1.18: To take a couple of examples, one from literature, one from music. The novelist, James Joyce, was commenting on the furore that was kicked up by the publication of his book, Finnegans Wake, which is a famously difficult book to read involving multiple neologisms and a very elastic use of language. It's very, very densely written. He would take words from different languages and combine them to make a new word and so on. He responded to this by saying, "I don't know what they're so upset about. They can have their English language afterwards, when I'm done with it."
1.19: Likewise, the German composer, Stockhausen, Karlheinz Stockhausen, was asked by a BBC journalist why he felt it was necessary to break things, why it was necessary to break the rules of music. Stockhausen said, "I haven't broken anything. I'm just adding to it. I've added a whole new room to the mansion," so to speak. So think of this as being a central body of knowledge that allows you, if you wanted to, to expand outwards or to remain right in the center. But this is a very broad enterprise.
1.20: So we're going to start at the very beginning. We're going to start with the basics of music notation, and we're going to understand how that works. Remember that there are lots of people who are successful in music who don't learn these things.
1.21: I gave the example in the Composition course of Paul McCartney, who can neither read nor write music and hasn't stopped him from being one of, if not the most, successful musicians of the 20th century. But that's partly because he sits on top of this 2000-year tradition that he's absorbed through his fingertips unconsciously through osmosis, if you like.
1.22: Knowing this material can help to speed things up for most people, I would say. I can't think of any circumstance in which it could possibly be a detriment to learn this. If your approach is more intuitive, if you're not accustomed to thinking music in this way, it's not going to cause you any harm. The additional knowledge can only be helpful. That would be the spirit with which I would approach it.
1.23: Let's start at the very beginning. We're going to look at the five-line staff. We're going to start with the notion of the staff. The staff in conventional music notation has five lines. Now, that being said, historically, if you go back, you'll see staves with two lines, three lines, four lines. You have to go back quite a way; it's farther back than a thousand years to see this.
1.24: But this was a technical problem that had to be solved, which is: How can you take something as nebulous as pitch? In other words, what is the frequency of a tone? Or in common parlance, how high or how low is it? How do you write that down? How do you give it a fixed form? That turned out to be a very, very complicated problem.
1.25: The solution, which started to stabilize approximately a thousand years ago, was to have this ruled staff, where you can have a spatial metaphor for the disposition of sounds. The farther you are towards the bottom of the staff, the lower the sound, and the higher you go, the higher the sound. That's a spatial representation of sound, if you like.
1.26: Now, that being said, you might also have staves, and this is increasingly common, that are intended not for notating pitch, but simply for notating rhythms, in which case you don't need five lines. One line is enough if you're just writing down a rhythm. If you look at percussion notation, as an example, you'll often just see a single line like this with a little clef at the beginning, and then you'll see rhythmic values on it. Because the pitch doesn't need to change, we don't need anything more than one line.
1.27: Let's look at the basics of staff notation. The first thing you need to know is that to the left of a staff is a symbol that looks like this, and this is called a clef. The clef tells you what register you're in. Is it high? Is it low? Is it medium? The origin of these different clefs, of which there are many, was to specify a vocal range. There are four basic human voice types: soprano, alto, tenor, and bass. Depending on which type of voice you had, you might want to situate a different clef on the staff in order to reflect that different range.
1.28: This is because the total range of pitches that it's possible to reproduce with the human voice is pretty broad. A baritone can usually sing down to an F [plays low F]. A bass might go a little bit lower than that [plays low E–D]. A basso profondo, which is a very rare voice type, might go down to [plays low C] or even lower. Then a soprano can sing up to about [plays high C] there, maybe a little higher [plays high D]. If you're a coloratura soprano, a virtuoso, then you might go [plays high F] up to the high F, which, to hear that sung by a human voice, is really something.
1.29: That's a pretty big range. But remember that our staff here has only five lines on it. How are you going to fit all those notes onto one staff? Well, the answer is you don't. You use different clefs depending on the range that you're working with. If that's the case for instruments, it also holds true for voices.
1.30: The clef that you're probably most likely to encounter is the treble clef. We're going to use the tone middle C as our reference point to get oriented in all these different clefs. The reason this is called middle C is that it lies directly in the middle of the piano keyboard [plays middle C]. That's middle C.
1.31: If you've ever taken a piano lesson, that's one of the first things you learn because you look at a piano keyboard and it's like this sea of keys. You don't know which octave you're playing in. It's very difficult at first to get your bearings at a keyboard because there's so many notes. So that's your orientation point, is middle C.
1.32: Once you know where that is, you can find everything else much more easily. It's the same with staff notation. With each different clef, middle C is positioned differently on the staff. In the case of the treble clef, middle C is here. You'll notice that it doesn't actually fit inside the clef. But I have to draw an additional line below the staff in order to put my middle C down.
1.33: This additional line, which looks like this—it's just a little fragment of an additional staff line—is called a ledger line. Ledger lines are used sparingly in order to notate pitches or tones that lie below or above what the staff can hold—there'll be more on that in a minute. So this tone here, one ledger line below the lowest line of the treble staff, is middle C. Now, that's for the treble clef.
1.34: Now, if I write in the bass clef, the bass clef looks like this. Now, with both of these staves, there's a little visual clue, again, to help you get oriented so that you know where you're at. We talked about middle C and how its position changes depending on the staff. But there's also one other thing.
1.35: You notice that the bass staff has this little nub here. If I zoom in a little bit, you can see it there, which is situated on the second line, reading from the top. Then on top of that, there are these two dots above and below it. The purpose of these symbols, and the reason the clef looks like this, is to draw your attention to this second line. If you place a note on that second line like that, then you get an F.
1.36: The old name for this clef, and actually the current name in French and other languages, is the F clef or the "clé de fa." More on that later. Likewise, if I return to the treble clef, the French term for this is the "clé de sol," or the G clef. These terms are not broadly used in English anymore, but it's useful to understand their historical origins. The G clef or the treble clef wraps around the second line from the bottom. If you put a note there, you get a G, hence the name G clef.
1.37: Those are the two most widely used clefs. The bass clef, which, as its name indicates, allows you to write notes from middle C downwards, and middle C on the bass staff looks like this. Now, you'll notice something. I'll write that down. Middle C on the bass clef also requires a ledger line or a supplementary line above the staff in order to be written down. These two tones are one and the same. This and this. But they're notated in different ways.
1.38: On the treble staff, the middle C is right at the bottom. You could think of it as being where that staff begins its range. And on the bass clef, it's at the top, and they're the same. Those are the treble and bass clefs, and there are two others that we need to know.
1.39: Now, this is kind of a funny-looking clef. Once again, you'll see that there's a particular design to this clef, which is intended to help us get our bearings. In the case of this clef, which is called commonly the alto clef, or in French, the "clé d'ut trois," the key in which C is situated on the third line. In the alto clef, middle C is found right in the middle of the staff on the third line.
1.40: Finally, there's a very similar-looking clef called the tenor clef, or in French, the "clé d'ut quatre," which looks like this. Almost the same, but it's a little bit higher on the staff, and middle C is located here. So these four different staves—sorry, these four different clefs, allow us to situate a range of a voice or an instrument in a way that it fits conveniently on the staff, whether it's a very low range, very high range, or something in the middle. The alto and tenor clefs have a more medium range, in between soprano and bass.
1.41: Different instruments use different clefs for their musical notation. If you're playing a cello, or a double bass, or a tuba, or a trombone, or some other low instrument, in all likelihood, your part is going to be notated using the bass clef. If you're playing a high instrument like a flute, a clarinet, or a violin, most likely it will be notated on the treble clef. If you play the viola, or sometimes the trombone, your part will be notated on the alto clef or possibly the tenor clef. With the idea, again, of making the notation easier to read so that the part fits comfortably on the staff.
1.42: Okay, so let's return to this five-line treble staff and how we can get oriented on it. Remember that middle C, again, requires a ledger line, and that this symbol here curls around the G, which is situated here [plays C–G–C]. There's middle C [plays C], and there's the G above it [plays G].
1.43: Now, fortunately, we have mnemonic aids to help us remember where the notes lie on the staff. Some of these are very silly, and some of them are less so. But the one I learned when I was a kid was F-A-C-E, "Face". The staff has both spaces and lines, which is to say that a note can be situated between two lines on a space like this, or it can be situated on a line with the line going through the note head.
1.44: If we're reading the spaces, then reading from the bottom to the top, we get F-A-C-E, "Face". If we're reading the lines, we get E-G-B-D and F. Now, the mnemonic for that, there'ss quite a few of them, that I learned, was "Everyy Good Boy Deserves"—— okay, you can decide what the last one is. How about Favors?? Whatever helps you to remember it. And so byy remembering these two mnemonics, you can find a notee head on a staff and remember what it is, when you're getting started. Eventually, this becomes second nature, and you don't have to think about it anymore.
1.45: And likewise with the bass staff, starting from the bottom space, we get A-C-E-G. And starting from the bottom line, we gett G-B-D-FF and A.. For some reason, I don't have a hilarious mnemonic for these. I don't know why.. They're less common. Maybe I didn't learn them for whatever reason. You can invent your own, in anyy case. But for now, we'll just stick with the treble clef just for the sake of simplicity. So F-A-C-E-E-G-B-D-F.
1.46: Once again, that gives you a fairly limited range. If I'm reading notation in the treble staff and I start with the bottom line, which gives me E above middle C [plays E], then I can play E-G-B-D-F [plays E–G–B–D–F]. And if I read the spaces starting on F, I get [plays F–A–C–E ] F-A-C-E. That gives you just over an octave [plays E–F–G–B–C–D–E–F]. Pretty limited range. Unless you're playing an instrument that only has six or seven notes on it, you're going to need more than that. That's where, again, we come back to the ledger lines.
1.47: So ledger lines, the idea is to use them as little as possible because they make the notation a little bit harder to read. Of course, professional musicians are accustomed to them, and it's not a problem, but it can make the learning process a little bit slower. So we try to avoid writing lots and lots of ledger lines unless it's necessary and there's no way to avoid it.
1.48: So just as the middle C in the treble clef requires one ledger line below the staff, you can also have ledger lines that appear above the staff. So remember that we have F-A- C-E. If we keep going, then we get G, that's above the staff there. If we want to go above that, we need a ledger line. Just like on the staff, the note can go above the line like this, or the line can go through it. And of course, we can have as many ledger lines as we want, in principle, although it gets very hard to read.
1.49: Now we should talk a little bit about the nomenclature of tones. Now, you have to bear in mind that music theory is a conception of sharing this knowledge that is located in a specific culture. In other words, it's not done universally in every country. If you were to talk about music theory in a French conservatory, that term doesn't have a wide currency the way it does in the English-speaking world.
1.50: The Germans have a term "Musiktheorie" that corresponds to music theory, but it's not taught as a separate subject as such in France. Instead, the body of knowledge that's grouped within music theory is divided into different subjects that have a more practical and less theoretical orientation, such as the notion of "écriture," which is music writing, and that immediately situates it as more of a practical than an abstract skill.
1.51: In North America, when you say, "music theory," it's understood that you mean, generally speaking, the rudiments of music, understanding staff notation, understanding how chords are put together, understanding the terminology, effectively. It's a body of knowledge that covers everything that you can do without ever touching an instrument, basically.
1.52: But again, different cultures will have a more theoretical leaning or a more practical leaning, depending on how their musical pedagogy has evolved. In Germany, you can do a doctoral degree in music theory. That doesn't exist in France. So some of the way that these disciplines are taught very much depends on the culture.
1.53: When I talk about the nomenclature of the tones, that is also something that varies from country to country. If you're in Italy, for example, or France, or Spain, most likely when you begin your musical education, you're going to be subjected to a form of torture called "solfège" or "solffegio." What that is, is a way of memorizing intervals and tones through the use of note names. These note names are very, very old. They're at least a thousand years old.
1.54: We're going all the way back to the early medieval era in which, as a mnemonic aid, theorists devised a set of six syllables called the medieval hexachord, which was used to help singers remember the notes that they would have to sing. And those sixsyllabus are ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la. Ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la. Now, those syllabus were chosen not by accident, but actually, they form an acrostic in Latin if you take the first letter of the six. On top of that, each one has a distinctly different sound.
1.55: Now, later on, centuries later, "ut" was replaced with the syllable "do," simply because there was a theorist who preferred the sound of that. And later on, a seventh syllable was added, which is" si" which is often called "ti" in North American nomenclature. So that's very common in the Latin countries: do, re, mi, fa, so, la, si, or ut, re, mi, fa, so, la, si, or ti.
1.56: In the German-speaking world, however, there's a completely different tradition where the notes are simply assigned the names of letters. We have C, D, E, F, G, A, and confusingly, H, which breaks the series. We don't have to get into all the historical and theoretical reasons for why this is the case and why it evolved that way. But "ha" or "H" is the German equivalent of our "B" or B-natural. So all these different nomenclatures, but all with the same intention, which is to help us remember the tones.
1.57: And so if you're learning solfège, you're learning to associate notation with the sound that you can produce with your voice reliably and consistently. Rather than do, re, mi, fa, sol, we go C, D, E, F, G, A, B. These are the basic tones of a seven-note or diatonic scale, which forms the basis of most of our musical tradition. Once you get to B, this series just repeats itself—C, D, E, F, G, A, B, C, D, E, F, G, A, B, et cetera.
1.58: Okay, so now that we've understood that on a staff, we have both spaces and lines, we can start writing out a simple scale. I'll show you what that looks like. If I start on middle C in the treble clef, I'm going to have to go up to the next space or line in order to produce the next tone in the series. That's our middle C. Then we go up to the space above C, which sits on a line. We're alternating lines and spaces, and then I just keep going. And that gives me C, D, E, F, G, A, B, C. So that's a complete scale with the bottom note repeated at the top [plays C scale]. C, D, E, F, G, A, B, C.
1.59: Now, the nice thing about the Italian and French systems is that when you're learning these materials, you're required to sing them. You don't simply understand the notation in an abstract sense, but you immediately have to externalize it. You associate the tone with a syllable, [plays C scale] do re mi fa sol la si do, and so on. In some ways, it's a difficult discipline because you can go extremely far with this, where you can learn to very rapidly sightread a piece of sheet music with all of the syllables in place.
1.60: To some degree, that's a matter of culture and taste and different historical traditions. A lot of North Americans are not accustomed to that system and find it quite challenging when they first encounter it. But again, for others, especially if you begin early in life, it can become second nature.
1.61: That's how you situate notes on a staff with spaces and with lines. Now, we've looked at the different clefs. We've looked at the different ranges of the clefs, and we've looked at some mnemonic aids that help you to get situated. We've also looked at ledger lines. Now we're going to continue a little bit.
1.62: We're going to talk about the grand staff, which looks like this. Now, music written for keyboard instruments or instruments that have a particularly large range, like a piano— a piano covers more than seven octaves. You can't fit all of that on a single staff, and it's not practical to change clefs all the time, especially since you might need to notate a very low sound and a very high sound simultaneously, in which case you need another system. If you look at piano notation, you're going to see something called a grand staff.
1.63: A grand staff consists of both a treble clef on top and a bass clef on the bottom. You need two staves, most of the time, to notate piano music. Remember, this and this are the same. They're both middle C. That's very convenient because it means the middle of the piano is situated exactly in between the two staves. Then, of course, you can expand upwards from there or downwards from there.
1.64: We've looked at percussion clefs. Remember that in percussion writing where you don't need to differentiate between pitches, you don't need five lines, you can just have one line. We've looked at the grand staff. There's also something called transposing clefs, which you probably won't need right away, but we'll just take a second to look at what those are.
1.65: A transposing clef looks like a regular treble or bass clef, except that there's going to be a little 8 above it or below it, ora 15 above it or below it. The 15 means quindicesima alta, which means two octaves higher than written. If I put a middle C down on a staff like this with the 15 added to the [top], then the sound is not going to be middle C, but it's going to be the C two octaves higher [plays high C].
1.66: That's very convenient if you're writing for instruments that are extremely high or extremely low, where you don't want to use millions of ledger lines all the time. You still want it to fit on the staff. But you also want to keep it easy to read by using a familiar clef, like the treble clef or the bass clef. If 15 uses the Italian nomenclature, quindicesima, the 8 means, octava alta, in other words, one octave higher. And the 15 is two octaves higher or lower.
1.67: Okay, so now we're going to have a look at notes and rhythms. We've looked at the basics of writing down pitches associated with either syllables or with note names. That allowed early theorists and composers to solve a very difficult problem, which is, of course, how do you take something as difficult to conceptualize as a tone or a pitch and write it down in some kind of a fixed form?
1.68: The next problem that had to be solved was: How do you notate rhythm? In some respects, that might be an even harder problem. The solution that eventually was come up with was completely transformative. But we have to back up a little bit here in order to understand the implications of it.
1.69: If you look at very, very early music—if you look at early medieval music— you won't see anything resembling the rhythmic notation that we use today. Instead, they used things called rhythmic modes, which would be specified in the score, which would tell you that the rhythms are meant to be played with this or that type of rhythm— either an equal rhythm, or an unequal rhythm, or some little rhythmic figure that would persist throughout the entire piece. That was fine if your piece was just going [sings a rhythmic figure] and it never changed, but it also had some limitations.
1.70: In very early musical notation, it's very ambiguous in some cases, exactly how the rhythms were meant to be performed. A lot of this would have been not written down because it was obvious to everybody at the time how it fit into their performance practice. Typically, you don't write things down that everybody knows. It's not necessary. But of course, if that tradition has been broken, or if we no longer understand what it was meant to sound like, then it's very difficult to reconstitute it after the fact.
1.71: Eventually, hundreds of years after the development of the five-line staff, a system called mensural notation took hold. The basic concept behind mensural rhythmic notation is this: you start with a large beat unit, and you divide it by halves. This beat unit is called the breve. Now, here again, there are different nomenclatures that are used in different countries. In North America, this is referred to as a double whole note. In the United Kingdom, you would say breve.
1.72: This is the longest note value that you can produce conventionally using this notation. Then you divide it by half. If you divide a breve into half of its duration, you obtain a semibreve, or a whole note. So one breve is equivalent to two semibreves. Then dividing further, we obtain a minim, or a half note in North American nomenclature. Just as you would expect, you can fit two half notes in the time of one whole note.
1.73: Continuing, you notice that the appearance of the notes is starting to change. The very long note values are an oval. The minim, or the half note, is an oval with a stem attached to it. And as we keep going, the note head becomes not open, but rather closed. We have a black note head starting with the crotchet, or the quarter note. Continuing the series, we come to the quaver, which is the same as the whole note, except that it has this little flag on it. This is also referred to in North America as an eighth note.
1.74: In some ways, the North American system is a little easier to remember because it's simply multiples. Double whole note, whole note, half note, quarter note, eighth note, 16th note, 32nd note, 64th note, 128th note, 256th note, and so on. You can keep dividing them into smaller and smaller and smaller rhythmic values, more or less indefinitely, although you do run into practical limitations with that.
1.75: If we keep going, we obtain the semiquaver, or 16th note. As you can see, we've added a second flag to the note. Of course, as you would expect, next we come to the demisemiquaver. These note names do get increasingly ridiculous as we get smaller and smaller. The next after that is the hemidemisemiquaver. This is also referred to as a 32nd note. And so that gives you an idea. So again, each of these rhythmic values halves each time. Now, that's for the notation of a single note.
1.76: If you want to group them together, as soon as you get to rhythmic values smaller than the quarter note or the crotchet, then when they are grouped together, you have something called a beam. The beam is a ligature. It's a visual symbol that allows you to see the grouping of the beats a little bit more easily. It makes them easier to read. In the case of two eighth notes, rather than having two flags, you would typically join them together with a beam, and likewise with 16th notes. If we go down to 32nd notes, it starts to look like that. Those are for notes, which tell us that a sound is meant to be played.
1.77: But in music, you're not necessarily playing all the time. In order to notate silences, we have a whole other repertoire of symbols, and these symbols are called rests. And rests obey the same basic logic as notes, note values, which is that you start with a large value. This is the breve rest or double whole note rest. Then we have the whole note rest. There's a bit of a subtlety here. This is something that is very easy to mix up. The whole note rest hangs downwards from the second line, and the half note rest sits on the third line. They're almost identical symbols, but one of them hangs down and the other sits on the floor, as it were. This is a half note rest.
1.78: The breve rest is a notch. It's a thin, narrow notch that lies between the second and third lines. Now, as we keep going down, we obtain the quarter note rest, which is a kind of a squiggle, and the eighth note rest. I'm going to stick to North American parlance for now. The 16th note rest. And so on and so forth.
1.79: That's quite a lot of ground to cover already if you're not familiar with music notation. It does take some time to become used to all of this. If you were taking a course in beginning music theory or solfège, or some other related discipline, then you would typically drill all of this, and the teacher would give you simple little notations with assignments either to sing or to play what you see.
1.80: I'm going to suggest we stop there for this lecture. In the next one, we're going to put all this into practice. We're going to have little examples of actual notation. We'll show you what they look like, and we're going to have to look at other concepts, such as the notation, not just of abstract pitches and rhythms, but of time signatures. We're going to take a break for now and resume with the notation of meter and rhythm. Are there any questions so far?
1.81: So, earlier, you said that the music notation from the Middle Ages was a bit limited compared to now. Do you think the notation we have now is limited compared to what we will have in the future?
1.82: Well, it already is limited because now, of course, we have digital audio workstations, we have electronic music. For at least 80 years now, composers have been working with electronic instruments— instruments that can produce not just the discrete tones that you see on a piano keyboard, but a whole continuum of pitches.
1.83: Once you get into electronic sounds, then this system of notation is absolutely inadequate. If you're getting into extremely precise fractional durations, people involved in media scoring, for example, will often think in terms of milliseconds, as opposed to quarter notes and 16th notes and eighth notes.
1.84: You could argue that MIDI, which is a language that allows musical instruments and computers to talk to each other, to have a common language, is in a sense a new form of notation. If you are involved in making soundtracks, for example, or many different kinds of electronic music, or commercial music, then you have to come to terms with what MIDI looks like, with how that's represented visually, and that's a whole other language. You could argue, again, that MIDI allows you to encode quite a lot more information than this system does, which is nearly always relative in the way that it conveys information.
1.85: For example, if I write down a quarter note on a piece of staff paper, that doesn't tell me anything about duration. The duration only comes into it once the notation is embedded in a whole expressive context and a time signature, a style, an era, a performance practice. Just a quarter note or a whole note on a page by itself tells me nothing.
1.86: But in MIDI, and no doubt MIDI will eventually be replaced by something else, but in MIDI, you can write down a sound, give it a numerical value from 1 to 127, which tells you the intensity of the note or the velocity of the attack. You can also specify the duration to a precision of milliseconds. That's a form of writing, in a sense, because you're fixing information in a way that can be reproduced. It's not necessary for everything. For concert music, you can't give a violinist a screenshot of a ProTools file. It's not going to help them. But if you're working in the electronic domain, then that might become a native tongue to you.
1.87: Is there a link between the different way countries learn how to write music and the fact that, for instance, the Germanic countries have emphasis on the orchestral, whereas the French more on the soloist?
1.88: I'm tempted to say no. The reason is that multiple different countries use the solfège system, and their musical cultures look very different from each other. If you compare the musical life of Spain and Italy, it's very different. Likewise, the German system and the Anglo-Saxon system are not identical, but they're much closer together, and the way music is practiced in Germany as opposed to the way it's practiced, say, in the USA, is not the same.
1.89: I suspect it has more to do with historical, cultural, possibly linguistic developments, and a whole complicated series of contingencies about the way musical life is organized in different countries. But you're absolutely right to assert that the Germans have tended to prioritize collective music making, in the form of orchestras, and a very robust amateur practice of ordinary people learning instruments to a high level.
1.90: Whereas the French system is more steeply hierarchical in its nature. It's more oriented towards a professional education with the goal of producing high-level musicians. Also, it's much more oriented towards the production of soloists. These are broad generalizations. You'll find examples of both countries doing the opposite of that. But as a general tendency, I think that that broadly holds true.
1.91: I guess one of the assumptions underlying the way that the system of notation works is separating the frequencies into semitones. Obviously, the piano that we have as a visual reference is also broken up into semitones. I guess I'm just wondering if the system that we use is based on semitones as a consequence of an approach to the physical aspects of playing—if it came from something like a keyboard instrument or afretted system or something like that—or if the approach to break it into semitones came first as a way to just organize frequencies.
1.92: Yeah, the two things are clearly interrelated. The musical culture, the instruments that are played and developed within that culture, and the need for a particular type of notation are all intrinsically linked. If you look at other cultures and the way that they've developed, you can compare them and see that they've often evolved along very different lines, depending on the way music fits into their society, the instruments they have, what their performance tradition looks like, and so on.
1.93: For example, if you look at the music of Bali or Java, they don't have a notated tradition for their music. The parts that are played in a gamelan orchestra are learned note by note by the beginner from a teacher directly, and they're memorized. The patterns, the rhythmic patterns, and the pitch patterns in those pieces are dizzyingly complicated, but they don't use notation.
1.94: Likewise, tuning systems change from one region of the world to another. Through a very lengthy historical process, we've settled upon something called equal temperament. We probably don't have time to get into a detailed examination of tuning systems and their implications. But basically what equal temperament means is that on this piano, the interval, the difference in pitch between each successive tone is identical.
1.95: If you take any two random notes on the keyboard and play them one after the other, the interval, the gap between those two notes will be the same. But that's not the case in every musical tradition. You can test this out very easily by listening to examples of folk music from Eastern Europe. Listen to traditional Balkan music—music of Bulgaria, of Macedonia. What you'll find is that it sounds very different to our Western ears because they don't use the same scales. Their scales may use intervals that we've never learned how to sing. They can do them perfectly in tune, but we don't have that in our ear.
1.96: Just as it's very, very difficult for a non-native speaker to pick up Mandarin and reproduce all the tones accurately—whereas for a native speaker it's effortless— it's the same with different tuning systems as well. The notation, or the lack thereof, reflects these different systems and traditions.
1.97: Finally, there are also musical cultures that rely much more heavily on percussion and rhythm than on pitch. Different cultures emphasize and prioritize different musical parameters, to the exclusion of others. You might have a culture, as is the case in large parts of sub-Saharan Africa, where the rhythmic repertoire is extraordinarily developed, but the music is either unpitched—so it's primarily preoccupied with rhythm—or if it does use pitch, it might use a very limited number of tones.
1.98: Likewise, Indian music—this is a very broad generalization because it's a huge country, obviously, and divided between a northern musical tradition and a southern one, which are very distinct from each other— but broadly speaking, there's little to no harmony in their music. There's a virtuosity of pitch and hundreds of different scales that they use, and different modes which have different tuning systems—far beyond anything we have. Their rhythms are complicated, but there's no harmony—or there might just be a drone.
1.99: Music has a very broad range of uses and different cultural traditions. Depending on how those traditions have evolved, then you're going to see very different notations or no notation at all. As it happens in the West, the development of our musical tradition has relied very heavily on the capacity to write things down, which allows you to have polyphony. It allows you to write down multiple different independent parts and to have each of them evolve differently.
1.100: It's very hard to do if you had to memorize every line. You could only really do that if you had tightly-knit communities that spent a substantial portion of their lives memorizing these things, and then transmitting them to the next generation—with, of course, the possibility that at any time that link could be broken if the knowledge were not passed down. But this way, a composer in 1450 can write down his idea, and 550 years later, we can read it. Lecture 2: The Time of Music At a glance — The time of music — rhythm and notation.
2.1: Now we're going to get deeper into music notation, specifically rhythm and how rhythm is notated. Remember earlier, we were looking at the system of mensural notation, which again was not an obvious idea; it had to be invented. So how do you capture something as nebulous as a duration in a fixed form? That's what it attempted to do.
2.2: Now, you might have thought to yourself that that's a good system because it's logical, and you can divide everything by half, and you get progressively smaller values. But it's also very limited in some ways because there are lots of rhythms that aren't articulated in terms of exact multiples of durations. In fact, generally speaking, rhythm doesn't work that way.
2.3: So it's a very abstract system that allows you to represent a series of proportional durations. It doesn't tell you exactly what the duration is, but it tells you the proportions between one value and another. But it still doesn't communicate anything about rhythmic feel, or a meter, or the relationship between the body and the gesture and the rhythm that we're hearing. This is where we have to get into time signatures, meter, and duration, which are three distinct but interrelated concepts.
2.4: Let me start by making a distinction. You can have rhythms that are subtractive or divisive, where you start with a big unit such as a breve, and keep dividing it in half— cutting it in half—until you get finer and finer bits of time, if you like.
2.5: You could also do things in the opposite direction, which is how a lot of Eastern European music works. So rather than subtracting time from a larger unit, you might start the other way around by adding little beats together to make larger beat units. If you listen again to the music of Macedonia as a good example, Turkey is another example; what you'll find is they don't subdivide a big unit, but rather they have beats of unequal duration, and those beats are not exact multiples of each other.
2.6: When we learn subtractive rhythms, we're thinking in terms of exact pulses [demonstrates beats at regular intervals: ta–ka, ta–ka, ta–ka, ta–ka], where the pulses are all equally spaced and they are exact multiples of each other. But what if you didn't have equal beats, but you had short beats and long beats, and instead of being exactly proportional to each other, they were more to do with physical gesture, and they were more predicated on the time it takes to perform an action of some kind?
2.7: We have an example of that actually in our Western tradition, which is the Viennese waltz. I've probably already mentioned this in the History of Western Music course, but I'm going to briefly recapitulate this because it's a very important point in coming to terms with rhythm.
2.8: If you listen to a Viennese waltz played by the Vienna Philharmonic Orchestra—take any random waltz by Strauss or any composer in that tradition, and listen to it carefully —you'll see that the beats, the three beats in a waltz, are not equal, it's not [demonstrates beats at regular intervals: pom–pom–pom, pom–pom, pom]. If you were to play a waltz like that, they would look at you as though you were from another planet because that's not how we do it at all. In the Viennese waltz, the beats are unequally spaced. The second beat is a bit early, and the third beat is a bit late [demonstrates beats at irregular intervals: pom–pom, pom, pom–pom, pom]; it's completely irregular.
2.9: Now, if you look at a notated waltz, it's going to be written in a time signature, which is 3/4, and on the page, it's going to look regular, but they don't play it that way. The reason they don't play it that way is because the waltz is, of course, a dance, and it has a step that involves turning, and it takes longer to do that. So the beats are unequally spaced in order to reflect the time it takes to perform these different physical motions.
2.10: Now, all of these things are difficult or impossible to take into account in a notation. These are things that are culturally encoded, let's say, that belong to our collective cultural memory. The notation cannot possibly take all of those things into account. It's of necessity incomplete and abstracted to a degree. This is the case in pretty much every culture.
2.11: Again, in the music of the Balkans or in parts of Turkey, what you'll find are beats that are like this [demonstrates irregular beats], which can then be subdivided. Now, that's hard to notate. It's hard to notate because you have a short beat and a long beat, and you make phrases by adding them together. Then you can subdivide them in different ways. It's a fundamentally different approach. Technically, if you were to try to notate it, which ethnomusicologists have tried to do using various different systems, it gets complicated very, very quickly.
2.12: This is the case also with all kinds of popular traditions. How would you notate a blues song? How would you notate swing rhythms? How would you notate ragtime? It's not straightforward. There are matters of feel, and that's simply a matter of physical embodiment—things that are not abstract, they're not intellectual, they are embodied. Notation is not very good at encoding that.
2.13: However, we still have to solve the problem of trying to write these things down so that a piece of music can be fixed in some form and transmitted through time and across different geographical locations. Before that was the case, if you wanted to have a composition, a piece of music to be played somewhere else, then you had to physically go there and teach the singers or whoever how to do it. Obviously, notation makes that a lot easier.
2.14: So what do you do about the problem of rhythm? The fact that there's something very intangible about this. It has to do with feel, it has to do with gesture, it has to do with the body. Well, the solution that eventually arose was to use something called a time signature.
2.15: The time signature is something that you'll see on the staff right at the beginning. Remember, we said that the clef goes at the left of the staff in order to tell us how to get situated. Where does middle C fall on that staff?— maybe it's here, maybe it's here, maybe it's somewhere in the middle. That allows us to orient ourselves with respect to our instrument and the range of the instrument on the staff.
2.16: But then we also need something to orient us rhythmically. Now, if I were to just sit and write a sequence of rhythmic values like this [writes musical notes on the staff], I could go on forever just writing values like that—two quarter notes, two eighth notes, two 16th notes, an eighth note, four more eighth notes, etc—then that allows me to write some rhythms, but it doesn't tell me anything about how these rhythms are meant to be interpreted, how they relate to a gesture, how they relate to a phrase.
2.17: So I can just write endless successions of rhythmic durations, proportional rhythmic durations like that, but it doesn't really help me to read it necessarily because I won't be able to imagine this succession of values in relationship to a gesture or to a phrase.
2.18: In order to do that, I need to have a system that allows me to set up a pattern, a pattern of weak and strong beats, or a pattern of accented and unaccented beats. This is fundamental to any notion of rhythm that is connected to the body. Dance has to do with periodic rhythms. Periodic rhythms set up a pattern and repeat that pattern. You can think of this as a predictable grid that continues indefinitely for as long as the piece is going. What you're actually playing or singing can line up with that grid, or it can be out of phase with it, and it can push against it, but the grid allows us to understand what the underlying pattern is.
2.19: You can think of it again as a set of weak and strong beats. For example, I might write a time signature that looks like this [writes time signature on the staff], and you'll see that right after the clef. If you look at the screen there, you'll see there's a treble clef, and immediately to the right of it, the numbers 4 and 4. That's a 4/4 time signature.
2.20: Time signatures have a numerator, which is the upper number, and a denominator, which is the lower one. The upper number tells you how many beats there are in the bar. The lower number tells you what is the basic beat unit to which you will be referring in the piece. In other words, what are we counting? Are we counting quarter notes as the basic beat unit, or eighth notes, or 16th notes, or half notes, or whole notes?
2.21: This 4/4 time signature tells me that the basic beat unit is the quarter note, and there will be four quarter notes per bar of music. And so once we get to four, we've completed a measure—or a bar of music, depending on whether you're using British or American English; you might say a measure or a bar, but they're interchangeable terms. Now, once we've got four quarter notes, we can't fit any more quarter notes into a 4/4 meter.
2.22: Now, I mentioned that there is an accent pattern in these different meters that tells the player what to emphasize and what not to emphasize and what shape to give to a phrase. It looks something like this—imagine that we are plotting a little graph in terms of intensity. The first beat is called the downbeat, and that relates to a physical pattern. If you're conducting a piece of music, you'll notice the conductor is doing patterns with their arms. Sometimes the patterns are quite wild and hard to follow. But the pattern is you go down on the first beat, over for the second beat, over to the other side for the third beat, and then up again for the fourth beat. And then down again.
2.23: The downbeat is the first beat of the bar, and it's the strongest beat. If we were to plot a graph, it might look something like this—the first beat is the strongest, the second beat is a weak beat, the third beat is stronger than the second beat, but not as strong as the first, and the fourth beat is the weakest beat. You can plot that in terms of a simple graph that just shows you.
2.24: Now, of course, nobody actually plays that way. You don't think, "Oh, yes, okay, it has to be exactly here on the graph." Nobody does that. It's simply an abstract representation to illustrate the point that although on paper we have four equal beats, in reality, they have different degrees of stress. Now, depending on the nature of the rhythmic figure that you're playing, of course, you might have something very different from that.
2.25: For example, in a lot of Baroque and Classical music, if you have a short beat immediately followed by a long held beat, it's common for the long held beat to be accented more than the first, even if the first beat is a downbeat. So, for example, in Schubert, you can have lines like this [plays the piano]. Now, that's in 4/4, but it starts like this [plays the piano]. Now, the first note I'm playing is on the downbeat. It's the first note of the bar, but it's immediately followed by a long note. It's customary and instinctive for performers to emphasize the long note, even though that breaks with the pattern.
2.26: So the notes are not emphasized equally in rhythm, but according to a meter. It's the same thing in classical poetry. Poetry also uses metric—what are called metric feet— which are a way of telling the reader effectively, or rather, allowing the poet to set up patterns of stresses, stressed and unstressed syllables. Of course, there are all kinds of different poetic feet, such as dactyls and spondees and so on.
2.27: There's a whole repertoire in poetic writing of figures that parallel but are not the same as the rhythms that we have in music. Remember that rhythm in music is, of course, an extension of rhythm in speech. These are closely interrelated ideas. You'll see parallels very clearly between poetry and rhythmic meter.
2.28: Now we have to talk about the different types of time signatures that exist because there are many of them besides just 4/4. Remember that the numerator tells us how many beats, and the denominator tells us what is the beat unit. Of course, you can modify that. As an example, rather than 4/4, I might change the top number to 3. So now I have a 3/4 time signature. In 3/4, rather than 4 beats per bar, I'm going to have 3, and that would look like this. Then, once I get to 3, I need a bar line, which is a vertical line that crosses the staff from top to bottom and tells me that another bar or another measure has to begin.
2.29: Now, the bar line is not merely a convenience to make it easier to read. The bar line also tells you at a glance what the phrase is like, what the character of the rhythm is going to be, where the downbeat is, and what beat is emphasized. If we didn't have that, then there would be no difference at all between 3/4 and 4/4. You could just keep writing beats forever, and you wouldn't be able to distinguish between one rhythm and another. The thing that allows you to distinguish between 3/4 and 4/4 is the accent pattern. So 3/4 gives us a basic waltz pattern.
2.30: So this example of 4/4 versus 3/4 allows me to make a preliminary distinction in meters between binary and ternary rhythms. And as the name indicates, a binary rhythm divides into groups of two beats: 2, 4, 8, 16, and so on. And ternary rhythms divide into groups of three beats. So 3/4, for example, or 6/4, or 3/8, or 6/8—and we'll get there in a minute. So we have binary rhythms and we have ternary rhythms.
2.31: A third category—which we probably don't have to worry too much about for now because it's much less common—but a third category combines both of those into a single meter. These are called asymmetric meters. They include rhythms such as 5/4, 7/4, and so on. Now, these are actually quite common in folk traditions. They're much less common in Classical and Baroque music, or unheard of, in fact, until you get a little bit farther into the 19th century.
2.32: We call them asymmetrical or sometimes compound meters, because even though it looks like we have five equal beats in a measure of 5/4, in fact, we have to subdivide into patterns of 2 + 3 or 3 + 2. It's called asymmetrical because those beat units are of different duration: 2 + 3 or 3 + 2, as opposed to 2 + 2 or 3 + 3 + 3 + 3; we have unequal subdivisions. The binary or ternary division is an important one to understand because you might have two measures that, in theory, can contain the same number of pulses, but in which the pattern is divided up very differently.
2.33: Let me give you an example. If I write a measure of 3/4—remember, again, that the downbeat or the first beat in the bar, which is this one, is going to be emphasized [counts 3/4 time signature].
2.34: Now, if we go backwards again to what we were talking about earlier today, where we had equal subdivisions of beats. Remember that one quarter note or one crotchet is equal to two eighth notes or two quavers. So if I wanted to, I could fill this bar with six eighth notes instead of three quarter notes, and that would look like this. So instead of [counts 3/4 time signature], I've got [counts different 3/4 time signature]. Now I've moved from three quarter notes to six eighth notes.
2.35: Now, let's have some fun. We're going to change the denominator from 4 to 8. We're going to change the numerator from 3 to 6. Now, we have a totally different time signature. This time signature tells me that we have six beats per bar, and the beat unit is the eighth note as opposed to the quarter. So then you might think, "Okay, well, that's going to be the same. It's going to look like this."
2.36: Remember, this is 3/4, and you can fit six eighth notes into a bar of 3/4, or you can also fit six eighth notes into a bar of 6/8. So what's the difference? The difference is that 6/8 is not a ternary rhythm, but rather a compound binary rhythm. What that means is it divides into two beats, each of which is subdivided into three. It's written like this. So yes, there are six eighth notes in a measure of 6/8, but they're grouped together differently with a different pattern of stresses. So that would look like this.
2.37: Now, notice that the beaming in my measure of 6/8—and I'm going to put this in red so that we can see it—the pulse is in two groups of three. The beaming in my 3/4 bar was in three groups of two. So that's the difference between [counts 3/4 time signature] and the 6/8 example [counts 6/8 time signature].
2.38: So in reality, our 6/8 bar has two main pulses, each of which is divided into three pulses. That's a binary rhythm that is a compound meter. It's taking two subdivided beats and putting them together. That's called a compound binary because we have one main beat, two main beats, and then it repeats. So a multiple of two.
2.39: As you would imagine, there's also compound ternary meters. Compound ternary meters will have a pattern of three beats subdivided into three in this case. That could look like this: 9/8. In 9/8—you can probably follow the logic at this point—three beats, each of which is divided into three [counts 9/8 time signature]. So there we've got three beats.
2.40: Now, of course, you can have even more complicated meters if you want, and many musical traditions and many composers do use them. You can put any arbitrary number of beats in a bar. You could, for example, have a meter that looks like this: 15/16. Now, we're getting on the esoteric side of things at this point. We don't have to spend a great deal of time there, but the point is that in a 15/16 measure, the composer has to tell us through his notation how those beats are meant to be divided up, because 15 is a large number. It's not obvious exactly how that's meant to be divided.
2.41: It could look like this—in this bar, we have five equal beats, each of which is subdivided into three [demonstrates 15/16 time signature]. Or—this is also possible—a bar of 15/16, divided like this, and you can see here that it's the same number of 16th notes. If you look at the screen there, there's fifteen 16th notes in both cases. In the top example, they're grouped into five pulse groups. In the lower example, they're grouped into three groups of pulses [demonstrates 15/16 time signature]. The question is, at a glance, the performer has to understand what the pulse groups are, how many of them are there per bar, and then how are the pulse groups divided up.
2.42: So that's a little tour of time signatures. To recapitulate what we've looked at. You have binary meters: 2/4, 4/4, 2/8, 2/16—anything where the top number is a multiple of two. Then you have ternary meters, where the top number is a multiple of 3—3, 6, 9, 12, and so on. On top of that, you can have compound binary or compound ternary meters in which the basic beat is further subdivided into smaller pulses.
2.43: We also looked at how it's possible to have asymmetrical meters in which the pulse groups connect together in groups of two or three. Now, in that case, again, it's necessary to make it visually clear to the performer whether we're meant to group it in 2 + 3 or 3 + 2 or 2 + 3 + 2 or 3 + 2 + 3, or whatever it might be.
2.44: So that would give you, for example, here's a measure of 5/8. Now, it could be like this, or it could look like this. In the first example, we have [counts 5/8 time signature in a 2 + 3 pattern]. Now, there's two beats per bar subdivided in the first beat in two and subdivided in three equal beats in the second part of the bar [counts the pattern again]. In the second example, we do the opposite pattern: 3 + 2 [counts 5/8 time signature in a 3 + 2 pattern]. So those are the asymmetrical meters, and in many of these folkloristic traditions, that pattern will change many times over the course of the beat, sometimes in dizzyingly complicated arrays of pulses.
2.45: The reason we put the clef and the time signature on the left-hand side of the staff is so that you can pick up the score and immediately understand both where the range of the part lies and also you can immediately understand what is the basic metrical pattern. At a glance, you can then much more rapidly decode the music. Those are two very important symbols to come to grips with.
2.46: Now, we also need to look at how these different rhythmic figures are meant to be written out. The reason for that is there's a bit of a subtlety here, which is for some reason not often taught when beginning music students are coming to grips with notation, and that is the stems and the beams.
2.47: Now, remember that as the written notations get smaller, you add first stems or a long vertical line to the bottom of the note head or the top of it, depending on where it sits on the staff. Then, as they get even smaller, you might add flags, and then the flags can be grouped together to form beams or ligatures. Let's just take a minute to show how those are meant to be drawn.
2.48: Let's say I'm in the treble clef—now, remember, the acronym is F-A-C-E. Let's say that we've got an E on the staff, and we want it to be a quarter note. The rule is that the stem of a quarter note should be one octave long. That means the bottom of the stem is going to come to a rest where the lower E would be if it were one octave lower than the top note. So the stem should be one octave long. Likewise, if I have a G here, then the stem is going to go all the way up to where a G would appear one octave higher.
2.49: That rule only changes when you get up to the upper ledger lines. If I'm writing a C here, two ledger lines above the treble staff, at that point, the stem is still one octave long. But as I add additional ledger lines, the rule is the stem always touches the middle line, no matter how high the note goes. So if you're dealing with very high or very low notes where multiple ledger lines are necessary, then the stem is always going to touch the middle line of the staff. If your note is located within the staff, then the stem is one octave long—it touches the span of one octave.
2.50: Now, as for beams and ligatures, let's imagine we have a rhythmic figure that looks like this. Again, it's going to be one octave long for the stem. Then we connect the notes together with a horizontal line called a beam. Beams are typically thicker than stems in notated music. You're going to need two beams in order to make it visually clear that these are 16th notes.
2.51: Now, in the case of more complicated rhythms, you might break this beam and make what's called a secondary beam. That would look like this. And notice that the 16th note beam does not go all the way through, but rather it's broken, so we have three subgroupings. You might or might not do that, depending on what you want to convey to the performer. If there's an ambiguity as to how the beats are meant to be subdivided, then you might want to have secondary beams.
2.52: In other instances, it's necessary to have secondary beams in order to make the notation easier to read. For example, if you have a stream of 30-second notes, which require three beams, then a group of eight of them starts to get really difficult to read. If you were to just draw the beam straight through like that, it starts to become visually confusing. You can't really see at a glance where you are within that figure, especially if the notes are changing.
2.53: In the examples I've written so far, it's just been a bunch of repeated notes. But if I were to write something like this, then in order to make it easier visually to parse this figure, I would break it up and have a secondary beam like this. Now I can see much more easily how to play this figure; otherwise, it would just be a disorienting mass of notes with no particularly easy way to read them.
2.54: Hopefully, it's clear by this point that all of these notations are a compromise between the need for precision and flexibility and the need to present a language of symbols that is clear because a lot of music in the professional world is sight-read, which is to say that the performers will show up to a rehearsal, and they may not have had a chance to look at the music ahead of time.
2.55: If you're playing on a Hollywood soundstage, for example, or if you're a gig musician in Los Angeles and you show up for a concert, you might be given the music a few minutes beforehand or the day before, and you might not have had time to read through it. Those musicians develop a skill of rapidly scanning and sight-reading. In order for them to be able to do that, the notation has to be clear; it has to be very precise the way it's written. And of course, they have to be highly trained in rapidly scanning a piece of music and instantly turning the symbols that they see on paper into a physical gesture.
2.56: So this system of notations we have is actually quite powerful because it allows us to do a lot and to write it down with precision and to communicate very effectively between the intentions of a composer and the performer who must realize the sounds that are implied or encoded within this notation. It can't do everything, though.
2.57: Now we come to a peculiarity of our notation system, which is, again, unlike many other musical traditions, the pulse groups are typically exact multiples of each other. The 16th note is exactly half as long as an eighth note, and the eighth note is exactly half as long as a quarter note, and so on. Well, what if you want to have note values that don't just divide by half? What if you want some other division? How do you write that?
2.58: In poetry, for example, you have triplets, and that's three equal pulses in the time of one beat. You need a notation for that because it might not be convenient or appropriate to change the time signature every time you want to change between beat subdivisions. Here we come to the concept, which is hilariously named, of irrational rhythms or irrational note values.
2.59: The rational note values, again, are the mensural system where it's one to two, two to four, and so on. Very, very simple. But we needed a way to account for other types of rhythms as well. One of the most common is the triplet. Let's look at what that looks like.
2.60: Here I'm drawing a 4/4 time signature, and I'm going to draw three equal beats to start with: three quarter notes. Now, let's imagine that in the fourth beat, instead of having either a quarter note or two eighth notes, I want to have three beats; I want that beat to be subdivided into three. Now, if I just write this, we have a mathematical problem, which is I now have a bar with 11 eighth notes in it—sorry, I now have a bar with nine eighth notes in it. How many eighth notes can you fit into a 4/4 measure? Eight. So that doesn't square; it doesn't quite work. What I want is not [counts uneven subdivision] because that gives me an irregular beat.
2.61: What I want is [counts even subdivision]. I want the last beat to be the same duration as all others, but to be divided into three instead of two. Now, if I didn't do that, once again, I'd have [counts uneven subdivision], and that's not what I want. I want [counts even subdivision], so the pulses are the same. In order to notate that, I need a triplet. The triplet is notated with a little numeral three underneath the last beat. That tells me that I meant to play three pulses in the time of one quarter note.
2.62: The phenomenon of irregular or irrational beat subdivisions that have to fit into a broader metric pattern, but only temporarily, is known as a tuplet. The tuplet allows me to write values that don't fit squarely into my time signature, and they're incredibly useful. Now, that allows me, among other things, to alternate between groups of two and groups of three if I want to do that. Then you can get into rhythms that are a little bit more interesting.
2.63: For example, here's a bar of 4/4. The first beat is a quarter note, the second beat is two eighths notes, the third beat is three eighths notes, expressed as a triplet, and the fourth beat is two eighths notes. That gives me [demonstrates rhythmic pattern]. Now I'm alternating groups of one beat, two beats, and three beats. Then you can start to have a much broader range of possible rhythmic expression. We're no longer confined to exact multiples, but you can have so-called irrational values that break with the underlying beat subdivision.
2.64: And of course, you can go quite far with that, as some composers have done. Large aspects of the romantic piano style, for example, the style of Liszt, of Chopin, of Charles-Valentin Alkan, A-L-K-A-N, who's a 19th-century French composer, of extraordinarily virtuoso piano music, and many other figures besides. A lot of that music is predicated on these very complex and very subtly nuanced rhythms.
2.65: In Nocturnes by Chopin, if you open the scores up, you'll see what looked like phenomenally complicated rhythmic subdivisions or polyrhythms, where on the upper staff, the pianist will have to play 17 or 23 or 25 16th notes in the time of 12 or 16. Complicated ratios like that. You look at the page and get completely, like, "How do I do that? How do you possibly make a subdivision like that?" Well, the answer is it gets turned into a gesture. The pianist isn't thinking in terms of, "I have to subdivide 17 into the time of 12." You work on it, of course. You work with the two hands separately, then you put them together, and then you turn it into a gesture. It encourages the performer to create something very fluid, something very subtle.
2.66: So tuplets allow us then to have a very broad range of extraordinarily subtle rhythmic divisions. In a bar of 3/4, I could write a figure that looks like this, and now I've got a quintuplet: I've got five equal beats in the time of four 16th notes. Why would you ever need to do that?
2.67: Well, in speech, we do it all the time without ever thinking about it. We do triplets, we do quintuplets. Take a word like university—five syllables, university. It allows you to have these pulse groups that don't divide neatly up into two or four and still fit them into the phrase. A lot of what this is attempting to do is to take things that we instinctively do in speech and allow us to notate them in a musical context.
2.68: We still haven't gotten to the bottom of what's possible in rhythmic notation because let's say that you're in 4/4, you're not going to just write four equal beats per bar in every single bar because, well, that would be extraordinarily monotonous very quickly. And real music almost never does that unless you're aiming for a special effect of some kind.
2.69: That was the case in the Bach prelude that we looked at in the composition course, where he sets up a little rhythmic figure and just repeats it over and over and over again throughout the piece. But most of the time, what you're likely to do is have phrases that have a certain flow to them. You might not have every pulse be articulated, and you might not have an absolutely regular array of pulses within the bar.
2.70: For example, I've just written out two bars of music, and you'll notice that this contains not just pulses, but also rests. The notation adds up to 4 beats per bar, but I'm using a mix of different rhythmic values and rests, and that gives me, ta, I'm not articulating all the pulses. I have some rests in there, and I have rhythmic values of different duration.
2.71: Now, sometimes you may need to extend the rhythmic value beyond the bar line. You're holding a note, and you want it to continue for longer than what's possible within a bar. Then you need something called a tie. I have a first bar that ends with a half note, and the half note has a tie that connects it to the first beat of the following bar. What that little symbol tells me is that when I arrive at the second bar, I'm not meant to rearticulate that note or play that note again. Instead, I'm holding it over from the previous bar. That's going to sound like this [demonstrates sustained note carried across the bar line]. I'm not actually articulating a note on the downbeat of bar two, but I'm holding it over from the end of the previous bar.
2.72: Now we're starting to approach a pretty complete idea of some of the things that you can do in rhythmic notation. This is by no means an exhaustive list—it would take multiple eight-hour courses to even begin to scratch the surface of all the subtleties of rhythm and all the things you can do within it, and all the different styles and dances and patterns and so on. But this is an initial foray into the possibilities of rhythm.
2.73: Remember, we have note values that tell us not an absolute duration, but a relative duration. The absolute duration is determined, among other things, by the tempo, by the context, by the style, and so on. Then we have time signatures. Time signatures allow us to break up the flow of beats into a regular pattern that we can parse much more easily, a pattern of stresses. We had binary and ternary time signatures, and compound binary and compound ternary time signatures.
2.74: Then we looked at the ways that you can combine different rhythmic values within a single bar and how you can allow for irrational values that are not exact multiples of the beats in the bar. Finally, we looked at ties, which allow you to prolong a rhythmic value beyond a bar line or beyond a written duration.
2.75: We're going to end with one more thing, which is dotted rhythms. We don't need to spend a great deal of time on this, but it's important to understand the concept. If I have any rhythmic value—it can be a quarter note, half note, even a whole note—I can extend the value of that duration by half by adding a dot to the right of the note, and that looks like this. And these are called dotted rhythms.
2.76: So a dotted quarter note is equal to three eighth notes. Why three? Because a "normal" quarter note is equivalent to two eighth notes. If I extend it again by half, then that gives me three eighths notes. Likewise, a dotted half note is equivalent to three, not two, but three quarter notes, and a dotted whole note is equivalent to three half notes.
2.77: Now, where that starts to get useful is in places like this—remember, we looked at meters like 6/8 or 9/8? Let's return to that for a second. If I have a bar of 6/8, and I don't necessarily want all six pulses to be articulated, maybe I just want two pulses to be articulated in a bar of 6/8. The dot tells me that I've got two beats, each of which is three eighths notes long [counts two beats, each subdivided into three]. So the dotted quarter, again, is equal to three eighths.
2.78: And finally, the dot allows you to have unequal rhythms. In French, there's a term which is valeurs égales or valeurs inégales. So a beat can be divided into equal values. In the language of popular music, that would be straight eighths: each beat is divided into two equal beats that are equidistant to each other [demonstrates equal rhythm].
2.79: In unequal values, one of them is longer than the other. You have a long beat, followed by a short pulse [demonstrates unequal rhythm]. So that is an unequal pattern, and it's notated with a dot. Now, it all adds up mathematically because the dotted eighth note in the example I've just written is equivalent to three 16ths. Then, at the end of the beat, we have a fourth 16th. So each of those beats is made up of four 16th notes. The first one is three times longer than the last one.
2.80: Now, obviously, I have to emphasize this once again—it would be a mistake to think that performers are constantly going, "One, two, three, four, one, two, three, four—" No. They don't count every single pulse within the 16th notes. It's a matter of feel, and it becomes instinctive after a while. But that rhythm there would be played [demonstrates long–short" skipping" rhythm]. You can think of that as a skipping rhythm. If you're skipping, you're on one leg for longer than the other.
2.81: All of these rhythms—and there's an immense repertoire of them—but they're directly derived from physical things: the momentum of walking, the momentum of running, skipping, jumping, riding a horse, turning around in circles. These basic patterns of physical movement that are fundamental to how we interact with the world are manifested in these different time signatures and rhythmic patterns that underlie this musical tradition. We'll stop there for now for rhythm. I've only begun to scratch the surface. We're going to regroup in a few minutes. Thank you very much.
2.82: You expressed that music notations are an attempt at crystallizing the ephemeral sounds into permanent writings. Is there any link between music notations and sign language, for instance?
2.83: Well, in the case of sign language, or Braille, or written text or music, what you have is a language of symbols, or in the case of sign language, of gestures.
