So a symbol can take many different forms—it can be written down, it can be something tactile, or it can be a gesture, provided that the gesture or the symbol or whatever it is, has an agreed-upon meaning that is shared between the person relaying the message and the person receiving the message. That's all. Whether you do that through smoke signals or through whole notes and half notes or through subtle bodily gestures, in a sense, is not the main question. There just has to be a commonality of reference between both parties. That's all. Lecture 3: Pitch and Intervals At a glance — Pitch and intervals.
3.1: We've been taking a tour through the basic rudiments of music, through the basis of the language that allows performers and composers and indeed, audience members to communicate with each other and to understand each other and to have a common written basis. We've looked at the essentials of the staff notation, where notes are located on the staff and clefs. We've looked at rhythm, we've looked at time signatures.
3.2: What we're going to do now is get a little bit deeper into pitch and the possibilities of notating pitch and intervals. So far, what we've done is we've taken a five-line staff and we've learned where the notes go, we've learned the names of the notes, and we've learned some mnemonics, some little acronyms to help remember where those notes are located.
3.3: We have to go a little bit farther now. As anyone who's ever glanced at a piano keyboard knows, we have both black keys and white keys. When I play a simple C major scale on the keyboard, I'm not playing every single tone on the keyboard. If I were, it would sound like this. What I just played there was a chromatic scale. The first scale that I played was called a diatonic scale.
3.4: Diatonic, in this context, refers to a seven-note scale. It doesn't contain every semitone —every black key and every white key. It contains a pattern of whole tones and semitones in a fixed order. The chromatic scale, however, consists of an equal sequence of semitones. Every single tone is present. Every tempered tone, that is to say, in other words, the tones that it is possible to play on a piano keyboard.
3.5: Of course, if you look at other musical traditions and other instruments, it may not be laid out as a sequence of discrete steps, but more as a continuum. You can do this very easily with your voice. Obviously, your voice doesn't have a keyboard. You can produce any frequency, any pitch within the range that you're able to sing. You can sing very, very small fractional intervals that are smaller than a semitone, which is the smallest interval you can play on a piano. But for now, we're just going to concern ourselves with whole tones, or whole steps, and semitones.
3.6: If I want to play anything other than the white keys on a keyboard, then I need to have some visual language of symbols that allows me to explain what I'm doing—that takes the form of accidentals. What accidentals are is they take one of the seven diatonic tones of a major or a minor scale—and we'll explain more about scales later on—but for now, all you need to know is if we take the seven basic tones that we described earlier: do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, si, accidentals allow us to alter that pitch either raising it or lowering it or canceling out a previous accidental. I'm going to show you what that looks like.
3.7: We need a whole new set of symbols for this. Remember that if I want to write middle C on a treble clef here, a treble staff, then I need a ledger line, and there's my middle C. If I want to play D, then I just go to the next space or line up, and so goes the sequence. However, I can also place a sign before the note that tells me if it's a natural, a sharp, or a flat. And these symbols look like this—natural [♮], sharp [ ♯], and flat [ ♭].
3.8: The natural sign and the flat sign are both derived from the letter B. In fact, if you know the French terminology—I know we keep coming back to this—the French term for flat is bémol or a "soft B." The French term for natural is bécarre, which means a "square B" or a "hard B." That also refers to—we don't want to get too deep into the history of this, but the seventh tone in the sequence do re mi fa sol, la, si, or B, has a somewhat ambiguous status.
3.9: The quality of that interval could be different depending on the scale you're using, depending on the era in which you are writing, your geographical region, and so on. Sometimes it sounded like this—this is a very crude demonstration of the idea, but just to illustrate it [plays a scale with hard B], and sometimes you would hear this [plays a scale with soft B].
3.10: In order to differentiate between the different ways that you could have this seventh note, this B, we developed these symbols over time, the soft B and the hard B, if you like. Then those symbols became abstracted into what we have today. The flat symbol looks a little bit like a B, and the natural symbol looks a little bit like a square B, like this.
3.11: Now, the sharp symbol indicates that whatever note it lies before is raised by a semitone. The flat means that whatever note it appears before is played one semitone lower. The natural sign means you play it as a white note. You cancel out any preceding alteration. The reason you would need to cancel is that the general rule broadly applied is that accidentals hold for an entire bar.
3.12: So if I write a D in my piece—imagine we're in 4/4 here; I've got C, D, E, D ♯, D ♯, E, D ♮, C —I have to write the natural symbol there in order to cancel out the sharp that we see on the first beat of the second bar. If I didn't have that natural sign, then the performer would assume that the D on the third beat would still be a D ♯. The natural sign allows you to clear up ambiguities, and it allows you also to cancel an accidental when necessary.
3.13: To recapitulate: if I want to write a G, let's say on the treble staff, then if it looks like this, you assume in the absence of any accidentals that it's a G ♮. If I add a sharp before it, that gives me a G♯. If I put a flat, now I've got a G ♭.
3.14: Here's my G♮. If I lower it by a semitone, I obtain a G ♭. If I raise it by a semitone, I get G♯. All of these notes are called G, but the accidentals allow me to alter it—to raise it or to lower it. Then that leads to an inevitable question, which is: If you can write a G ♭ and the note below G is F, then you can also write an F ♯, and they're the same.
3.15: If I have an F here, I can also write an F ♭ and an F ♯. Now, in terms of just pure frequency, all other things being equal, without any context around the notes, this F ♯ sounds identical to this G♭. In both cases—start on an F, add a sharp, it becomes F ♯. Now, if I take the G and lower it, I get that note. It's the same in either case. Why would you spell it F♯ or G♭?
3.16: Well, we'll have to get into that a little bit later because we're getting into questions of harmonic functionality, but as a brief explanation and a simplified one, it partly depends on your direction of travel. If you're going down, then you use flats. If you're going up, then you want to use sharps. We'll use that as a heuristic for now.
3.17: For example, if I wanted to write an ascending line like this, this gives me a little chromatic sequence. Remember, we talked about the difference between chromatic and diatonic scales. Chromatic scales include all the semitones—all the black keys, all the white keys on the keyboard. If I start on an E and go up chromatically, then I can write that as E, F, F♯, G.
3.18: If I do this in the opposite direction, I start on the G, then I'm likelier to spell it G, G ♭, F, E. It's the same thing played backwards, but because the direction of travel is different, I'm going to use a flat to lower the G as opposed to an F ♯ to raise the F. That's a concise introduction to intervals—sorry, to accidentals. But that doesn't bring us to intervals just yet, which is the next thing we need to discuss.
3.19: I mentioned that these scales—the major and minor scales—are the two most widely used ones in the Western tradition, and that has occurred over a very lengthy process of historical refinement. These scales are based on a pattern of seven notes, as I mentioned, in a fixed order. So if we take a C major scale, we have the following sequence [plays C major scale].
3.20: Now, again, if you look at the pattern of black and white notes on the keys, you'll see that in order to go from C to D, I have to skip over the C ♯. I'm just going to play C to D and then D to E. But I'm not going to play [plays semitone sequence C, C ♯, D, D ♯, E]; I'm going to skip those.
3.21: When you have two notes played one after the other, if it's a sequence like that, then you have what's called a melodic interval, and that is the distance, or the difference, between the first note you played and the second one. If I take two tones and play them simultaneously, you obtain a harmonic interval. So you have to distinguish between melodic intervals, one after the other, and harmonic intervals, which are two tones played simultaneously.
3.22: Now, in the order of tones I play, the interval is determined by the distance, if you like, between the first note and the second. In the case of C to D, that is called a whole step because we're going from one natural note to the adjacent one and skipping the semitone in between. If I went from C to C♯ or C to D♭, that interval would be called a semitone. If I look at the resulting pattern, that gives me tone–tone–semitone–tone– tone–tone–semitone.
3.23: There's a pattern of intervals that I can remember. Let's write out that scale. The first interval from C to D is a whole tone—we're going to abbreviate that as T. Then, from D to E is another whole tone. Now, from E to F, there's no black key in between, so that's the smallest interval you can play—that gives us a semitone. E to F gives us a semitone —we'll abbreviate that as S. Then F to G is a whole tone. G to A is a whole tone. A to B is a whole tone. Then, if we continue to C, then we get another semitone. But the easiest way to remember this sequence is tone–tone–semitone–tone–tone–tone– semitone.
3.24: Now, if I want to start on any other tone on the keyboard and play a scale, all I have to do is remember that sequence, and I can reproduce exactly the same scale. That's called a transposition. So it's the same sequence of intervals, but starting on a different note. Here's my C major scale, and here's a D major scale. Exactly the same sequence of intervals, but starting on a different note. That gives us a little introduction to the concept of transposition.
3.25: But of course, we haven't made tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands of pieces using only a single scale. One of the things you learn very early on when you're learning an instrument and learning about music theory is that we use both the major scale and something called the minor scale.
3.26: The minor scale, as its name implies, has a different sequence of tones and semitones than the major scale. The easiest way to form a minor scale is to begin on what's called the relative minor of the major scale that you've just played. Remember, if we're in C major [plays C major scale], I can form the relative minor by starting one-third lower than the C that I began with. So, I'm going to start on A rather than starting on C, and that gives me this [plays A minor scale].
3.27: Like the C major scale, the A minor scale only uses the white keys on the keyboard. But the sequence of tones and semitones is different. We call this the relative minor because C major and A minor share the same key signature—that's a concept that I'll be explaining a little bit later. If there's anything you're not following up to now, don't worry. We're going to cover a lot of this stuff again.
3.28: C major has no sharps or flats. We're only playing white keys on the keyboard. Therefore, the key signature is zero sharps and zero flats—pretty straightforward. If I move down to A minor, A minor also has no sharps and no flats, but starting on a different tone and with a different sequence. So, A minor looks like this. Here, the sequence is tone–semitone–tone–tone–semitone–tone–tone.
3.29: Why do we call them major and minor scales? Why is this C major [plays C major scale], and why is this A minor [plays A minor scale]? The major and minor refer to the size or the quality of the third interval in this scale. Before I explain different qualities of intervals, we have to look at what the intervals are. Let's look at that for a minute. Let's start with C. Just a plain ordinary C. We're not going to worry about sharps or flats for now.
3.30: Now, if I move to the next tone up directly—C to D—remember, that gives you a whole tone. This is also called an interval of a major second. If I start on the C and move up to an E directly without any notes in between, then that gives me the interval of a major third. If I start on C and go up to F, that gives me an interval called a perfect fourth—or P4, the abbreviation. Continuing the series from C to G gives me a perfect fifth. From C to A gives me a major sixth. From C to B gives me a major seventh.
3.31: Now, so far, you'll have noticed that some of the intervals are called major, some of them are called minor, and some of them are called perfect. This connects back to what I was speaking about in my composition program, or forward to it if you're seeing them in the other order, which is that for historical and acoustic reasons, some intervals are referred to as perfect—the unison, the fourth, the fifth, and the octave are considered to be perfect consonances. They are simple consonances. They are very simple ratios of each other. Another way to think about this is that they're simple, or they're considered perfect because they're very easy to relate to the lower note of the interval. So think of these as simple or perfect consonances.
3.32: Then we have major intervals, minor intervals. Major second, major third, major sixth, major seventh. Now, you can also play minor seconds. For example, C to D ♭. If I take my C to D interval there and add a flat sign on the D, this gives me a minor second. Likewise, if I take it C to E and put a flat symbol there, that gives me a minor third. Remember, this is the major third [plays C–E], and this is the minor third [plays C–E ♭].
3.33: The A minor scale—if I take the first and the third note in that scale and play them together, I obtain a minor third. Major and minor refer to the quality of interval between the first note of the scale and the third, among other things, but that's the most immediate distinction. So, so far now, we've looked at how intervals can be major, minor, or perfect. There are other possibilities, too, but we'll get to those a little bit later.
3.34: The other thing we need to know is that in any scale—any diatonic scale, that is—the notes are assigned names, of course, and if you create intervals between one note and any other note in the scale, then you can describe it in terms of a perfect fourth, a perfect fifth, and so on. But you can also assign the notes of a scale Roman numerals, or degrees: I, II, III, IV, V, VI, VII, and so on, such that, if we're in C major, and I play an A, I can refer to the A as being the sixth degree of the C major scale. I can refer to the E as being the third degree. You can think of this as almost like steps on a ladder. You can imagine it as being an almost spatial movement between one step and another.
3.35: If I'm playing my scale and I play only adjacent tones in the scale, then that is called stepwise motion. I'm moving by step, which is to say I'm only moving between adjacent tones. Now, the instant I have an interval that's larger than two adjacent notes, I'm moving by leap because I'm skipping over some of the notes in between. And generally speaking, melodies, in order to be interesting, will contain a mixture of both steps, stepwise motion, and leaps.
3.36: Music is obviously a very complex phenomenon, and harmony in particular. Part of the reason that harmony can be difficult to get a handle on, intervals can be difficult to get a handle on, is that they change depending on the context. Remember how I said that you can spell that tone there as F♯ or as G♭, depending on the direction of travel. C, D, E, F, F♯, or a C, B, A, G, G♭. Both are possible. That's called an enharmonic spelling. Enharmonic means that the sounding pitch is the same, but it's spelled in two different ways: F♯ or G♭.
3.37: Now, what today counts as an enharmonic spelling would have actually sounded quite different during the Baroque. The reason is that this equal temperament that I described earlier, where all the semitones on a piano are tuned to the same ratio; they're all the same interval. But on older instruments, before equal temperament became the norm, various different systems existed simultaneously, which allowed for either perfectly tuned thirds or perfectly tuned fifths, which necessitates some amount of compromise because you can't have both in the same scale for acoustic reasons.
3.38: What we've opted for is a totally artificial system, which is a compromise, where if we base our tuning system on acoustics, on the actual physical properties of vibrating strings or air columns in a pipe, then you need a very specific ratio to produce a fifth that's exactly perfect, that's exactly in tune. The octave has to be exactly double the frequency of the lower note, for example, and so on and so forth. The third, in order to be precisely in tune, needs to be in a specific frequency ratio between the bottom note and the upper note.
3.39: However, if you try to make a scale out of only acoustically perfect intervals, what will happen is your octave won't be in tune with itself. Your scale will be completely lopsided, and you won't be able to reproduce it in higher octaves. If I start here, I can just keep going the entire length of the keyboard, and it all works. But if you try to do that with exactly perfect intervals, the notes would be subtly rising and getting out of tune with itself. It wouldn't work.
3.40: In older music, they tried to get around this problem by making some intervals a little smaller than they needed to be in order to try to fit them within perfectly in tune octaves. The compromise that we've landed upon is making all the intervals very slightly out of tune. That's what we have here. The fifths on this keyboard are not exactly acoustically perfect, nor are the thirds, nor are the fourths. They're slightly flat, but the octaves are precisely in tune.
3.41: What that means is on a keyboard like this, you can play in any key. I can play in C major, I can play in D major, I can play in A flat, I can play in G ♭ major, I can play that scale, that C major scale or the A minor scale, starting on any key on the instrument and working my way up and down, and all of it will be in principle in tune.
3.42: If you try to do that on an early instrument, like a 17th-century harpsichord, the way it would have been tuned at the time, you would find that as you venture from keys like C major or A major into keys with lots of sharps or flats, like A ♭ or D ♭, that the farther you get from C major, the more out of tune it gets. You can't actually play in every key on those instruments. You can try it, but it's going to be extraordinarily out of tune once you get too far from C major. It's a compromise.
3.43: On those keyboards, if you're playing in a key that has a relatively small number of sharps or flats, then the intervals—the octaves and the fifths that are meant to be perfect—will be exactly in tune, but there are going to be some funky minor seconds and minor thirds that are going to sound really strange to your ears. So here we have something, again, which is homogenous. It's not perfect. It's very slightly out of tune, but that gives us the flexibility of playing in a broad range of different keys.
3.44: Let's continue with intervals. Now, intervals for beginning musicians can be tricky to get a handle on because at a certain point in your training, you have to be able to not only remember what each interval sounds like, but you have to be able to reproduce it with your voice. If you wake me up at 3:00 in the morning, I have to be able to sing an augmented fourth. I have to be able to do that. I have to remember the interval, I have to be able to externalize it, and I have to, of course, also be able to write it down. That takes a certain amount of your training to be able to do that effortlessly.
3.45: We've looked at major intervals and minor. We've looked at perfect fourths, fifths, octaves, and unisons. Now, there are a couple of other concepts we need to know. Let's make this simple. I'm going to start with the C above middle C on my treble staff here, and I'm going to put a D next to it. If I keep it like this, remember, I obtain a major second. Now, if I add a flat, remember, this gives me a minor second. This is the major second [plays C–D]. This is the minor second [plays C–D♭].
3.46: Now, if I put a sharp next to the C, I also obtain a minor second. However, this is where it gets a little bit weird. If I start with C and go to a D ♯, I get this [plays C–D ♯]. Then you might say, "Well, that sounds like a minor third. Isn't that the same thing?" It's not the same thing. The reason it's not the same—I mean, it's the same acoustically, but it's not the same thing functionally because I've spelled these notes C and D. The fact that the D is sharp gives me an interval larger than a second, but spelled C to D, and C to D is always a second. Even if it's D♯, D♭, C♯, C♭, it's always a second because the size of the interval, if you like, is determined by the distance between two adjacent tones in my scale—C and D in this case.
3.47: Now, if I alter them, I alter the quality of the interval, but I don't alter the interval, if that makes sense. I'll try to explain. If I move from C to D ♯, I've now got an interval that's larger than a major second. The next step up from a major second is an augmented second. Augmented, meaning even larger than a major second; it's the next step up.
3.48: Now we're getting into some seriously weird theoretical territory because it's possible to go even farther. This symbol that I've just placed next to the D in my next example is a double sharp [𝄪]. And a double sharp, as you may have guessed, is one step higher than sharp. And that gives me this [playsC –D𝄪]. So now you're getting seriously irritated. You're like, "Well, that's obviously not a second. That's a third. That is now a major third." Well, yes, except I've spelled it C to D𝄪, and C to D𝄪 is a double augmented second.
3.49: This is where we get to one of the more confusing or counterintuitive aspects of music theory, which is that there's a gap between the acoustic reality of what you're hearing and the actual function of the interval, depending on how it's written and depending on the harmonic context. If I spell that C to D𝄪— which you might think nobody would ever do that, but it actually does occur—then I get a double augmented second.
3.50: If I go the other direction, C to D♭, then we have a minor second. If I go C to D𝄫, which looks like this [𝄫], then I obtain a diminished second. The diminished second sounds like this [plays C–D𝄫]—yeah, it sounds like I'm playing the same note twice, and acoustically, that is what I'm doing. But again, I've spelled it as C to D𝄫, and that gives me this—still a second because of the way I've spelled it.
3.51: You get these strange occurrences—this is another one: B ♯ to C, where the two notes sound identical, but I spelled the first one as B♯, so I'm raising the B by a semitone, and that gives us the same tone as C. The point is to understand that there's a distinction, again, between the function and the acoustic reality of what you're hearing. The reason this is important is that, depending on the key you're in, the same frequencies will be spelled, will be written, in different ways. Depending on the nature of the harmonic motion, you might spell an interval in many different ways.
3.52: I want to return now to the A minor scale that we were looking at previously. Remember that the quality of the third, which in this case is minor, in an A minor scale, goes some ways to determining whether it's a major or a minor scale. It's not the only difference, but that's the most immediately noticeable one. Now, in reality, if you're writing a piece in A minor, you're not only going to use the white keys all the time. Part of the reason for that is that there is a very special phenomenon in tonal music—in other words, music that's written in a key in the Western system, which is called the leading tone. This is a very, very important concept. Here we're getting into questions of harmonic and melodic functionality.
3.53: Let me write out that A minor scale again. The bottom note here—the first note of the scale, the first scale degree, if you like—is A. Then, when I get back to the top again at the end, I get back to another A. Now, the interval between the tone immediately below it and the first note of the scale, in this case, is a major second. That ends up being a bit of a problem. The reason is this phenomenon called the leading tone. The leading tone is the note that lies directly below the first note of the scale.
3.54: Now, let's back up and go back to C major for a second. There's the leading tone. The leading tone has this peculiar property: it really wants to go up. It wants to lead you back to the beginning of the scale. That's why it's called the leading tone. And in major scales, the leading tone is a semitone below the first note or the first scale degree. That first note has a name, which is the tonic—the tonic being the strongest or the first note in the scale. The leading tone is directly below the tonic and wants to lead back up to it.
3.55: The fact that you have this leading tone and this tonic gives you this strong sense of orientation and attraction and stability when you do and back up on the tonic again. The minor scale gives you a leading tone that is a whole step lower than the tonic—G to A. That gives you a much lesser degree of upward push, let's say, this desire to resolve, this desire to lead us back to the tonic.
3.56: This gives rise to something called the A melodic minor [plays A melodic minor scale ascending], which raises the sixth to F♯ and the seventh to G ♯ in order to preserve that sense [plays A–F♯–G♯–A] of something sharply leading you back to the tonic again. When you go back down in the opposite direction, you're going away from the tonic, but you don't have that motion towards the tonic again, so you lose the F ♯ and the G ♯ [plays A melodic minor scale descending]. The A minor scale has the peculiar property that you don't necessarily have the same notes going down as going up.
3.57: One of the things you want to do if you're coming to terms with music and you're starting to learn an instrument, you're starting to get familiar with all of these concepts, is you learn to, first of all, identify the intervals by ear so that if I wake you up at 3:30 in the morning and go like this [plays C–G], you're like, "Oh, perfect fifth," or [plays G ♯– C♯] "perfect fourth," or [plays C–C♯] "that's a minor second," or [plays B ♭–D] "major third." You can instantly recognize both the size of the interval and its quality, and you can reproduce it with your voice. That is fundamental to musicianship—to have that capacity. That's something that you do by training your ear. At the end of this course, tomorrow, we're going to look at some exercises to work on that.
3.58: The other thing you learn is you start thinking in terms of sequences of intervals, which makes it easier to transpose. You start learning about moving around between different keys, between C major and D major and F [major]. You can play the same scales and the same chord patterns, but starting on a different note.
3.59: All of this, of course, takes a great deal of practice. What you want to do is start with very, very simple little exercises, just playing scales in different keys, memorizing the patterns. Eventually, what happens is they become gestural; you're not thinking of them intellectually as you're playing them. You're not thinking, "Okay, C goes to D, D goes to—" No, you remember it as a sequence, a physical sequence. It becomes encoded in your muscle memory and you don't think about it.
3.60: But it takes a while to develop that fluency, just as it takes a while to learn a foreign language so that you're not constantly thinking about grammatical constructions and syntax and vocabulary. But like anything, when you're acquiring a new skill, it's usually best to not torture yourself by trying to go too fast or trying to cram all of this information in your head in a short period of time.
3.61: All the more so, depending on your aptitude and your interest in music, you might find this extraordinarily tedious to learn. You might find it effortless and natural, but in any case, you want to make sure that when learning skills like this, that you go at a pace that allows you to progress, but without it being torture. If it's torture, you won't keep doing it. You're going to give up and do something else because why torture yourself? But if you can make it where it's stimulating and enjoyable and it's stretching you a little bit, but not to the absolute limit of your capability all the time, then you're much likely to retain it, and eventually it becomes second nature.
3.62: So, in this lecture, we've looked at intervals, we've looked at qualities of intervals, and we've looked at some basics of how you can put together major and minor scales. As with all of the things that we're looking at, of course, we could go into much more detail, much more depth, but I think that's a reasonable introduction to the topic.
3.63: We've looked at how in minor, you can have the A natural minor scale, which is simply formed from the same tones as the C major scale. You can alter it to obtain a harmonic minor scale or a melodic minor scale, depending on the context and depending on, of course, what type of piece you're writing. Lecture 4: Keys and Harmony At a glance — Keys and harmony.
4.1: We began our deep dive into the wonderful and strange world of intervals earlier, and we also looked at how the way the interval sounds acoustically, and what its function is and how it's written can be different things depending on the musical context. Now, what I want to do is to get into one of the most fundamental concepts of Western music, which is the concept of a key or a key signature.
4.2: Now, we've looked at the A minor and C major scales. We've looked at how they're related to each other—A minor being the relative minor to C major, and inversely, C major being the relative major of A minor—relative in the sense that they share the same key signature, which is to say the same number of sharps or flats that are needed in order to play a scale in that key.
4.3: Now, if we were content to just write pieces that consisted of seven notes played over and over and over again, running up and down the keys and so on, which you could do indefinitely if you wanted to, but it might be quite boring and homogenous, and it might not afford you many possibilities to write a longer piece. In order to have a broader range of motion in a piece of music and a broader range of contrasts and harmonic effects, we need to be able to move around a little bit harmonically.
4.4: To a degree, you can do that, as we looked at earlier today, with accidentals— sharps and flats—which allow you to change the quality of an interval. But it's also necessary to have a key. You can think of a key as being an organization of pitches around a central tone. If you see that there's a Beethoven symphony in C major or in B ♭ major or in A major, then you might wonder what exactly that terminology means, and why would you bother putting that in the title?
4.5: Well, the A major or the B♭ or whatever it is tells you what the key of the piece is. In other words, what is the central tone against which all the others are heard? This gives us a sense of both harmonic stability and a sense of harmonic motion, because you can move harmonically in a piece of music away from home base, if you like, or the tonic, the first scale degree. You can move away from it; you can have a centrifugal movement away from it.
4.6: Or you can move back towards it—a centripetal force that draws you back. That allows you, again, to create very long-range harmonic and dramatic effects in a piece of music. If your piece were static—in other words, all you could do were to play the tones of C major all the time—well, you'd be limited. You could do it, though [plays improvised passage on the piano]. I could do that for four hours. It might be nice. There are some genres of music where that harmonic stasis goes on for a very long time, but it's not suited for all styles.
4.7: You might want to actually move somewhere else. You might want to have a range of harmonic motion [plays improvised passage on the piano]. Now, what I just improvised there takes me away from C major into different keys, sometimes very fleetingly, sometimes for a longer duration. Maybe I end up in a different key and I stay there for a while, and then I have to work my way back to where I started again. But in any case, in order to allow for that movement, I need to have the possibility of moving between different keys.
4.8: First, we have to lay out what these keys are and how they relate to each other. To illustrate this concept, I have to explain about something called the circle of fifths. Now, you might have heard about this already. It's a foundational concept in music theory. Well, it's foundational, but it wasn't actually formalized straight away. But let's have a look at how this works.
4.9: If I start on C, and then I continue to move upwards in a sequence of fifths, where each successive tone is a fifth higher than the previous one, if I keep doing that, eventually, I'll get back to where I started again, and it completes a circle. I'm going to have a C, followed by a G—a fifth above the C. Then, if I keep going, I get to D, and then I get to A, I get to E—now, I'm going to have to change octaves because obviously this is getting a little bit high—then I get to B, F♯, C♯, G♯, D♯, and then A ♯, F—this is where the sequence starts to get a bit funny—and then end up back on C again.
4.10: Now, you'll notice something in this little sequence here is that if I keep going in fifths [plays sequence of fifths], eventually, I get back to where I started again, in a circle. Having done that,, I've played every single semitone. If you take all of these 12 notes and group themm together, it gives you a complete chromatic scale.. Not in that order, obviously, but that gives you the collection of all 12 semitones that you can play on the keyboard. That is called a circle of fifths.
4.11: Now, if I want to build keys, or scales on each one of these tones, preserving the same order: tone–tone–semitone–tone–tone–tone–semitone, that characterizes the major scale as we saw earlier, then I have to keep adding sharps or flats to play those interval patterns. Remember, C major [plays C major scale], no sharps, no flats, just the white notes on the keyboard.
4.12: If I go up a fifth and start on G [plays G major scale], I can't play an F; I have to play an F♯. That means I have to add an F♯ to what's called the key signature. The key signature looks like this: on every staff of every page of this piece, as long as I'm still in G major, I'm going to put an F♯ on the top of the staff there, and it's going to appear on every line. What that means is, unless I include an accidental or cancel out the sharp somehow or modulate to another key, every F is going to be an F ♯. That just makes it a lot easier because you don't have to constantly write out F ♯ every time you want to play that note.
4.13: Now, if we continue the sequence, we go from G to D [plays D major scale], I still have the F♯ from G, but now there's a second sharp, which is C ♯. If I want to write out a D major scale, I'm going to need a key signature with an F ♯ and a C ♯, and then I can write the notes like this. As you keep going up the cycle of fifths, you keep adding an additional sharp to the key signature. The order is F♯, C ♯, G ♯, D ♯, A ♯, E ♯, B ♯ .
4.14: Now, remember, we have these helpful acronyms. How are you supposed to remember this? F C, G, D, A, E, B. The most common one that I've encountered is "Father Charles Goes Down And Ends Battle." Okay, it's not the world's most clever acronym, but for some reason it's stuck: "Father Charles Goes Down And Ends Battle." No doubt there are better ones, but this will do for now.
4.15: If you're trying to remember, let's see now. I'm in A major. There's three sharps in A major. What's the order of sharps I need to write? Father Charles Goes: F, C, G. Then you can write the sharps on the staff: F, C, G—that's for sharps. But you run into an issue, which is that if you just keep going up in fifths and adding sharps all the time, you eventually are going to run out of sharps or you're going to need double sharps, and it's going to get seriously weird.
4.16: If you're in G♯ major, then you need how many sharps? Eight. That's more than there are notes. You can do that technically, but it's much better to use an enharmonic equivalent at that point. So instead of writing the key signature of G ♯ major, you would spell it as A♭ major. A♭, conveniently, has four flats. It's a lot easier to read, it's easier to write, and it's simpler. The order of flats for key signatures that use flats is B, E, A, D, G, C, F. Another silly acronym is "Battle Ends And Down Goes Charles' Father."
4.17: Now, in order to create a cycle of increasing numbers of sharps in a key signature— remember, you go up in fifths from C to G to D to A and so on. Now, you might want to use key signatures that use flats instead of sharps, in which case you would start on C and go up in fourths rather than in fifths. So start on C, then you go up to F, then to B ♭, E♭, A♭, D♭, G♭, C♭, F♭— again, by that point, you start needing to use double flats, and it starts to get a little bit complicated. Had I pursued the logic all the way to the end, then here in my sequence of sharps in the cycle of fifths, I would actually need an E ♯ rather than an F♯, and so on.
4.18: This gives you the sequence [plays cycle of fourths]. So it also gets you back to C, but you're going in fourths instead of fifths. So C, once again, no flats; F, one flat; B ♭, that's two flats; E♭, that's three flats; A♭, four flats, and so on and so forth. So these keys are arranged in cycles. You add a flat each time.
4.19: So with this contemporary piano with equal temperament, I can play in any key I want. I can play in A♭, I can play in D♭, I can play in B♭, F, G, whatever. I just have to remember what the key signature is. If I know that, then I can instinctively figure out what notes to play. If I'm in E♭ major, then I remember my little acronym. It starts C, B, E—"Battle Ends And"—that brings me to three flats. I can remember the order of flats from my little acronym: B♭, E♭, A♭. Then I just have to, every time there's an E, play an E♭. Every time there's an A, play an A♭, and then aB ♭.
4.20: This is, again, the thing where it can be very counterintuitive to learn it, and you just have to drill these sorts of things. It's a bit of memorization involved. Remembering the key signatures, circle of fifths, the number of sharps or the number of flats in every key, and then you just drill it so that you think, " C ♯ has seven sharps, and B major has five sharps, and A♭ has four flats," and so on. It becomes second nature after a while.
4.21: That's a pretty fundamental concept because, again, it allows you to play in different keys, and it allows you to modulate. If you're writing a piece in C major, you can move to another key, and then you can eventually work your way back to where you started again. It gives you a much broader range of possibilities. Now that we've looked at melodic intervals, we've looked at scales and how they're put together, and we've looked at key signatures in the cycle of fifths, now we can look at chords and how chords are assembled.
4.22: I've previously given a series of lectures on musical composition for Peterson Academy, and I gave a lecture on chords, on harmony, in that course, but that was very much practically oriented in the sense of, "Here's a bunch of ways that you can take a simple chord and transform it and obtain a whole bunch of different sounds by changing the voicing, by changing the register, by doubling certain tones and so on."
4.23: I'm not going to duplicate that material here, but I'm going to talk to you a little bit about how chords are formed in a more abstract sense and the different ways that they can be transformed. Finally, we're going to look at the qualities of chords. Remember that intervals have qualities—they can be major, minor, perfect, augmented, diminished. We're going to look at chords and the qualities that they can have as well.
4.24: So first, we have to understand how a chord is constituted. A chord simply means two or more tones that are played simultaneously. It can be any two tones, or three, or four, or five, or however many tones you're able to play at the same time. The two tones could be C and D♭ played together. Or it could be [plays a combination of tones]. Any combination of tones that you can possibly imagine can make a chord.
4.25: In the vast bulk of what's called the musical common practice period, or rather the bulk of codified practices that characterize the Baroque, the Classical, and the Romantic eras, and more. Besides, it's not as though this era has, by any means, come to an end. But let's say there was an era in which the basic grammar of music was very broadly and widely applied throughout the Western world, with very few meaningful deviations.
4.26: Of course, the world of music has expanded quite considerably. The technical means of music have turned into a vast ocean. So it's less easy to speak in terms of generalizations. But nevertheless, for the sake of tonal music, music written in keys, a triad is the most fundamental harmonic unit. A triad is constituted of the first, third, and fifth notes of a scale. Let's look at this again. Here's my C major scale— remember that you can assign Roman numerals to each scale degree: I, II, III, et cetera. If I want to make a C major triad, then I take the first scale degree, the third and the fifth—or the root or the tonic, the third and the fifth, and I play them simultaneously. That gives me this [plays C major chord].
4.27: So here's my scale: I, II, III, IV, V, VI, VII; do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, si; C, D, E, F, G, A, B. Of course, you can use whatever term you want within reason. We're just going to take the first, the third, and the fifth, and that gives me a triad. The triad is one of the most absolutely fundamental building blocks of Western harmony.
4.28: I can construct a triad built on the first, the third, and the fifth note on any scale degree. I can do that on the first scale degree or the tonic. But I can also build a triad on the second scale degree, which is D. That gives me a sequence of triads: I, II, III, IV, V, VI, VII. Now, those are the triads in their most basic, fundamental, undiluted form. Totally simple presentation.
4.29: But of course, you can also skip between one and the other. You can move from scale degree I to IV, and IV to V or I to II and then II to VI, and so on. You can have any sequence of triads that you like. What we have here, what I've just played at the keyboard, are a sequence of root position triads, where each successive chord is built on a different scale degree, but always with a root, a third, and a fifth in every chord. These are known as root position triads— root position because the lowest note of the chord is placed on the bottom; there's no change in order of the tones.
4.30: Now we come to inversions. I've covered this slightly before in the composition program, but not everybody's going to have seen both courses. Just a brief recapitulation: if I play a triad in root position—that means I have the first, the third, and the fifth, or the tonic, the third and the fifth. If I swing the order around where I put the third on the bottom and then the fifth on top, and the tonic, or the root, on top, then I obtain this [plays E–G–C]. That's called a first inversion, triad. It's written like this: E, G, and C.
4.31: So this is the root position. This is the first inversion. Then, of course, there's also the second inversion, which is where the fifth is the bottom note. That gives me this: root position [plays C–E–G], first inversion [plays E–G–C], second inversion [plays G–C–E]. And this gives me many more possibilities. I'm not obligated to put the root every time in the bottom position. Now, here, what I'm doing, this little sequence I'm playing, I'm playing a sequence where sometimes the root is in the bass and sometimes the third is in the bass.
4.32: That allows me to have a much smoother and more interesting bass line than if I were obligated to always put the root of the chord in the bass every time. So I can use inversions to put a note other than the root in the bass. Here I've got the third of the chord in the bass [plays a chord with the third in the bass]. And now I've got the root [plays a chord with the root in the bass]. Now the third [plays a chord with the third in the bass], and so on and so forth. So that opens up the musical possibilities considerably.
4.33: One of the things, again, that you do when you're coming to terms with music and the language and grammar, if you like, of music is developing the capacity to recognize instantly these different inversions. So if I play a first inversion triad, you can hear instantly, "Oh, yes, that's not a root position triad. It's in first inversion because I don't have an F as the bottom note." That's one thing that you can do with a triad. You can permutate the order of the notes or rotate them rather so that the bottom note goes on top and you keep going.
4.34: The other thing, of course, that you can do is you can alter the quality of the chord by using accidentals to change the intervals. We're going to stick with a C major triad for now. I'm going to take the third and lower it using a flat symbol. So now we have a minor third between the root and the third of the chord. You want to get in the habit of listening very closely, not to this chord as just a single thing, but as an entity constituted of three different tones, and you want to hear each tone. You can do that by singing the tones.
4.35: The way to remember and to incorporate all of these different concepts effectively is to externalize what you're doing. You have to sing; you have to use your voice. Even if your voice is hideous, which right now is the case for me. So this gives us different qualities of triads: major, minor, augmented, and diminished.
4.36: To make an augmented triad, start with a C major triad once again, and I raise the fifth to a G♯. That gives me this [sings C–E–G♯]. It's hard to sing; augmented intervals are difficult to sing. Hard to sing in tune as well. All of these have C as their root, but there are different qualities of chords. Now, I can also make a diminished triad by lowering not only the third, but also the fifth. That gives me C, E ♭, and G ♭. That gives me a diminished triad.
4.37: So now we've covered some of the basic ways that you can alter or that you can present a triad. So here's our major triad in root position [plays C-E-G], in first inversion [plays E-G-C], and in second inversion [plays G-C-E]. Then we've got a major triad [plays C-E-G], minor triad [plays C-E♭-G], diminished triad [plays C-E ♭-G ♭], augmented triad [plays C–E–G♯]. This is where we start getting into a combinatorial explosion, because if you consider that each of these different chord qualities can also be inverted, and of course, you can play this in any key on the piano, on any scale degree, it becomes truly vertiginous.
4.38: A minor triad can also be inverted. I can put any note in the bass. I can put the root in the bass, the third, the fifth, and it's the same with the diminished triad. And of course, the augmented triad. So starting from just a simple chord, suddenly we have tens of thousands of possibilities, perhaps. So it goes very, very quickly. The difficult thing here, again, is to develop the capacity to recognize chord qualities instantly. So that if I do this or this, or this, or, or [plays various triads], you can say without hesitation, "You just played a diminished triad, an augmented triad, a minor triad, a major triad," and so on. That's without getting into questions of inversions.
4.39: If all of that sounds dizzying, you can take some relief in the fact that there are methods to work on this that are actually extremely effective. We're going to talk about that a little bit tomorrow, about some of the ways that you can train your ear to recognize these intervals. Of course, sitting down and playing for hours a day helps as well. It just helps to familiarize yourself with these concepts.
4.40: We've looked at the different ways that you can construct three-note chords. There are many, many other possibilities, of course. There are possibilities that aren't triadic. You can have three-note chords that aren't made up of stacked thirds. All of the chords that we've looked at— major, minor, diminished, augmented—are built around two thirds stacked on top of each other.
4.41: But you can have other qualities of chords as well. You can have chords that are built on fourths or chords that are based on seconds. Those sorts of sounds are very common in jazz and many other expressive contexts. They're not triadic in nature, but they are three-note chords or four-note chords.
4.42: Another thing you can do is you can continue to add thirds to your chord. So remember that the C major chord is built on the root, the third, and the fifth. I can also add the seventh to the chord, and that gives me, logically enough, a seventh chord [plays C-E-G- B]. And you can keep going. You can add a ninth, an 11th, 13th, and so on, and end up with chords like this [plays extended chords].
4.43: Now, if I am on C, if I'm in C major, and I move towards the fifth degree of C major, which is G, now we're getting into another concept that we need to understand, which is the harmonic functions. We've looked at how you can take any scale and count off the tones: I, II, III, IV, V, VI, VII. In Roman numeral notation, those are the scale degrees. We've looked at how you can give them solfège syllables: do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, si. But we haven't looked at the harmonic functions yet. So let's explain what those are and how they work.
4.44: I need to, yet again, write out my beloved C major scale. Now, I did teach you one term, one harmonic function already, which is the tonic, which refers to the first scale degree, the first tone in my scale. In C major, the tonic is C. Now, if I move towards the fourth scale degree, the harmonic function, the term for the fourth scale degree, is subdominant. If I move to the fifth scale degree—I'm going to start with these three for now—then I'm moving towards the dominant. What we're going to do is we're going to build a triad on the tonic, the subdominant, and the dominant or I, IV, V in C major—I, IV, V, andthen back to I.
4.45: The term harmonic functions refers to the fact that if I just play you a random chord with no context around it and just leave it hanging there, then that chord is harmonically ambiguous. It doesn't tell me anything. It doesn't give me a sense of movement. It doesn't tell me what the tonic is. It doesn't tell me even what key we're in. I can play a C major triad, and it could be the dominant of F major. Or it could be the tonic of C major, or it could be the subdominant of some other key, and it keeps going.
4.46: The important thing to understand is that the most stable scale degree in any key is the tonic. The tonic is—you can think of it as being like home base. You're at home. You haven't moved anywhere. You're just sitting at home. The polar opposite of the tonic, in a sense, the scale degree towards which pieces tend to gravitate as a secondary place, is the dominant. In the case of C major, the dominant is on the fifth scale degree, which is G. That gives you a stable place and an unstable place.
4.47: If I just play these two chords, there's this sense that I've moved away from somewhere, and I'm not quite done. I've created an instability. The subdominant, which, as the name implies, lies directly below the dominant, gives me an intermediary degree of instability. So think of the tonic as the most stable harmonic function [plays C major chord]. The subdominant [plays F major chord] is an intermediary degree of instability. The dominant [plays G major chord] is quite unstable. And then we want to get back [plays C major chord] to where we started again.
4.48: The amazing thing is you can tell a very simple, archetypal story in music through sounds with those three chords. A stable place, an intermediary or transitional place, and an unstable place. That's enough to tell a story. There's this cliché—it's kind of true —that pop music is based on a three-chord structure. Now, not all pop songs literally have only three chords, but they tend to gravitate around that basic progression: I, IV, V—that's also a blues progression.
4.49: I think the reason for that is that the I, IV, V progression is the simplest chord progression you can write that has a sense of movement away from your starting place, and then that allows you to get back to where you started again—avery, very simple little story. What all of this has to do with are the dynamics of centripetal and centrifugal motion away from and towards your center of gravity. These forces, which we might not understand consciously— we might not be thinking about them when we're listening to a piece of music—but they're a large part of what gives it its sense of dynamism and its sense of movement.
4.50: Composers who have completely mastered harmonic tension, harmonic movement, can tell extraordinary stories with tones by moving away from or back towards some either permanent or provisional landing spot in the piece. That's why Beethoven can write a 25- or 30-minute-long symphony movement that has a complete sense of coherence dramaturgically, and it takes you on a journey, and you can go very, very far from the starting point and then end up where you began at the end. You can hold your attention for 30 minutes without necessarily understanding why. A big part of it is because of that coherence on the harmonic scale.
4.51: A simple way of thinking of tonic, subdominant, and dominant, again, is in terms of their function within the key. So stable place, intermediary place, and a secondary place. Every one of the seven scale degrees has a different term that assigns it a function within the scale. The others are supertonic— the supertonic is the scale degree immediately above the tonic; that's easy to remember. The third is the mediant —mediant because it's halfway between the tonic and the dominant. If we go to sixth scale degree or A, if we're in a C major, then we end on the submediant. Finally, B, which is immediately below the tonic, is the leading tone, which is a concept we've already looked at.
4.52: So then you start to see that this seven-note scale, which seems so simple, is not actually that simple. Every single tone in that scale has a function, a function relative to where you started—on the tonic. So tonic [plays C], supertonic [plays D], mediant [plays E], submediant [plays F], dominant—sorry, I'll start over again. I must be getting tired. Tonic [plays C], supertonic [plays D], mediant [plays E], subdominant [plays F], dominant [plays G], submediant [plays A], leading tone [plays B], and then back to the tonic again [plays C]. Those are theoretical terms that allow us to describe the function of different scale degrees within a key. We're almost done with this.
4.53: I wanted to get back to what we were talking about. We looked at a very primordial, very important progression. Now, a chord progression implies that we're moving towards a goal of some kind. It implies that there's a directed motion between one place and another place. In order to have a progression, the movement has to be palpable; we have to have a sense that we're going somewhere.
4.54: If you string together chords without thinking in terms of a progression, in terms of a goal-oriented motion of some kind, then you end up with a succession of chords. It's not the same thing. And I, IV, V is a very simple progression, but there are many others, too. One of the things you can do when you're getting a handle on these materials— starting to understandhow keys work and how you can join chords together—is to make little progressions and to play them in different keys.
4.55: So you can say, "Well, okay, play a I, IV, V progression in B ♭ major" [plays a I, IV, V progression in B♭ major]. " Play it in A major" [plays I, IV, V progression in A major]. "Play it in F major" [plays I, IV, V progression in F major]. You can do that in any key, and it's the same progression every time, and the functions of those chords are the same; they're just transposed to a different key.
4.56: Of course, you can move between any two scale degrees. You can make any progression you want in principle. You could say, for example, we're going to go from I to VI to II to V. So I to VI to II to V—that's a very, very common pop song type of sequence [plays C major–A minor–D minor–G major chords]. So again, by creating progressions out of sequences of triads, you can create phrases that have musical coherence and harmonic coherence. Those are just two simple examples.
4.57: What you do, again, when you're starting out, you play those sequences in every key. You learn to do them, learn to drill them. It becomes second nature. The advantage of that is it sharpens your ear and it allows you to link up your eyes, your ears, and your hands very rapidly. We'll stop there for now. That was a little tour of triads. It's not an exhaustive one. There's much more we could add to it, but that's probably enough for now. Are there any questions?
4.58: Is it possible that music, as the dramatization of deep search into our experience, has led to the birth of more sophisticated feelings or associated values?
4.59: Well, music is a mirror of the human psyche, so it's possible to express almost any facet of human experience through music. And what has happened, really, is that that range of expressive capability has just expanded and expanded and expanded. I don't think it's music itself that's driving that expansion; it's the desire of humans to express an ever-broader range, not only of emotions, but also of thoughts and sensations. What I find absolutely incredible about that is that music can always do it. You can express any conceivable interior state, any conceivable character through a piece of music.
4.60: The materials of music have sometimes needed to expand in order to encapsulate some of these sensations. You see this certainly with the Romantics. The Romantics were interested in emotional paroxysm in extremes of interior states. This led to Expressionism, which was interested only in the extremes: intense anger, intense happiness, intense horror, intense anxiety. Whether they're positive or negative emotions, Expressionists and the Romantics before them wanted to convey the limit cases—how far can you go in that direction?
4.61: In order to convey those extreme emotions, sometimes you need to draw upon unconventional musical resources. When we get into the Bach course, which I'm going to be presenting in a few days, we're going to see examples of this, of how Bach had to sometimes have recourse to extraordinarily sophisticated and unusual progressions and melodic contours in order to convey some of the experiences that are related, for example, in the passion stories, where sometimes a simple triad isn't enough, a simple diatonic scale isn't enough. You need to find something more intense, more stranger, in order to convey the nature of that experience. Lecture 5: Motion in Music At a glance — Motion in music.
5.1: Music Wants to Move—that's going to be the topic of our lecture today. I've spent my life now trying to work out exactly what lies at the bottom of the musical phenomenon. Different styles of music have different points of emphasis, as we've seen already. Some music is intensely rhythmic. Other pieces seem to be strangely static. Others are full of surprises and non sequiturs and contrast. Others are much more continuous. But there seems to be a constant at the bottom of this phenomenon, which has to do with motion.
5.2: Music provides us with an infinite array of possibilities for expressing ideas of movement. Of course, this can be literal, embodied kinetic movement. In fact, that is how perhaps a majority of people engage with the musical phenomenon. But other aspects of music move in a way that is sublimated, which is to say we're not literally moving, we're not literally dancing while we listen to it. But there seems to be, nevertheless, a very profound feeling of forward motion. That motion, of course, can take all kinds of forms. That seems to be something that's absolutely central to the development of this art form through the centuries.
5.3: Now, what harmony does, and we started looking a little bit at individual chords yesterday, and we looked a little bit at some simple progressions: I-IV-V, I-VI-II-V-I, and so on. We looked at the basic harmonic functions, the fact that there's a stable function, you might say, an intermediary function that allows you to move, and an unstable function, which allows you effectively to have goal-oriented motion, a meaningful sense of progression using nothing but sounds, nothing but tones on a piano, which is quite extraordinary.
5.4: But we haven't quite gone into detail yet about precisely how the mechanics of that work. In order to understand that, we need to talk a little bit about consonance and dissonance. Now, those are terms that you've probably come across before. For many people, dissonance has an emotional connotation of something unpleasant, something cacophonous, something that might strain the indulgence of your ear. But consonance and dissonance, as well as being aesthetic concepts to a degree, can also be defined technically in terms of the musical phenomenon. We're going to look at that.
5.5: Consonance doesn't mean pretty or agreeable, and dissonance doesn't mean ugly or disagreeable. Rather, consonance can be thought of in a musical context as something stable, something that doesn't need to move. And dissonance is something that creates a need for movement or possibly a need for resolution of some kind.
5.6: To a degree, these are contextual ideas. So the dissonance in one style might, in fact, sound relatively consonant in another style. It comes back to what I said yesterday when I was answering a question, which is that you can think of this as a dance between the world of natural acoustic phenomena and the world of culture, which is a world of artifice. To some degree, you can explain consonance technically in terms of the simplicity of a harmonic ratio.
5.7: Remember, if you take a length of string, a vibrating string of some kind, stretch it between two posts that hold it in place, and then divide it into exact multiples— divide it in half, divide it in thirds, divide it in fourths, and so on—divide it into exact ratios— 1:2, 3:2, 4:3, 5:4, and so on—you obtain a series of simple harmonic intervals. The simpler the ratio, the closer the sound is to the fundamental of that string, which is to say the tone that it produces when the string is undivided, when you're hearing the full length of the string.
5.8: It's easier for the ear to relate those simple ratios, those simple intervals, to the fundamental. Let's try this again. I have to keep returning to this point because it's a fundamental property of acoustics, and it informs our experience of music, certainly, and also the music that we produce. If you take all of those ratios in sequence and present them one after the other, you obtain the harmonic series.
5.9: The harmonic series is going to start with the fundamental tone. We're going to start on a C here [plays C]. If you divide that string in half, that gives you a ratio of 2:1, and that produces the octave [plays C–C]. Frequential tones, this octave, the upper note is exactly double the frequency of the lower note. It's a very simple ratio. The only thing simpler than that is 1:1, which is a unison, two notes sounding at the same pitch. That gives us this octave [plays C–C]. All of these successive octaves stand in that very simple relationship to each other.
5.10: We're not in the arena of culture; we're not in the arena of artifice here. This is a natural phenomenon. Next comes the fifth [plays C–G]. Now, this is something that you can train your ear to be sensitive to because any harmonic sound, that is to say, a sound in which the various frequency components stand in a certain ratio to each other, let's say, and have a certain periodicity to their frequencies, any harmonic sound is going to be made up of some combination of these overtones.
5.11: But you don't experience that directly when you're listening to it. What you hear is a synthesis, and that synthesis in the particular distribution of intensities and of dynamic curves that it contains—because some partials, some overtones will die away faster than others, some will be more intense than others—the particular way that those sounds evolve over time and their frequency distribution, their intensity, creates timbre. That's how we're able to tell the difference between instruments, between a piano and a trumpet, and so on.
5.12: If I take these natural harmonics [plays C–C–G–C–E ascending], especially if I play the lower partials louder than the upper partials, what you hear is an enrichening of the sound, but you don't necessarily hear it as a chord [plays C–C–G–C–E ascending]. That's how they blend together and create almost a single synthetic sound.
5.13: So if you just take these simple ratios, then you can use that to create consonances that are very stable. But music abhors constant stability. I could just sit down and play that sound for four hours, and it would go nowhere. There'd be no story. Nothing would happen. You can try to imagine a narrative that would be like that, where you're just sitting there eating cupcakes or something, andeverything's fine.
5.14: So we need a stable entity of some kind, whatever that is—it can take the form of a pattern, it can take the form of a sound— and we need a destabilizing force applied to that so that we can move. This is why we have these progressions that want to take us somewhere.
5.15: We've looked at concepts such as the circle of fifths. We've looked at how that gives us this whole network of different keys with different amounts of sharps and flats, and that gives us the capacity to move around in music and create a more interesting sense of motion. In theory, you can get extraordinarily far from your starting place and still work your way back there. This is why the symphonies of Beethoven are so long and complicated and emotionally absorbing. It's because of the sophistication, the complexity, and the daring with which he's able to get progressively farther and farther from his starting point, but without ever completely losing his way.
5.16: Let's return to consonance and dissonance. We've looked at how consonances are formed. We've looked at the fact that they are technically made out of stable things— simple ratios, sounds that don't particularly have a need to move.
5.17: What can you do to create a dissonance? Well, the dissonance is something that, again, pulls our ear. This is a contextual phenomenon to a large extent. I could sit and play very beautiful seven-note chords on the piano that may technically be dissonant chords, but if I play them in a certain way, they might not necessarily need to move all that much. It's partly to do with context, and it's partly to do with matters of style, and also what comes before and what comes after.
5.18: If I just sit here and play something like [plays dissonant chords]. Both of those are very dissonant chords, but by carefully manipulating rhythm, timbre, register, and dynamics, you can make something that doesn't create the impression necessarily of an unpleasant or discordant sound, but rather that creates a certain atmosphere, let's say.
5.19: Now, in a harmonic context, let's try to set up a situation where we have the need for a resolution. I'm going to go back to my program here, and I'm going to write a simple triad—we're going to start that again. You remember how triads are made? It's constituted of the root, the third and the fifth. In this case, we're going to be in C major. This is going to be the first scale degree. So it's a triad built on C, E, and G [plays C–E– G].
5.20: Now, I'm going to make a very small change to this chord. I'm going to take the G and add a sharp. That's going to look like this. Now, as you might remember from yesterday, if you take a triad, raise the fifth up a semitone, you obtain an augmented triad [plays C–E–G♯]. Now, it's possible to imagine chords that are considerably more dissonant than this one, this augmented triad. But notice the difference in quality and the difference in apparent stability [plays C–E–G, C–E–G ♯]. Now suddenly, we're going somewhere. That's what dissonance is.
5.21: Now, that G♯, that can resolve in any number of ways. For example, I could take it up another semitone, and here we start to see a little melodic progression [plays C–E–G, C–E–G♯, C–E–A]. That's called chromatic voice leading—chromatic voice leading because the top note of the chord is proceeding stepwise up by a semitone each time [plays C–E–G, C–E–G♯, C–E–A, C–E–A♯, B–D♯–B, B–D♯–A, B–E–G]. Now that I've done that, I've landed on a mediant chord, an E minor chord in C major. That gives me a feeling of moderate stability. It's more stable [plays B–E–G] than the augmented triad [plays C–E–G♯], which really wants to go somewhere, but it's not completely stable because I'm not on the tonic; I'm not in C major.
5.22: Music is this continuous dance between provisional stability, provisional stasis, and an experience of foreignness, an experience of not being where we started. And there are all these subtle degrees. So if I play that progression again [plays C–E–G, C–E–G ♯, C–E– A, C–G–A♯, B–F♯–B, B–D♯–A, B–E–G], I can eventually get back, but because of the nature of this little story I've been telling through sounds, I don't feel that this has been completely resolved. There's a strong possibility that I'm going to keep going and end up somewhere else, and you can just keep doing that in a piece of music.
5.23: So how do we know when we've arrived at asignpost, let's say? We've arrived at somewhere intermediate? Imagine that you're driving from Paris to Prague or something like this. You're going to stop at various points along the way. You might go through Switzerland, or you might go through Germany, or you might go through Italy, even. There's all kinds of routes you could take, and you might stop at different cities along the way. You haven't reached your destination, but you've reached a stopping point temporarily. The way that this is signaled in music is through cadences.
5.24: Cadences are a form of punctuation—we've addressed this a little bit in the composition class, but we need to get into a little bit more detail with this idea here. Cadence is a term that means a close. It relates to, among other things, the French word "cadenas," which is a padlock. It's something that closes. It's a signal to your listener that we've arrived at a pause. Just like the period at the end of a sentence or a comma or a semicolon, it's a form of punctuation, if you like. It allows us to create a continuous sense of movement, but a movement that is articulated by different arrival points.
5.25: Yesterday, we looked at a simple progression, which was I, IV, V, and I want to look at that again. I'm going to draw a simple bass line here. Remember those Roman numerals? I, IV, V. If I stop there, at least temporarily, if I go from I and I move towards V, towards the dominant, what that gives me is called a half cadence or an imperfect cadence—imperfect because I've arrived somewhere else, but I haven't arrived back home. It's a temporary or provisional resting place [plays a sequence of chords].
5.26: That characteristic, I, IV, V, motion [plays C–F–G], or even just directly I to V [plays C major chord, then G major chord], very often signals a moderate degree of break in a phrase. As you might imagine, the opposite movement from V back to I is a perfect cadence. So, movement from I to V gives you an imperfect or half cadence; movement from V to I, or dominant to tonic, gives you a perfect cadence. Notice how the feeling of suspension is always there when you move from I to V directly [plays C major chord, then G major chord]. When you move from V to I [plays G major chord, then C major chord], you have a feeling of closure or finality [plays G major chord, then C major chord].
5.27: One thing that people, students, coming to grips with music theory in the early stages, have to work on is cadences. And so what you do is you pick a random key—it could be an A major or a B♭ or A♭ or a D or whatever, and you practice playing cadences. This process of drilling them, first of all, helps your ear to become accustomed to the function of these progressions, and it also helps you to attain a certain degree of fluidity.
5.28: Now, there are other types of cadences. In fact, there's many of them. Cadences change throughout the centuries. If you listen to medieval music, Renaissance music, you're going to hear a variety of cadences that sound very little like these. But that, nevertheless, within that context, within that cultural and stylistic context, create a palpable feeling of closure.
5.29: One of the other effects you can produce with a cadence is called the deceptive cadence. This is a cadence that doesn't do what you're expecting, but takes you somewhere else. The deceptive cadence, or interrupted cadence, as it's sometimes called, ends with a motion from V to VI. Remember, we're in C major here. That means moving from G to A in the bass, from the dominant to the submediant [plays G major chord, then A minor chord].
5.30: Now, what you might be expecting to hear if you're coming to the end of a phrase is this [plays G major chord, then C major chord] . And what the deceptive cadence does is it gives you a little trick [plays G major chord, then A minor chord]; we haven't ended up where we're expecting to go.
5.31: That allows you to do a couple of things. One is that you could just keep going from there. Now you're in the relative minor, you're on A minor, and you could say, "Well, that's the new key for a while. I didn't go where you expected me to go; I'm going on this supplemental journey." Or you can use the deceptive or interrupted cadence as a way of prolonging the eventual return back to the tonic again [concludes the phrase in C major]. So it can form part of a larger phrase unit that gives us a little bit of a more elaborate formula.
5.32: One of the things to be careful about in music, generally, is avoiding things that are too obvious or that happen too many times with a minimum of variety, a minimum of change. Just as how you would be justifiably exasperated if a movie you were attending did exactly everything you were expecting with absolutely no surprises and always took the shortest route to the exit, as it were. It's the same in music— we have a variety of different effects that allow us to create feelings of stability, instability, and movement between things. That's the deceptive cadence, which is a move from the dominant to the submediant.
5.33: One other type of cadence we need to look at is the plagal cadence: P-L-A-G-A-L. The plagal cadence is associated with early music, which is to say, medieval and Renaissance music. What characterizes it is a sense of close, but a somewhat weaker sense of close than V to I. Instead, the plagal cadence moves from IV to I, so the subdominant to the tonic. That looks like this [plays F major chord, then C major chord]. All of these different cadences have different functions that orient our ear differently and create different expectations and different degrees of release or tension.
5.34: So we've been looking at how you can join these chords together, how you can make simple progressions, how you can signal the end of a phrase or a pause in a phrase through cadences. Now we come to a concept called voice leading.
5.35: Voice leading is a very important concept to understand because you have to remember that European art music for centuries was based exclusively around the voice, which is to say that all music was conceived in some manner or another in terms of an actual voice. Even when pieces were played on instruments, they were generally adaptations of vocal music.
5.36: So if you wanted to stack two or more sounds together, you would be thinking in terms of individual voices, where every tone in the chord is one component of a polyphonic texture. It's one voice that has its own trajectory independent from the others, which gives you a fusion, if you like, of the horizontal and the vertical—the horizontal being the melodic dimension and the vertical being the harmonic dimension. Horizontal, one sound after another; vertical, two or more sounds heard at the same time.
5.37: Why this is important is that it's easy to just sit at the keyboard and play block chords like this [plays a sequence of chords]. You can chain chords together like that without there necessarily being any particular notion of a voice. What you're hearing there are block sonorities that you can shove together, like blocks of granite, effectively. There's not a sense of organic connection between them where every note is leading to some other note, but it can actually be quite disjunctive, like this [plays a sequence of disjunctive chords].
5.38: It's not that the chords themselves or the harmonic functions are necessarily completely disjunctive. It's that the gap between one tone in one chord and another tone in another chord is so great, so disjunctive, that you can't relate them with your ear as belonging to the same voice. So we're going to look at some basic principles of voice leading. What voice leading aims to do is to take the principles of combining voices in vocal polyphony and apply them not only to voices but also to instrumental situations. That has a further benefit, which is an ergonomic benefit.
5.39: If you look at old harmonic treatises—treatises on thorough bass, for example, from the 17th century, it's quite interesting.
