There's a shift that goes on in the world of music theory—particularly in Germany, but not only— where at that time, if you wanted to learn how to harmonize a bass line, if you wanted to learn how to join chords together and make smooth progressions, a lot of it was actually predicated on ergonomics, on shapes that fit the hand, the natural shape of the hand. It had an abstract dimension, but it also had to do, very pragmatically, with limiting lateral hand motion on a keyboard so that you're not having to do this all the time.
5.40: One of the basic principles of classical voice leading—in other words, how do you move from one tone to another in a set of different voices so as to obtain a smooth result— one of the basic principles is you move as little as you need to. So if there's a tone in common between two chords, then you don't move it; you don't move it to another octave. You keep it where it is, and the other fingers move as little as possible.
5.41: Let me give you an example. I'm going to write out a very, very simple little progression here, just two chords. For the sake of clarity, I'm going to also point out that vocal polyphony tends to be articulated in terms of four voices, the four basic human voice types, which are soprano, alto, tenor, and bass. You'll often see that abbreviated as S, A, T, B: soprano, alto, tenor, and bass. You'll see references to S-A-T-B choirs—that means two of each voice type. Generally, soprano and alto are female voice types, and tenor and bass, or sometimes tenor and baritone, are male voice types. That's called a mixed choir [plays C–F].
5.42: That's my bass voice. The soprano, or the highest voice, is going to stay put—it's going to play a C, and it's going to stay on C. That's going to sound like this [plays C–C, F–C]. That's not a complete harmony; we need to fill in the gaps a little bit. My alto voice is going to be on the G, just below the C of the soprano [plays G–C]. It's going to move up a whole step to A. My tenor voice is going to move from E to F. That's going to look like this [plays E–G–C, F–A–C, E–C, F–C]
5.43: Now, you can start to sensitize your ears so that you can hear that not in terms of one big chord, followed by another big chord, but rather in terms of voices. The tenor is doing this [plays E, F]. That's pretty smooth. The bass is doing this [plays C, F]. The alto is doing this [plays G, A]. The soprano, which has a common tone between I and IV, the C [plays C, C], isn't moving.
5.44: A couple of things to observe there. The first is that we have a four-voice texture: S, A, T, and B. There's our S, there's our alto, tenor, and bass. But triads only contain three notes. That means you have to double one of the tones. The doubling can take the form either of a unison, where you have two voices singing the same tone in the same octave at the same time, or you can take one of the three notes of the chord and have it present in another voice in a different octave.
5.45: In the case of the first chord here, which is [plays C–E–G–C], the bass and the soprano are both singing a C [plays C–C]. We consider that to be a doubled tone. In order to produce the most stable and the simplest result, the order of priority is you double the root or the fifth, and generally speaking, you're not meant to double the third. Sometimes in exceptional circumstances, it will happen, but it's the absolute last priority. And the reason is that the third is harder to tune, and it's a less stable interval than the root and the fifth.
5.46: Therefore, I've decided to double the root in this case. In both cases, in fact, because the bass and tenor voices in the second chord are both going to sing F [plays C–E–G–C and F–F–A–C]. And notice how these inner voices, the alto and tenor, just move a tiny bit [plays E–G, F–A]. And the soprano on top [plays E–G–C, F–A–C].
5.47: That's exceptionally easy to play because your hand hardly has to move at all, which makes it both ergonomically comfortable and easier on the ear because it's very easy for the ear to hear the individuality of each voice. Whereas if I were to have all sorts of large leaps in there and disjunctive movement and dissonant melodic intervals all over the place, then it would be much more difficult, both for a singer—you can do this experiment yourself. It's very difficult to sing large intervals. It's difficult to sing dissonant intervals, and it's difficult to have multiple skips or leaps in a row.
5.48: If you can keep the voice leading smooth, it's easier to sing, it's easier for the ear to relate the chords together, and it's also easier ergonomically. It's quite interesting to me that those two things are connected, that what's easy to sing also ends up being what's easy to play on a keyboard, even though, mechanically speaking, there's nothing in common between the two.
5.49: So well-written vocal music tends to translate extremely well to keyboard music, interestingly enough. The ranges are not that dissimilar. If you're dealing with the four voice types, you've got a range of maybe three octaves, something like that, maybe three and a half octaves, which is a very comfortable range to play on the keyboard as well. Those are some basics of voice leading.
5.50: Generally speaking, the ear is drawn to the outer voices, primarily. This is the same reason why when you listen to a song, you are going to be primarily focused on the voice. The voice is usually, although not always, front and center in the texture. If it's a high voice, a soprano, then it's going to sit on top, and you're going to hear it without any difficulty. Your ear tends to be drawn to the highest note in a sonority. That's where you're going to be focusing your attention. That tends to be where the melodic interest is.
5.51: Likewise, you're also going to be drawn to the bass because, in tonal or classical harmony, the bass determines the function of the tones that lie above it. The bass gives you a strong sense of movement, and everything that happens above it is related by the ear, acoustically, to whatever is happening in the bass.
5.52: Now, the inner voices will tend to attract somewhat less attention. They matter, obviously, for all kinds of reasons, but it's not where your ear is going to be focusing the most necessarily. In actual practice, in actual compositions, what you'll find is that as a very skilled composer, we'll never neglect the inner voices. They'll always have nice lines for them to play— that's regardless of if it's a keyboard piece, a vocal piece, or something else. But you want to attend to all the details in a texture; they're all important. A skilled composer, again, will make sure that the inner voices are not boring. They're not just moving in circles doing nothing, but there will be an interesting, distinctive line in every single part.
5.53: So we've talked about the fact that you need to double a tone in four-part vocal writing. If you're writing triads, primarily, then you have to double a tone in order to complete the four-voice texture. We've looked at some basic principles of voice leading, about how you aim to have common tones remain in one voice, if possible, to keep things smooth, and the inner voices should not move more than is necessary.
5.54: There's a couple of other principles we have to look at. The first is that, in general, you want the voices to remain stratified in their own space, so to speak, so that the soprano doesn't impinge upon the alto line, so that we can always hear the distinctness of each individual line. The voice leading principle there is avoiding the crossing of voices, so you don't have the soprano dipping below the alto, and you don't have the alto singing higher than the soprano.
5.55: Of course, you could do that technically. There's a certain amount of overlap between all the vocal ranges, which makes it possible. Again, with all of these things, it comes back to what I said in the first lecture on the first day: you have to look at these as descriptive rather than prescriptive. Anything I'm saying here, you can easily find countless examples of composers not doing what I'm saying to do. You can think of this again as a normative practice that is based around ideal voice leading, let's say, but expression isn't so straightforward.
5.56: There will be instances where for technical reasons, for expressive reasons, the composer may decide to go against those principles. Notice I don't say rules, but rather principles. And provided that there's a reason for it, an expressive reason, and it works musically, then you accept it, but you have to be doing it consciously and have an understanding of what the normative, let's say, process would be.
5.57: So we avoid crossing voices in order to make it so that the distinctness, the individuality of each voice, is not impinged upon. You will find examples of voice crossings, sometimes as a special effect, sometimes because, for one reason or another, maybe for reasons of range, or maybe because the composer wants to preserve a certain melodic contour in the tenor or in the alto, where you may occasionally see that, but it's a general principle to avoid doing that.
5.58: For example, in this instance, I'm going to color-code the voices so you can see what I'm doing a little bit more clearly. You can imagine the soprano doing this [plays C, G (below), A]. Then we're going to write an alto voice, and the alto is going to be written in red. If I just played on a piano where it's a matter of hammers striking strings, obviously, the effect is a little bit harder to hear. You would have to hear singers attempting to do this.
5.59: I've got my alto moving up [plays G, B, C] and my soprano doing this [plays C, G (below), A]. That gives me [plays G-C, B-G, C-A]. You would have to look at the diagram on the board to see that, in fact, the alto is moving above the soprano and the soprano is moving below the alto. In reality, there would be almost no reason you would want to do that in the first place because it's quite simple for the soprano simply to go C, B, C, like this [plays C, B, C]. But nevertheless, it's a mistake to be avoided in voice-leading exercises. One of the basic principles of voice leading in terms of texture is to preserve the autonomy, the independence of the voices. This is why we don't cross the voices; we try to keep them relatively smooth most of the time.
5.60: There are another couple of rules to observe. One is that you avoid having an interval of more than an octave between any voice pairs. You won't see a gap of more than an octave between the note that the soprano is singing and the note that the alto is singing, with one exception, which is that you can have a gap larger than an octave between the tenor and the bass.
5.61: All of these principles, all of these practices, again, it's not useful to think of them in terms of rules that have been dreamt up by a pedagogue or by a theorist, but rather as principles that serve a particular function. The reason you can have a larger gap between the tenor and the bass is so that you can preserve the independence of the bass line and have very wide-ranging basses that are interesting to hear. Also, simply because if you try to do that in the inner voices, you're very likely to end up with voice crossings.
5.62: So generally speaking—and this also relates back to an acoustic principle. Remember that when we looked at the harmonic series, the intervals between successive partials or overtones get smaller as you go up. As the ratios get more complex, as you get farther from the fundamental, the intervals get smaller.
5.63: That seems to be something like a natural acoustic law, which is that the voices on the lower end of the spectrum, in the bass, tend to sound better if they're more widely spaced, and the voices on top tend to sound better if they are more closely spaced. So you'll see a larger gap between the bass and the tenor. As you get into the middle voices, the voices get closer together. It seems to be easier for the ear to assimilate and to fuse those different voices together with that texture.
5.64: So we've looked at principles of voice spacing. You can see here, for example, that I've got a distance of a perfect fourth between my soprano and alto [plays G–C]. There's a third, minor third between tenor and alto [plays E–G]. And an interval of a 10th between bass and tenor [plays C–E]. So we have both harmonic intervals here, or vertical intervals, and melodic intervals when I move from one sound to another.
5.65: Now, another principle that serves also to preserve the independence of voices is the avoidance of forbidden parallels. Forbidden parallels have a very lengthy history. Here again, we come to issues of artifice. There's no natural or acoustic reason why you wouldn't have certain types of parallel motion between a voice pair in a four-voice texture.
5.66: As you move through the different historical eras and listen to music of different centuries, you'll find that the tolerance for or avoidance of certain parallels changes over time. There were certain parallels that were considered to be very dissonant and unpleasant in the medieval era that are completely commonplace today. But in their most fundamental form, students beginning to learn about voice leading and joining chords together, learn to avoid what are called parallel fifths and parallel octaves, primarily. That means that if two voices are moving together, then you don't have two successive intervals of a fifth between the voices.
5.67: Now I've got this [plays G–D, A–E]. It doesn't sound horrible, but in a continuous four- voice texture, what that does acoustically is if you have these parallel consonant intervals like that, like an octave or a fifth, what happens is the voices start to lose their independence. They start to fuse together acoustically in a way that disrupts the fluidity of the texture. It's something that you might not even necessarily notice right away, but it does have the effect of subtly damaging that texture somehow, impinging upon its fluidity and the independence of the voices. It's not that they sound bad, exactly, but it's not ideal.
5.68: When you're learning to do these kinds of exercises, you're taught that consecutive fifths in two different voices are to be avoided. And likewise, consecutive octaves are to be avoided. That would look like this [plays D–D, E–E]. So no consecutive fifths and no consecutive octaves.
5.69: Once again, if you really go looking, you can find subtly hidden examples of that in the works of classical composers. Beethoven, for example, was quoted as once having said that there's absolutely no reason to avoid consecutive fifths. They don't sound bad. The justification is that it sounds bad, but in certain contexts, it's very difficult to even hear.
5.70: So you always have to look, with these things, at: What is the purpose of this principle? Why does it exist? Then you can see for yourself, you can train your ear to recognize that phenomenon and decide if it indeed sounds disturbing or if it somehow does not create the effect you want. So always try to understand the reason behind the principle, and then if you need to break it, you'll know why you're doing it, and you'll be aware of it.
5.71: So those are a few basic principles of voice leading. We've looked at the need to keep it smooth as much as possible unless you're aiming for a special effect. We've looked at the need to be very cautious about the spacing of voices, avoid having the voices cross, and then we've also looked at the avoidance of forbidden parallels.
5.72: That's just the beginning because we haven't really talked about seventh chords and the resolutions of dissonances and all the different ways you can join various different chords together. We haven't looked at chromatic voice leading. It's an extremely vast subject, but I think this is at least a fairly concise introduction to the subject.
5.73: In practical terms, what that means is you can try this out as an experiment—sit down at a piano keyboard and just move one finger at a time. Try to keep it smooth and see if you can create little progressions by moving from I to VI or I to IV to II to V, and so on. And what beginner students will do is they'll take a little bass line like that [C, E (below), F, G, C], and they'll have to harmonize it in four voices, or rather add the missing three voices: the tenor, alto, and soprano above that bass line, bearing in mind all of the different voice leading principles we've looked at previously.
5.74: So that's a pretty big topic. We're going to leave it there for now in terms of voice leading, and I'm happy to take any questions.
5.75: As someone trains himself to become more sensitive to nuances in music so that he can understand it better, does this heightened sensitivity also translate into his persona in usual life?
5.76: That's where art is extraordinarily interesting, because what happens is you develop your senses to a very, very high degree of sensitivity. You become hyper-aware of phenomena such as the joining of two chords together. Then that does spill out into everyday life as well.
5.77: There is a Canadian composer called Murray Schafer, S-C-H-A-F-E-R, for example, who was very active in the 1970s and 80s in Canada, who pioneered the concept of the soundscape, which was developing an intense awareness of all the sounds that are going on around you at all times and how that affects you psychologically and how that affects you also physiologically and thinking about what our actual sonic environment is like. To a large degree, that also comes from people like John Cage. But to a large degree, that's a result of this sensitivity brought to bear upon the acoustic phenomenon. You start to notice things.
5.78: It completely conditions you. I think it's so useful, it's so enriching, it's so fascinating to concentrate on these phenomena. See what your senses are able to distinguish. Find out what the threshold, the perceptual threshold is. What can you hear? How far can you push that? Then see what happens to the rest of your life as well. You become much more attentive. Lecture 6: Structure in Music At a glance — Structure in music.
6.1: We've been looking at the way we can create a palpable sense of movement using the progression of tones, voices, voice leading, harmony—the ways that this creates either a sense of stasis or movement. We talked about the technical definition of dissonance, both its acoustic reality and also its more aesthetic or cultural dimension.
6.2: What I want to do in this lecture is talk now a little bit more about other ways of creating a sense of movement in music. What we're going to do here is to start with the very small and zoom out to the very large. We're going to look initially at questions of duration, and then we're going to look at musical forms.
6.3: In one of my earlier lectures in this series, we looked at rhythm. We looked at the rhythmic values, how they're notated, how we start with a large unit and divide it by halves successively. We also looked at different ways of putting rhythms together, how you can use time signatures to create a sense of pulse and a pattern against which a performer or a composer can push and create interesting rhythmic sensations.
6.4: But we also have to look at duration as a phenomenon in a little bit more detail. For this, we're going to look at both pulsed and unpulsed rhythms, what that means technically, and we're also going to look at how you can use that simplest of devices, which every musician has, a metronome, in order to practice different rhythmic patterns and also to understand the way subdivisions work. We're going to start with the very small, and then we're going to look at musical forms, which is the largest scale on which we can imagine phenomena of movement and of change.
6.5: This is also a very important thing to come to grips with if you're studying music theory because you need to understand formal articulation in a piece of music. When you understand that, when you understand that forms in music aren't just there in order to give you some abstract, idealized pattern that you have to follow, but you can think of them as an eternal push and pull, an eternal subtle balance between repetition, transformation, and contrast, all of which are necessary in order to, again, create a sense of movement in a piece of music.
6.6: Let's start with duration. I want to start by talking about the distinction between pulsed sounds, sounds that can be related to an underlying pulse grid— if you're working on a digital audio workstation, then you'll be accustomed to this concept because those platforms, whether it's Pro Tools or Cubase or whatever you're using, the rhythms are quantized, which means they're expressed in terms of milliseconds.
6.7: What you can do, of course, with those programs, which are pretty incredible, is you can make it so that the pulses in a rhythm are exactly equidistant to each other in terms of milliseconds. You can have this absolute precision. You can have a pulse grid, and if your drummer is slightly out of time, then some producers will go in, cut every little individual beat apart from the others and make sure they line up with the grid, which I don't recommend you do because it really kills the rhythm of the music, but that's a technological possibility we have now.
6.8: You can think of pulse as being something regular and iterative. You can think of unpulsed sounds, the sounds that we do not hear in relationship to a grid. Now, this brings us to a perceptual limit case, which is that we're able as humans to distinguish between values that are short but that are slightly different from each other. As the pulses get longer, as the ratios get more complex—and this relates to the acoustic phenomenon we were talking about earlier—it gets almost impossible, and in some cases, literally impossible, to distinguish between two long, but very similar, but not identical durations.
6.9: Let me demonstrate what I mean. If I play you a pulse like this [snaps a short rhythmic pulse], that gives me a simple periodicity. Imagine I play or snap out a pulse like that, and then the second pulse is a little bit longer than the first. I'm going to do this [snaps a longer pulse]. Now, anyone can easily tell that the second pulse is longer.
6.10: You can try this as an experiment and see what the threshold is. If I tap out a sound that's one second long and then one that's two seconds long, that's pretty easy. If I do one that's one second long and then another one that's three seconds long, even easier. You can try these different ratios. How about 2:3? Can you still tell? As you get into longer and more complex ratios, let's say 9:10 [sustains note for 9 seconds]— approximately 9 seconds; it's probably a bit fast. In 10 seconds [sustains note for 10 seconds], it's very difficult to tell the difference.
6.11: That's when we're no longer dealing with rhythm, at that point. We're dealing with durations. We don't hear them in relationship to any audible pattern or ratio to each other. It's too complex. Duration can take many different forms in written music. There are some notations that you'll see where the duration is not explicitly given. We're going to look at a few of those and see what they look like.
6.12: If we stick with the conventional rhythmic values that we've looked at already: a quarter note, a half note, a whole note, and so on. Then, once again, we're in the realm of rational durations, but that doesn't tell me what the actual speed is or what the actual length of time that I have to spend on each note is. In order to know that, I need to have a tempo.
6.13: A tempo is expressed in terms of the number of beats per minute or BPM. A tempo marking looks like this. Here at the top of this staff, you see the notation quarter note or crotchet equals 60. That means that in one minute, I'm going to have 60 pulses. In other words, each pulse is going to last for one second. That's a very useful tool for a musician because it allows you to do, among other things, a quick calculation of how long a piece is going to be. You look at the number of beats per minute, you count the number of beats, and you can estimate that this piece is going to be approximately two or approximately three minutes long.
6.14: The other thing is it gives performers and musicians an exact reference point so that the composer can say, "I want this piece to be played at this metronomic speed: 60 beats per minute." Any performer who plays the score can pick up a metronome and find that speed without any difficulty.
6.15: The other advantage of it is it allows us to think in terms of what is actually possible to play at a certain speed on a given instrument. Because I can turn on a metronome, I can check for myself if a given figuration or a given rhythmic value is far too fast to be played. That's also a very important thing for composers or anybody dealing with a performance situation to understand is you want to know what the pulse speed is, and then from there, you can work out what is the range of figures that are possible in that tempo.
6.16: If my tempo is quarter equals 60, which is approximately like this [demonstrates tempo at quarter note equals 60 bpm], then I can subdivide that pulse in all kinds of different ways. I can go [demonstrates subdivision into eighth notes at 60 bpm] in eighth notes. I can divide it into 16th notes [demonstrates subdivision into 16th notes at 60 bpm]. And I can divide it into irrational values like quintuplets [demonstrates subdivision into quintuplets at 60 bpm] in equal groups of five in each pulse. I can also keep going. You can divide it into thirty-second notes [demonstrates subdivision into thirty-second notes at 60 bpm].
6.17: There does come eventually a point where you reach a practical limit in terms of the figuration speed that's possible. Musicians have to understand what the limits are. You look at the piece of music and you see, "Okay, this is the smallest pulse that I have, and I have to be able to execute it in a tempo that is consistent."
6.18: That can also help you to figure out how to play a piece of music so that the pulse speed or the tempo isn't always speeding up and slowing down, unless that's a particular effect that the composer is asking for. Generally speaking, you want those things to be constantso that there's an audible relationship between the underlying pulse speed and the figurations, the different subdivisions that you hear rhythmically within that.
6.19: But not every rhythmic value, as we saw yesterday, is a rational rhythmic value. We've looked at tuplets or triplets, quintuplets, septuplets, and so on. But there are other forms of notation that you're going to encounter that break with this regularity. One of them is the whole category of ornaments.
6.20: We don't just have structured, rational rhythmic values in pieces. An easy demonstration of this is that there are a lot of pop singers who are constantly embellishing the lines that they're singing. A good example of that would be the singer Mariah Carey, who can never just sing one line where there's one note connected to another, but there always has to be a florid ornamentation in the line at all times. That's a very particular vocal technique. It's extremely old. It's more present in some than others, but it's called ornamentation.
6.21: The ornamentation breaks us out of the regularity of the pulse grid. The way to notate that is, among other things, with what are called grace notes. Grace notes are notes that are not assigned an exact rhythmic value or a proportional rhythmic value, but rather sit outside of that framework. We're going to look at what that looks like.
6.22: A grace note is a smaller note head like this, with the stem going up and a little slash through it—you can see that notation there. The grace note typically precedes the main beat; it's played before it. Often, grace notes are connected to the main note by a little slur or a little tie like that. The grace note doesn't have a definite rhythmic value. It's not counted towards the 4/4. Even though this grace note is, at least on paper, it looks like an eighth note with a slash through, it is not counted as an eighth note.
6.23: You could have a figure like this, for example. Now I've got a very simple rhythm in 4/4, which, if I were to subtract the grace notes, I would have this [plays four equal quarter notes], just a very simple succession of four equal pulses. That gives me a periodicity— these are pulsed as opposed to unpulsed sounds.
6.24: Now, I can make that subtly ornamented, let's say—this is a very basic form of ornamentation—by having a grace note precede each pulse [plays four equal quarter notes with preceding grace notes]. That little ornamentation adds a supplementary degree of rhythmic interest and also melodic interest, since it consists of two different tones, the B and the C.
6.25: Depending on the style of music and the tempo, the grace note might be articulated; it might be played in very different ways. If you're in a slow tempo, it might sound like this [plays slow ornamental grace notes]. It might even be slower than that. What you're doing there is you're taking a main note and embellishing it. If the tempo is very fast, then you might have something where you almost can't quite distinguish the two notes [plays fast ornamental grace notes], where they almost sound like they're being played simultaneously.
6.26: Grace notes and ornaments, generally, have a very, very broad range of applications in virtually every musical style you can think of. But you can go farther than that. Now, I used the term melisma earlier to describe vocal flourishes. So that if you don't want to sing something straightforward and banal like this [plays C, D, E, D, C], you might want to ornament it using runs of grace notes that might look something like this [plays ornamented C, D, E, D, C], for example.
6.27: That's not a perfect demonstration of what I'm talking about, but it at least gives you the idea that there is a distinction between what you might call a structural level of a melody, which is just the basic tones, the basic movement, if you like, the basic direction of the line, and then the capacity to add little ornamental figures that make the connection between tones a little bit more fluid.
6.28: The way this might be notated, you could have groups of grace notes connected by a beam with a little slash, and that would sound like this. So first, without the ornamentation [plays C, E, E, C]. And now with [plays ornamented C, E, E, C]. One more time [plays ornamented C, E, E, C].
6.29: Now we're again in a phenomenon where we're not thinking in terms of pulse exactly, but rather of something much more fluid. We still know that there's a pulse there, but we're able to break the regularity of that pulse using grace notes, using ornamentation. If the music gets extraordinarily embellished with these grace notes, you can end up in a situation where the pulse essentially disappears. You don't really hear it anymore. You can end up with something that sounds improvisatory and completely free [plays highly ornamented passage] and so on and so forth. In other words, you can get very, very, very far from any regularity of pulse.
6.30: This concept of push and pull, of polarities, and of a balance between two opposing forces is absolutely central to music. We looked at, in harmony, the fact that you can have consonances and dissonances, and that you need both. You can't have a piece that consists of nothing but one perfect consonance after another—you could, of course, but it's not going to necessarily be very interesting.
6.31: Likewise, you might not want to have a piece that consists of completely homogenous dissonances without any flow, without any regulation of the degree of dissonance. That would result in a very gray sound where we have this impression of constant agitation, but no particular sense of direction. Likewise, in rhythm, there's a continuous push and pull between the regularity of pulse and either ornamentation or local disruptions of the regularity of the pattern.
6.32: My sense, having studied music my entire life, is that these polarities are fundamental. They're fundamental to our experience of music, our perception of music, and it can take a very broad range of different forms. To a large degree, again, they're contextual. The composer will make it clear, if they're skilled, within seconds, what we're dealing with. Are we dealing with something pulsed? Are we dealing with something unpulsed? Are we dealing with music with a lot of dissonance? Are we dealing with relatively consonant music?
6.33: Once we have a context, an expressive and a musical context that's established, then you can start to play with that. You can start to move around within that space, and that creates a feeling of a trajectory. What's amazing is that it operates on every level simultaneously—it operates on the level of rhythm, on the level of texture, on the level of harmony, melody, and so on.
6.34: So we've looked at the world of the very small, of these little pulses and rapid melismas, rapid ornamentations, which there are many, many kinds. If you were to open a Baroque manual on keyboard playing, for example, you would often find page after page of detailed descriptions of ornamental figures. That's a whole science in and of itself. If you play early music, then you have to learn the whole repertoire of these different ornamental figures, and how to apply them, how to improvise them when you're executing a piece of music.
6.35: Let's zoom out now to the largest scale. Form also gives us a notion of periodicity and a notion of ratios, let's say, between different durations, but it's on a much, much larger scale. It's on a scale that you don't apprehend consciously, but that nevertheless articulates and differentiates your experience of a piece of music.
6.36: I've already laid out in the composition course some of the basic categories of musical forms and how they operate. But I attempted to present those in a much broader manner so that a creative person can think in terms of, let's say, what do you want the trajectory of a piece of music to look like? What do you want the sensation of that trajectory to be like? Do you want it to be bumpy and unpredictable? Do you want it to be smooth and continuous? Do you want it to be highly dynamic? Do you want it to be much more meditative in nature? And so on. That's a more general or a more applied way of thinking in terms of musical forms.
6.37: But let's get specific about what those forms are in Classical, Baroque, and Romantic music and how exactly they work. Remember how we talked about binary and ternary rhythms? Those basic divisions exist in musical forms as well, on an obviously much, much larger scale. Perhaps the simplest directional musical form is binary form, that is to say, an AB form. We're going to look at what that consists of exactly.
6.38: Binary form, again, is the absolute simplest way that you can create this sense of a push and pull between the same and the different, between something continuing and something changing. Stasis and contrast. So ABA forms in classical music look like this— sorry, AB forms in classical music look like this.
6.39: We talked about the fact that harmony allows us to differentiate between a stable place and a secondary place that is less stable towards which we move. You can have a meaningful sense of harmonic motion using the opposition: tonic and dominant. That is one of the fundamental polarities of classical music: tonic-dominant opposition. When you have that as a central feature of your harmonic language, it inherently creates a strong sense of teleology because you can have a movement towards a place or away from where you started, and then you can move back towards it.
6.40: What gives the classical forms their intense dynamism, their sense of forward motion, is the fact that you start on the tonic—you have all sorts of adventures, you modulate, you go towards different keys, you visit different scale degrees— but there's a magnetic attraction back to your starting place. That's why, again, if you're in C major or you're in D major, that means that the action, so to speak, begins and ends on that tone. It's like a magnetic pull towards which everything is attracted, or you might be repelled away from it for a time.
6.41: That trajectory can be very, very, very long-reaching. It can be extended as long as you want, as long as your ability to imagine a complicated trajectory can be stretched. But in order to have that dynamism, that sense of forward motion, that sense of directed motion, then again, there needs to be strong magnetic poles, as it were, a strong sense of opposition between these scale degrees.
6.42: In the Western tradition, that has coalesced around the tonic-dominant opposition. Now, if you look at really early music, early medieval music, for example, that opposition isn't there. It starts to coalesce towards the end of the Renaissance and becomes much stronger in the Baroque era. In a lot of more recent music, if you look at some jazz, even some popular music, that polarity is severely weakened. You can think of this not as a heaven-sent rule, but rather as a cultural construction that mirrors the dynamism of the culture that produced it.
6.43: So this tonic-dominant opposition gives us, in an exploded form, the basic outline of an ABA or an AB form in a piece of music. That looks like this. Again, for the sake of simplicity, we're going to argue that we are in C major, once again. We're going to start by establishing the tonic, and then we're going to gradually move towards the dominant. Once we've done that, we will have made a move from I to V; we will have modulated. We're no longer in C, but we've moved towards G—so I to V, and we'll call that our A section.
6.44: Now, you'll notice that at the end of my A section, there's a little repeat bar line, the double bar line with the two dots, which indicates to the performer that you have to start over and repeat the whole section again. We're going to move to I to V, and we're going to jump back to the beginning and do the whole thing a second time.
6.45: Then, once we've done it a second time and we're on V, we need to round out the form by proceeding to a B section. The B section moves from V back to I. It's difficult to come up with anything simpler than that, but there are tens of thousands of Baroque pieces that follow that exact, precise pattern over and over and over again. You see it today still— hundreds of years later, we still have countless pieces that are built upon this basic pattern.
6.46: If I were to improvise some simple little phrase, I could show you what that sounds like [plays A section, I to V]. Now, I've moved from I to V. I've ended here. I've made that little trajectory. Now, what I have to do is I have to start on V again, or rather keep going [plays B section, V to I]. Now, this is not a great piece. The point is to show you what that trajectory sounds like. Move away from where you started, move back again.
6.47: Okay. Now, that's a very, very rudimentary form, a very effective one. The contrast there is not necessarily one of melody or texture; the contrast is simply a dramatization of the movement towards this other place. That's a binary form, a simple binary form with a repeated A section and a repeated B section.
6.48: Now we come to ternary forms. Ternary forms are slightly more complicated. In a ternary form, we might have an A section, a contrasting B section, and then a return to C at the end—sorry, a return to A at the end. In terms of musical analysis, typically a return of a section that we've heard previously is demarcated with a little asterisk. So we have AB, and then the second occurrence of A at the end. That's a nice little symmetrical form. It allows you a few more expressive possibilities.
6.49: The B section in an ABA form takes the form of a little contrasting episode. Of course, the composer can decide exactly what form that contrast takes. The contrast can be on the level of harmony. You might start in C, and then maybe you move to the parallel minor of C, which is C minor—we have a contrast there in terms of the harmony; we move from major to minor. Then we go back to the A section at the end, and we return back to C.
6.50: Very often in ABA forms, the "reprise" or the repeat of A at the end is slightly varied; it's not identical to the initial appearance. That gives you, again, this very nice little balance between something that's the same, something that holds the form together, and something that provides variety and a sense of change, and you need that balance.
6.51: Let's see if I can quickly improvise a little demonstration of that idea [plays phrase in ABA form]. I've moved from C major [plays C major chord] to C minor [plays C minor chord]. Then all I have to do is repeat my initial idea, and then I've created a little symmetrical ABA form. The level of contrast there is not very great because I've mainly just moved from major to minor. But of course, you can also have any degree of contrast you want. In principle, the B section in an ABA form can be different in every respect from the A section. It could be different in terms of tempo, in terms of key, in terms of rhythmic figures, in terms of the texture, melody, and so on. Everything could be very different.
6.52: So that's a very simple example that gives you a tiny little trajectory, A to B and back again, or A to B. Now, what that gives us is the embryo of some of the more sophisticated classical forms. We'll start with one of the simpler ones, which is the rondo. The rondo in itself is a classical form, but it's derived from much earlier forms. It's derived from old poetic forms, and it's also derived from a form called the ritornello, which is very widespread in the Baroque.
6.53: What all these forms have in common is a continuous alternation of refrains and episodes—refrains being the fixed element and episodes being the contrasting element. In its simplest form, rondo looks like this: ABACA, and so on. You can continue that series as many times as you want. You can have any number of episodes. You could go ABACADAEA, et cetera, the idea being that in between each repetition of A, there's a little contrasting episode.
6.54: You can think of that as an expansion of the ABA principle into a longer series of contrasting episodes. That's the rondo. But in its essence, what that really is is a circular form in which you can keep returning to a central idea again and again and again. To a degree, that simple alternation between refrains and episodes, again, is the skeleton; it's the embryonic skeleton of the contemporary pop song with its verses and choruses.
6.55: We looked at ABA forms—those are also known in the Germanic tradition as Lied forms, L-I-E-D, Lied, or the plural form Lieder, being German art song. German art songs, as practiced by Hugo Wolf, Franz Schubert or Schumann, many composers who wrote songs in that tradition, very often are patterned in that ABA form. You might think of them as formal archetypes that can take a lot of different forms.
6.56: Now, eventually, those binary and ternary forms in the Classical era, animated by the intense teleology, the tendency to move away from the tonic towards the dominant, became expanded into a much more complex form called sonata form. You have to think of sonata form again, not as something that just appeared out of the blue, but as an extension of this principle, and as something that is almost an inevitable consequence of setting up your musical system in terms of a fundamental polarity or a fundamental opposition between tonic and dominant.
6.57: All of these forms are effectively ways to play out and dramatize that opposition. Again, you're not thinking of that consciously when you're listening to these pieces, but nevertheless, it's orienting and forming your experience of the work. Let's look at how sonata forms operate.
6.58: First, just a couple of words about where you're likely to find sonata forms. In the Classical era, the first movement of a symphony, of a string quartet, of a piano sonata, is very often written in what's called a sonata-allegro form. This is a dialectical form in which you have different contrasting ideas that are initially presented as a simple opposition and that are later brought into dialogue with each other, and eventually, you end up with a synthesis.
6.59: If that idea sounds familiar, it's because it's a very ancient idea. As I've mentioned previously—I'm going to restate it here because it's such an important point— that is the dialectical principle; that is the Socratic ideal of a discussion between two people with opposing viewpoints. Person A thinks one thing. Person B has a different point of view. They have a discussion. They hash it out. Person A moves a little bit towards the position of person B and vice versa. Ideally, in an ideal scenario, you end up with a synthesis of the best features of both arguments.
6.60: Now, that's an Enlightenment idea also. It ties in with the search for rationality, order, and logic. You present this again, initially as an opposition. Then you combine the ideas, you fragment them, and you put them into a dialectical opposition, and a synthesis arises out of that. Then you restate the ideas at the end of the piece again, but within a unified framework this time.
6.61: I'll show you how that works, how that plays out in terms of an actual piece. In a sonata form, you may begin with a first theme. The first theme is typically presented or exposed on the tonic. Then you have a little transition— the transition allows you to move, usually towards the dominant, not always, but very often. Then there's a little double bar line, and you repeat that, and that's called the exposition—the exposition allows you to lay out the basic thematic materials and the essential harmonic trajectory of the piece. There's your exposition.
6.62: Once you arrive at the dominant, typically, although not always— we're talking about idealized, almost platonic forms here. In reality, virtually every sonata form ever written deviates from this to some extent. It's very rare that you'll find a piece that just follows this as though it were a recipe, but look at this as an idealized form. The first theme: transition, move towards the dominant. Then you have a second theme, a contrasting theme, one that has a different character from the first one. The first theme in a stereotypical idealized sonata form might have, for example, an assertive character. The second theme might be more ornamented. It might be more introverted, it might have a very different form of expression.
6.63: For example, if I wanted to improvise a first theme, maybe I'm in F major this time [improvises the first theme]. That might be my opening theme. Now, it's got that very articulated march-like rhythm. It's very simple. I might move towards the dominant, end up on C [plays C major chord], and once I'm on C, I might have something very, very different [improvises the second theme]. Something like that.
6.64: Again, take all of this with a grain of salt. This is a demonstration of the principle. In reality, you're going to find many exceptions. For example, if you look at the music of Haydn, you'll find that he often uses only one theme—he states a theme, moves towards the dominant, and states the same theme again. If you look at Mozart, you'll find that there's a profusion of different melodic ideas— there's a first theme group where he might lay out three or four themes, each of which might be loosely interrelated, or they might be fairly different from each other, and then he moves to the dominant.
6.65: So in reality, composers, of course, will take this basic framework and treat it any number of ways. But this is the basic shape of it. The fundamental concept is a dialectical one. Once we've been through the exposition, we've had the A-theme, we've transitioned towards the B-theme or towards the dominant. Then we have a middle section, and this middle section is usually called the development.
6.66: Why do we call it development? The German term is Durchführung, which means to lead through, a little bit of a different concept. Effectively, what it means is you create a trajectory. You create a harmonic trajectory that takes us on a journey away from where we started towards somewhere else. You might modulate to multiple different keys. But the main thing to retain from this is not so much the modulations and the different keys that you pass through, but the idea of instability, of getting far from your point departure.
6.67: During the development, all sorts of things are going to happen to these materials. They're going to be fragmented, they're going to be superimposed, they're going to be played in different combinations, and then you'll have little episodes and little transitions and various things that happen. That part of the piece is quite free. The composer can give full rein to their imagination and hit you with one surprise after another. Remember, these forms are intensely dynamic, they're very full of contrast, and they're always moving.
6.68: Once we've had our development section, which is not repeated, unlike the exposition, then typically that will lead us back to the recapitulation. The recapitulation is a restatement of the materials that we heard in the exposition, but with one major difference—remember how we said that the exposition starts on the tonic, moves towards the dominant? So we've got a movement away from our point of departure. Then we have this whole adventure that happens in the development. In the recapitulation, we present the same thematic materials as we heard in the exposition, but without modulating, without transitioning to the dominant.
6.69: So these ideas that were initially pitted against each other, posed with their contrasting qualities clearly laid out, are synthesized into something unified. And so then we have our first theme. Usually, we keep the idea of the transition, except that the transition just leads us back to where we started again. We're not actually moving to the dominant, but we stay on the tonic, and then we hear the second theme again, and without moving to V. So these oppositions, which create dynamism, which create movement, are reconciled and synthesized at the end of the piece.
6.70: I find it so phenomenally interesting that that basic principle became the central motor of the high classical style. It's a very narrative idea; it maps onto stories. It's simple, simple, archetypal story-like forms, but expressed entirely through sounds, entirely through tones and rhythms. It's, in a sense, the most abstract possible embodiment of that principle of goal-directed motion, opposition, contrast, synthesis, all within this form.
6.71: So that's a brief introduction to some of the basic categories of classical forms that you'll likely encounter. In short forms, for example, in Baroque or Classical dance suites, what you'll have is a succession of pieces, each of which is oriented around a particular dance rhythm. You might have a bourrée, and then a gigue, and then an allemande, or there are all kinds of dances you see in the Baroque: minuets and so on, sarabandes. You might have five or six of those pieces strung together in what's called a suite.
6.72: The dance suite is, again, one of the most typical and one of the most commonly found ways of articulating a piece in the Baroque. Dance suites tend to be made up of short, little movements that contrast with one another. Within those movements, you're likely to see lots of binary and ternary forms, a very simple form.
6.73: Then, as we move into the Classical era, the narrative ideas, which are becoming more and more popular and more present through the genres such as opera, start to infiltrate instrumental music and animate it—again, always through a form of sublimation. There's no literal movement; you're not literally dancing when you listen to it. You're not literally following a story. Those concepts, those patterns of movement, are sublimated into pure sound.
6.74: The next time you're listening to a piece of music, no matter what the genre is, no matter what the era is that it comes from—if it was written yesterday, if it was written 600 years ago— try to think about it in terms of the formal articulation, in other words, the division into parts, where you can clearly hear a section coming to an end, or you can clearly hear a contrast between one material and another, between one form of rhythmic movement and another, one theme and another, and you can start to understand the formal articulation of a piece.
6.75: Just as how our limbs and fingers are articulated—we have joints—it's the same in musical forms as well. That, of course, gives us flexibility and movement and possibilities for contrast. All of these things have a theoretical basis. But what you want to do is to link up your ears, your perceptions, with these different concepts so that you understand them, not just in an abstract sense, not just in an intellectual sense, but you can relate them to your perception.
6.76: That was our journey from the world of the extremely small, from very tiny little iterative pulses all the way up to large-scale forms, sonata forms that can take 30 minutes or longer to play out. We're going to stop there for now. I'm happy to address any questions you may have. Yes.
6.77: Hello. Music has always been a profoundly human experience. Now, during this class, you've broken it down to almost a science, almost mathematical formulaic. I was wondering: in the age of AI, if you feed it all of these principles and patterns, will AI be able to replace the human creator of music, to provide the same experience to listeners as previous composers? Or in your opinion, is there something profoundly human about music that cannot be artificially created, and what would that be?
6.78: Well, here's one simple distinction: humans have a physical body, and machines do not. So that's, I think, an insoluble technical problem. If you're going to try to have machines duplicate some aspect of human art. All of these things that I've been describing, these different forms of movement in music, can be embodied kinetically in terms of dance, and they can also be sublimated. But I think for these concepts to make sense, for them to affect us, then you have to imagine it on some level in terms of movement.
6.79: This might be the limits of my own imagination, my inability to imagine what lies over the horizon, because things are moving quickly. It's anybody's guess what things will look like in five years, let alone 10 years or 20 years from now. Who knows? But from my present-day vantage point, I have trouble understanding how somethingdisembodied can replicate a phenomenon that is an embodied one. That's the first thing.
6.80: I personally am not particularly concerned about the advent of AI as it pertains to creative endeavors. The other reason for that is that music isn't a thing that you go and buy. It's not a commodity. It's something that you do. It's a process. That's a very intensely personal thing. Each of us has a personal relationship to the music that we're interested in, an autobiographical relationship to it that can't be duplicated any other way.
6.81: On top of that, if you have any engagement with music, either as a listener or as somebody who performs or composes, you'll know that it's a process, and there's no goal at the end of that process; it's something that is continuous and ongoing. That's why you can read interviews with very old composers who will tell you that they get the sense that they're just starting to figure out what music's about. There are so many artists where they say exactly that at the end of their life, that "I would need four more lifetimes, I need five more lifetimes." There's so much more to explore. It never stops. There's no end to that.
6.82: The other thing is—and I think this is very interesting—what AI is going to reveal to us is that some of the things that we think are uniquely the result of our particular form of intelligence are actually maybe not ultimately all that distinctive or personal. Those are going to be the things that are very easy to model. Something that we might imagine as being a unique expression of our subjectivity might turn out, in fact, to be very easy to replicate because it's actually less complex than we thought. Other things, I believe, are going to be very difficult and perhaps impossible to model in that way.
6.83: What might happen—this is a hypothetical—what might happen is it might bring us closer into contact with the things that are uniquely ours, that only humans can do. We'll see. It'll certainly be disruptive, but probably not in the ways we imagine.
6.84: You talked about the structures and that they repeat: ABA, and so on. Is this the same for every type of music, or do the structures tend to work better for a certain type of music, and for others, a different structure works better?
6.85: Right. The forms that I've just shown you are forms that are prevalent in the high classical style. If you think about 10,000 years of human music making, the high classical style is one step along that development, and it was a fairly short-lived one, actually. That style brings you, roughly speaking, from the end of the 18th century to maybe the beginning of the 20th century, something like that. So it's not a very big span.
6.86: As it happens, there were tens of thousands of symphonies and sonatas and concertos and suites and so on that were written during that period. There's an immense body of work, most of which is forgotten, some of which we've retained and have entered into what we call a repertoire, where orchestras and chamber ensembles and soloists have a certain— what would you say—selection of pieces that have, for one reason or another, survived to the present day and are still being played.
6.87: Sometimes that selection process is profoundly unjust. There are, no doubt, countless very interesting pieces languishing in libraries that are no longer played. But nevertheless, that's a process that is inevitable because you can't, as a culture, retain everything you produce. This particular form of dynamism of teleology that you see in the classical forms, as I tried to lay out in my lecture, is a consequence of the polarity, the opposition between tonic and dominant. And not every musical culture has that as a central feature of their music.
6.88: For example, if your music is highly predicated on rhythm and minimally involved with pitch, then you're going to see very, very different musical forms, different musical phenomena coming out of that. Likewise, if your music is not particularly oriented towards harmony, if you have a virtuosity of melodic elaboration, and that's the focus, then you're likely to see much less dynamic forms. Or you might see forms that heavily rely on external factors, such as the music being embedded in a social ritual of some kind. That's a little bit different.
6.89: I think one of the particularities of the classical style is that those ritualistic dimensions, the dance dimension, let's say, are all sublimated. There is a ritual involved in putting on a suit or whatever you do, going to a concert, sitting there and listening for 2 hours, and then going home—I suppose that's a form of a social ritual, but it's not the same thing.
6.90: So, depending on the broader culture, the role of music within that culture, whether or not it's embedded within some form of ritual, it might have a more or less greater degree of abstraction to it. Some of the forces that animate music might be more abstracted or sublimated as opposed to physically embodied. So no, there's a very broad range. These are forms, again, that find their expression most commonly and are most strongly associated with the European classical tradition. But I believe that they have aspects to them that are archetypal and that stem from things from the ancient world that have persisted.
6.91: But again, I keep coming back to this point: it's really a conversation between irreducible archetypes—God knows how old those are—and the aleatoric dimension of the evolution of our culture, which has all kinds of things about it that are over- determined or very complex and impossible to predict, and that change over time.
6.92: You were mentioning the polarity between the tonic and the fifth. I think it was medieval music that you were saying wasn't as reliant on that polarity. I was curious about what they were using instead, or maybe even a musical example of what that would sound like.
6.93: Okay. We looked yesterday at the phenomenon of the leading tone, remember? How the leading tone is immediately below the tonic? [plays B, C] The leading tone, again, gives you that sense of movement, and it stems, at least in part, from the V–I progression. So if you have that leading tone as a central feature of your scale, then it's going to have that strong inclination towards movement and resolution.
6.94: We looked at how the relative minor [plays A minor chord], if you do nothing to alter the scale and present it as a natural minor scale [plays natural A minor scale], it doesn't have a semitone below the tonic; it has a whole step. That little difference [plays G, A] changes everything. There's much less of a sense of tension there or movement.
6.95: That's why you have this variant of the minor scale—there are two variants, one of which is [plays melodic A minor scale] you raise the sixth and the seventh degrees in order to have that semitone below the tonic. Or [plays harmonic A minor scale] you might only raise the seventh degree.
6.96: Medieval music has a broader range of different scales or modes that it uses. Today, we think in terms of the minor or the major scales, but in medieval music, there were at least six different modes that were used, each of which had a different composition of intervals. Some of them have a leading tone, and some of them don't, but it's not predicated on that opposition. You might have a mode that sounds like this [plays D Dorian mode], or one that sounds like this [plays A Mixolydian mode]. There are many, many different examples, but we don't have that distillation into major and minor modes.
6.97: I would have to play you some examples of early motets, like 15th-century music, to illustrate the concept. But I might refer you to the History of Western Music course in which I do that, and you can hear the difference. The music is much less directional, and it has to do fundamentally with the use of different modes and with that fundamental lack of opposition. Lecture 7: Musical Exercises At a glance — Musical exercises bridging theory and practice.
7.1: Now we're going to attempt to bridge the theoretical concepts that we've been looking at and the world of actual practice of musical performance and practical skills. We've been taking a tour through concepts such as motion as expressed in music, the different ways that you can do that. We've looked at all these different parameters of how you can do that in melody, how you can do it in harmony, how you can do it rhythmically, and also how you can differentiate and articulate time, both on the micro level with individual short pulsations, and also on the macro level with musical forms that allow us to have this wonderful dialectic between the same and the different.
7.2: We mentioned at the outset of these lectures that one of the peculiar aspects of music theory, as it's conventionally taught, is that it pertains to everything except for playing and listening to music. It's an abstract set of ideas that we're learning: how these systems work together, how the notation works, and so on.
7.3: But remember, I said that in different countries, the body of materials that's covered under music theory is constituted somewhat differently. We talked about the fact that music theory, as I'm describing it, is somewhat of an Anglo-Saxon concept, which also has a certain existence in the German system. The French and Italian systems are very different. They're much more focused on solfège and écriture or music writing, which is, again, they cover some of the same technical aspects, but in a more practical application.
7.4: What we're going to do today is we're going to look at some simple techniques that anybody who is interested in music, wants to perform music, wants to learn about it, can try out to sharpen their skills. A lot of what we're going to cover basically falls under ear training. But I don't particularly like the term ear training because it sounds fairly rebarbative. It's not necessarily something that you would enjoy doing, or at least not from the term itself.
7.5: What we're going to look at—these are really elementary skills that can be not only beneficial, but are necessary for musicians. In a sense, it doesn't really matter if you're working in commercial music, popular music, the fine art musical tradition, or something else. These skills are, I think, fairly universal.
7.6: Now, again, this is where questions of individual aptitude for music come into the equation. I believe anybody can improve on these exercises that we're going to look at. It's true that some people will pick them up more easily than others. Don't let that stop you. If you're finding this difficult or if it's taking longer to get into it, I've worked with so many students over the decades, I can say with 100% confidence that absolutely anybody can improve their skills in these areas. It might take a little longer; it might be a little bit more painful for some than for others. Ultimately, that doesn't matter. What matters is your capacity to work on these things and make measurable progress.
7.7: What this does is it covers all the basic aspects of musicianship that can make you a flexible and competent musician. Of course, as with anything, you can take this as far as you want to, or you can learn the basic skills, and that might be enough. It falls under a few different types of exercises, and they involve rhythmic dictation, melodic dictation, harmonic dictation, and also rhythmic clapback.
7.8: Fundamentally, what all of these different skills have to do with is developing the capacity to externalize a musical idea or to reproduce a musical idea using your voice, using your hands to clap out a rhythm, or using an instrument. So it's very, very important to develop these skills because as a musician, what you want to do is to link up your eyes, your ears, and your fingers, or your feet, or whatever you're using to play your instrument. Those three things have to work together.
7.9: Let's start with some basic rhythmic dictation. Some of these things are going to be exercises that you can do by yourself. Some of them are things that you're going to need either a book or an online tool to help you with them. Fortunately, it's now possible to go online and find all kinds of exercises like this without having to sign up or have a subscription or anything.
7.10: What you want to do is you can go on to either a website called musictheory.net, which is a fantastic resource, has all kinds of ear training exercises, and they're graduated from very simple things all the way up to much more advanced concepts. Or, alternatively, you can just practice by getting some sheet music at whatever level is appropriate for you and practicing sight-singing—this is where you're away from the instrument and you attempt to reproduce with your voice what you see on the page. All of that, of course, presupposes that you've spent the time to familiarize yourself with musical notation.
7.11: As you start doing these things, you will inevitably find that it is extraordinarily slow and painful and clumsy, and you're going to feel incompetent, just as you would feel if you were beginning to learn German and you walked into a coffee shop and tried to order a coffee—every sentence is going to have 15 mistakes in it. That's fine; that's completely what you expect. Don't expect anything higher than maybe a 15% success rate at best with some of these exercises at first. That's completely to be expected.
7.12: So let's start with rhythmic dictation. What happens in a rhythmic dictation is that a teacher or an online assistant, or whatever it might be, will set up a pulse, a regular recurring pulse, and then they'll dictate a simple rhythmic figure on top of that. Then the student has to write down the rhythm that they've just heard. This is a very simple exercise.
7.13: For example, I can just start clapping a simple 4/4 rhythm. What I'll do is say in advance what the meter is, so you know what the time signature is. I start clapping a pattern, maybe for one bar. Then, with my voice, I'm going to sing this very simple rhythm. Then the student has to write that down, using what they know about rhythmic values.
7.14: For example, I might go [claps 4/4 time signature and sings contrasting rhythm over it], something like that. Simple rhythm. Then, what you would do—I'll go back to my app here—remember, I said this is going to be in 4/4, so we're going to start by writing out our time signature. Then I have to first remember what I've heard—it's partly a mnemonic exercise because you have to be able to remember the figure that I just played. Then you think, "How would I express that in terms of musical notation?"
7.15: Now, in some instances, you'll get to hear it more than once, which is helpful because one of the hardest things at first is remembering what you've just heard and then being able to mentally convert it into rhythmic values [claps 4/4 time signature and sings contrasting rhythm over it]. Once you've done that, you might need to hear it two or three times, then you convert it into notation. It's going to look like this.
7.16: In order to do this exercise accurately, you need to be able to remember things like dotted rhythms. Remember, we spoke about how if you take any rhythmic value and add a dot to it, you increase its value by half. So a quarter note with a dot added to it is equal to three eighth notes. Then that gives you that characteristic unequal rhythm that we talked about previously. The unequal rhythm being this [sings long pulse, followed by two short pulses].
7.17: You notice how one of the pulses is longer and one of them is shorter. Over time, this will become completely instinctive, where you will hear that figure and immediately think, "Ah, yes, that's a dotted rhythm, and you know how to write it down." At first, it's a conscious intellectual effort to relate these things, but after a while, you start to absorb the patterns. They become second nature, and you don't think about them anymore.
7.18: As you go through these rhythmic dictations, you'll get into exercises that are progressively more difficult, and they might include a wider variety of rhythmic figures. For example, you might have something like this [claps 4/4 time signature and sings contrasting rhythm over it].
7.19: Now, that had a simple—you might have noticed—a simple triplet rhythm. Then you think back, "How do I write down a triplet?" And you have this. Now, the way I performed that was, I suppose, slightly ambiguous in the sense that it would have been hard to tell if the last pulse that I did with my voice lasted for two beats or one. So you could legitimately write that down as a half note at the end or as a quarter note, followed by a rest; either one would be acceptable.
7.20: So that's an example of what rhythmic clapback looks like, or rather, rhythmic dictation. You hear a pulse, you relate it to a pattern, and then you try to write down the figure. That's a very good place to begin with ear training. It's forcing you to pay close attention to what you're hearing, remember it, and reproduce it. That's an example of rhythmic dictation.
7.21: We also have melodic dictation. Melodic dictation is the same basic idea, except you also have pitch to deal with. You're going to hear a little melodic fragment, and you're going to try to remember it and write it down. In most instances, when you're doing an exercise like this, you'll get a chance to hear it at least two or three times, especially if you're beginning with this kind of exercise; it's necessary to hear it multiple times.
7.22: What you want to do is begin by focusing on the direction of the line. Even if you can't tell the exact interval, even if you can't name the notes, focus on: Is it going up or is it going down? What's the basic shape? From there, you listen again a second time, you see if what you remembered was accurate, if it really corresponds to what you heard. Then the third time, you try to work out what all the intervals are.
7.23: In other words, you start from a bird's-eye view, a broad impression of the shape of the line, and then progressively, you fill in the details. It's like starting with one of those connect-the-dots drawings where you at first just see a field of dots, and then you start to gradually fill it in. You can see a bit more detail in it.
7.24: You might have a simple line like this—usually, the teacher in that scenario would start by giving you the first pitch. Let's say that it's middle C [plays C]. If you're beginning, you're going to mostly have stepwise or conjunct melodies that have no skips or that might have only one skip in them or one leap. Let's try a little line [plays C, D, E, F, E, D, E, D, C]. Very simple. Hear it again [plays C, D, E, F, E, D, E, D, C]. Try to reproduce it. Try to sing it [sings C, D, E, F, E, D, E, D, C], hopefully better than me.
7.25: This is such a primordial skill for musicians. If you're a jazz musician, if you play the trumpet or the piano or the double bass and you're improvising, you can't play a line until you can hear it first. You have to be able to hear inwardly what you're trying to do, even if it's just a split second before you do it, but you have to be able to audiate it. You have to be able to hear it inwardly before you can reproduce it.
7.26: If you can't imagine a line, if you can't imagine what the interval sounds like, you won't be able to hit it, and that's particularly crucial on instruments where the intonation is not fixed. If you're a singer, for example, or if you play the violin, the violin has no frets. The violin just has a fingerboard, and there are various positions, of course, that you learn, but there's no fixed place to put your hand on the fingerboard. You have to be able to hear the intervals inwardly with precision before you play them. If you can't do that, your playing will be out of tune, even if you have an excellent mechanical understanding of the positions on the violin.
7.27: If you can't hear the interval, if you can't reproduce it on some level imperfectly with your voice, then it's going to be very difficult. Let's hear that little phrase again [plays and then sings C, D, E, F, E, D, E, D, C]. What you'll find is that if you can sing it back, you're much likelier to retain it; it'll be much easier to write it down.
7.28: Then we're going to go to our sheet of music paper here. Now, remember that when I started the exercise, I said what the first note would be—the first note was middle C [plays C]. That gives us a starting point. Now I can put a middle C on the treble staff. Then I can go from there, and I can think, "Okay, it goes up [sings C, D, E, F]; that's just a stepwise progression. If I just write a series of adjacent notes, then that should give me the line.
7.29: Then I have to go, "Okay, what happens next?" [sings C, D, E, F, E, D, E, D]. Okay, remember the shape? It's not that many notes, not that many distinct pitches in this line. Then the last note sounds like it's the same as the note that we started on [sings C, D, E, F, E, D, E, D, C], and then you write it down. There's our melodic dictation.
7.30: Now, again, that's an exercise that can be as simple or as difficult as you care to make it. That line that I just played is 100% conjunct. There are no leaps anywhere in that line. But if I were to play something with larger intervals or a line that was more disjunctive, then that would significantly increase the level of difficulty. That's something that you want to work towards progressively.
7.31: Another thing that can, of course, make it very difficult is if you have chromatic intervals. In other words, tones that do not belong to the natural diatonic scale, but rather chromatic tones. For example [plays C, D, E, F, F ♯, D, G, G (below), C]. That's far more difficult. But there again, what you do is you practice with your voice [sings C, D, E, F, F♯, D, G, G (below), C] until you can reproduce the sounds reasonably accurately. It might speed it up to sit at an instrument so that you can play it again and try reproducing it. That's a progressive exercise you can do. That's melodic dictation.
7.32: We've looked at rhythmic dictation, and there's also harmonic dictation. Harmonic dictation has to do with reproducing chords, either at an instrument or with your voice, or simply identifying the quality of a chord based on hearing it once or twice.
7.33: Remember that when we were looking at triads and how triads are built—these three- note chords that are built on stacked thirds—we looked at the different ways that you can alter a triad and obtain major, minor, augmented, and diminished chords. If we're going to use A flat this time as our reference point, what you want to do is to develop the capacity to recognize instinctively if what you're hearing is a major or a minor triad.
7.34: This is a little bit more tricky because it's harder to relate it to something like a shape. If I just play you an isolated chord, then you're getting into qualitative aspects of sound. There's not anything else to compare it to. You're just hearing a sound, and you have to identify it. [Plays A♭ major chord], there's my A♭ major triad. [Plays A ♭ minor chord], there's my A♭ minor triad. [Plays A♭ augmented chord], there's my augmented triad. [Plays A♭ diminished triad], and there's my diminished triad.
7.35: That's an exercise that just takes a lot of repetition and gradual familiarity with these different types of chords. You can speed things up to an extent by sitting down at a keyboard and figuring out how to form these different chords. Choose any random key on the piano—maybe it's C♯ [plays C♯]. Can you build a triad starting from that note? You think, "I need to have a major third" [plays C♯–F], and then I have to have a minor third on top [plays F–G♯]. You practice building triads like that, different types of triads. You practice playing them all throughout the range of the instrument.
7.36: You can do this on other instruments, too. It's a lot easier on a keyboard because you can actually visualize the patterns; you can see them on the keys. On an instrument like a guitar or a harp, for that matter, you can do that, too. There's a visual dimension, but it's not quite as instinctive as it is on a piano keyboard. I want to get into some example exercises for chord dictation. But I also want to look at recognition of intervals because, in a sense, this is one of the most fundamental skills.
