When we had that little melodic phrase [plays C, D, E, F, E, D, E, D, C], remember that it was all stepwise. So the range of intervals that you have to recognize in there is very, very limited.
7.37: But what you also want to do is to practice recognizing intervals, not just the size of the interval, but also, as with these triads, recognizing their quality. For example, if I play a random note on the keyboard, let's do a G [plays G], and then I play a second note after it, so I'm playing a melodic interval, then you have to try to identify what the interval is [plays G–C]. There's simply no substitute in this case for singing and playing so that your ear can become accustomed to the intervals.
7.38: One trick that works amazingly well is to associate the interval with a particular song or piece of music that's familiar to you. If there's a song that you've heard 100 times and you can effortlessly sing it, then you'll have a much easier time recognizing it when it occurs in an exercise like this. For example, one exercise that's often given is to recognize the sound of a perfect fifth [plays C–G]. Can you think of a song that starts with that interval, with that sound? Then you remember that, you file it away in your memory, and if you have to reproduce the perfect fifth, you think, "Oh, yes, that's the opening of—" whatever it might be.
7.39: With tricky augmented or chromatic intervals like this [plays G–C ♯]. That is a tritone. The tritone is a famously difficult interval to sing. It's called a tritone because it covers three whole tones [plays G, A, B, C♯], very, very tricky to reproduce with your voice [plays and sings G–C♯]. Conveniently, those are the first two notes of the theme song from The Simpsons [plays G–C♯–D]. There you go; it works every time [plays G–C ♯–D]. That's the mnemonic aid or trick you can use to remember these intervals. Then you just go through them.
7.40: We're going to look at the different intervals that you're going to need to familiarize yourself with. We're going to start on F. Starting from the beginning, we have a minor second. That's written as a lowercase m with a 2. We have a major second, so uppercase M and 2. Then we have the minor third in ascending order, major third, perfect fourth, so P4, augmented fourth, perfect fifth, and augmented fifth or minor sixth—actually, I'm going to spell that as a D♭ to make it a little simpler.
7.41: Now we have a sequence of melodic intervals that you can practice singing. [Plays and sings F–G♭]—that's the minor second. Major second [plays and sings F–G]. Minor third [plays and sings F–A♭]. Major third [plays and sings F–A]. Perfect fourth [plays and sings F–B♭]. Augmented fourth or tritone [plays and sings F–B]. Perfect fifth [plays and sings F–C]. Minor sixth [plays and sings F–D♭]. You can just drill those.
7.42: What you can do is just pick a note anywhere on the keyboard and a random interval. You say, "I'm going to start on this note, and then I have to sing a perfect fourth, an ascending perfect fourth, starting on that note." [plays and sings C ♯–F ♯]. Now, remember, intervals can go up or down. They can be ascending intervals or descending intervals. You want to make sure that you're including both in your exercise. So I could start on an A [plays A] and say, "I have to sing a descending tritone" [sings and plays A– D♯]. You have to reproduce it with your voice. Or a rising major third [sings and plays E– G♯].
7.43: If you can get to a point where you can do that effortlessly, starting from any pitch, then you'll be well on your way to developing fluency with these sorts of ear training exercises. A lot of musicians, funnily enough, never get there. They don't work on these skills very hard. That's going to make things harder and slower for you. It's not that you can't do anything in music without those skills, but it certainly makes things a lot easier.
7.44: It makes it faster. You can retain things more easily. You can reproduce things more easily. You can explain your intentions to musicians that you might be working with more easily, and so on. If you want to sit down at a keyboard and start to play or improvise, developing the capacity to externalize your idea, even if it just means hearing the next sound before you play it inwardly, then it's going to be much, much easier for you to sit down and extemporize something.
7.45: We've looked at the melodic intervals—some of them anyway, the ones that you're at least likely to encounter as you first start working on these exercises. We've looked at melodic dictation and rhythmic dictation, and we've started to talk also a little bit about chord dictation or harmonic dictation.
7.46: The exact nature of a chord dictation exercise is going to depend somewhat on the teacher and on the particular pedagogy that they're following. But very often, what you do is you start by hearing a chord—and it might be arpeggiated or played one note at a time—then you try to reproduce, you try to sing back all the tones in the chord [plays and sings F–A–C–A–F]. In other instances, the chord might be played just completely straight like this [plays F major chord]. Then you have to try to separate it out into its component tones, hear them inwardly, and then try to reproduce them with your voice [plays F major chord and sings F–A–C].
7.47: Again, you can do this exercise by yourself to an extent, by sitting at a keyboard and saying, "I'm going to start on B♭ [plays B♭]. I'm going to play a diminished triad [plays B♭–D♭–E]," and you sing it back. As I understand it, there really is no substitute for sitting and doing this until you get to a point where you can link up what you're hearing with your voice. It all goes through the voice.
7.48: Now, because of the particular nature of this exercise, because of the fact that it's partly physiological, and it's partly got to do with your perception and your ability to distinguish sounds, you're going to find that there's a practical limit to how long you can spend on these exercises. That limit is going to, of course, vary from person to person. Some people will have a higher tolerance for them. Some people will learn them more easily. Others will find it very slow going. It doesn't matter that much.
7.49: But what you want to do, ideally, is to not torture yourself to death with these exercises, because as I mentioned at the outset, they can be rebarbative and they can be tedious to work on. You want to set this up in a way where you could actually conceivably enjoy it, where you're going to stop at the point where it's going relatively well and you're not getting frustrated.
7.50: I've had students make excellent progress by working on ear training exercises 10 to 15 minutes a day. That might not sound like much, but anything that's difficult, if you're actually sitting and concentrating on it and giving it everything you have, 10 minutes is actually—you can do a lot in 10 minutes if you're really focused. But it's not a major commitment in terms of time, even though the focus and the concentration might be challenging.
7.51: What I would recommend doing is just sitting with a timer. Let's set a timer for 10 minutes, try doing some of these exercises, and see how it goes. If you're having the absolute time of your life, then you can do a bit more than 10 minutes. But if that's enough and you'd rather do something else now, you can stop. That's the deal.
7.52: What also seems to be very effective is to have multiple different working sessions over the course of the day. And they can be very short. They could even be as short as maybe five minutes. But if you do it three times, then you're starting to condition yourself through regularity and through repetition, and that can be quite powerful. So it's not the amount of time that you spend practicing; it's not the amount of time you spend sitting at the piano, croaking out these out-of-tune intervals, but rather how effectively you're working and training yourself to listen, to hear. There's an art to listening.
7.53: Remember that listening and hearing aren't the same thing. Hearing is an indifferent physiological phenomenon, like a glass falling onto the floor and shattering. It's just something that happens in the physical world—airwaves hitting your eardrum. Hearing has nothing to do with culture or understanding. Listening requires culture, intention, and understanding. What you're learning to do is to move away from passive hearing, where the vibrations are hitting your eardrum, but you're not necessarily receiving, you're not necessarily understanding, you're not differentiating, and you want to learn how to hear. That's an art, and you can spend your life on that.
7.54: Those are a few practical exercises that you can do. Again, depending on how far you want to go with them, you can get into things that are more challenging. But I want to show you another couple of exercises that you can do that will improve your fluency with reading notation. A lot of the things we've looked at so far have had to do primarily with training your ear to recognize and differentiate intervals and rhythms, and then to be able to reproduce them. Those exercises largely bypass notation; you're not necessarily needing to deal too much with the language of symbols and note heads and rhythms and so on.
7.55: With some types of exercises, however, what you want to work on is your fluency with reading sheet music and instinctively recognizing and being able to reproduce rhythms that you see on paper. That will start with a rhythmic clapback. This is where you will have a sheet of rhythmic exercises. You'll have the time signature, and you have to reproduce them: you have to clap them back or sing them back.
7.56: If you look on the board there, I've got four rhythmic exercises: one, two, three, four. In actual fact, I'm the author of these exercises, but I'm going to pretend that I didn't write them and that I have to sit down and reproduce them. The first thing to do is to check the time signature and make sure you understand the pulse groupings within that time signature. We've got an exercise in 6/8, one in 4/4, one in 3/8, and one in 3/4 —four different time signatures.
7.57: You'll remember that we talked about binary and ternary beat patterns and compound meters. Remember that 6/8, although it has six eighth notes in it, it is actually articulated into two pulse groups, each of which is subdivided into three [counts six eighth notes with emphasis on beats 1 and 4] like that. You have to have that pattern in your ear before you start working on this.
7.58: Then you're going to think, "Okay, I've got two pulses, and I can subdivide them" [counts six eighth notes with emphasis on beats 1 and 4]. If you don't do that first, if you don't know what the pulse is, and if you don't know what the order of weak and strong beats is in that meter, then you're going to have a really hard time with these exercises. So make sure that that's clear. And then you can read and start to read it at a comfortable tempo [demonstrates rhythm as written on the board], et cetera. As you get more advanced, you can, of course, get more fluent with that, and you can experiment with faster tempi.
7.59: Now, some of these exercises are relatively straightforward. Some of them are a little bit more difficult. In exercise number two, you'll notice that I've got quarter notes, eighth notes, there are some rests in there, and there's also a triplet. So that means you're going to have to switch between different pulse speeds many times over the course of this exercise. The first thing, again, remember that we're in 4/4, so we have to remember what that rhythm is like [counts 4/4 time signature]. Then we're going to start to try to reproduce the rhythm [demonstrates rhythm as written on the board].
7.60: These are not particularly easy exercises because number two contains what's called a syncopation, and a syncopation is a beat that doesn't line up with the underlying pulse grid. Another way to think of it is as an offbeat. If you're doing [demonstrates syncopation], that thing. Syncopations are a fundamental part of dance styles around the world and different popular genres as well. We might understand them instinctively without necessarily being able to reproduce them accurately. Then you just work through the exercises. Again, these can get extraordinarily difficult. You want to start with very, very simple, straightforward ones as you start getting familiar with notated rhythms.
7.61: So next, we have an exercise in 3/8. So 3/8 is a ternary rhythm, so that means we're going to have three pulses per bar, three eighth notes per bar, and I have to try to reproduce this rhythm. So choose a tempo, one that's comfortable. Think about the pulse, think about the time signature [demonstrates rhythm as written on the board]. Then you try it again if you need to. You might have to do them 10 times. You might want to slow them down if it's difficult.
7.62: As you get into particularly advanced rhythmic clapback, you'll find that there are going to be examples where the time signature changes. The whole piece isn't in 3/4 or 4/4, but the meter will change partway through the example. Number four is an instance of that. In number four, we start off in 3/4, and four bars in, it switches to 2/4, and then it switches to 3/8, and then back to 4/4 again. The challenge there is that the fundamental beat unit changes between 2/4 and 3/8, where we have to move from thinking in terms of a quarter note to thinking in terms of an eighth note pulse.
7.63: If I'm moving from 3/4 to 3/8, then I have to do [demonstrates a pattern of 3/4 followed by 3/8]; that's switching from a pattern in 3/4 to a pattern in 3/8. The exercise from beginning to end is going to sound like this [demonstrates rhythm as written on the board]. There, not only did I have to deal with triplets and rests, but I also had to deal with this shifting meter. All of it takes practice, but that's a very good method anyway for learning to read rhythmic notation and achieve fluency with it.
7.64: The next exercise, which we're not going to do just yet—we're going to do it after the interval—is in many respects the most challenging of all. But the thing is, as these exercises get more difficult, you're going to find that they stretch your musicianship and they're amazingly effective. I really recommend anybody who wants to work on their basic musicianship skills to practice all of these different exercises: externalize with your voice, sing what you hear, what you see on the page, reproduce it, tap out the rhythms through whatever means work best for you.
7.65: There are also some resources that you can use to work on these in a more concerted way. I mentioned that you can go on musictheory.net and you can find lots of examples where you can just click on something and you'll hear a chord or a short little melodic phrase or rhythm, and then you have to reproduce it or write it down.
7.66: But there are also a number of resources that can be incredibly helpful, such as sight- singing exercises that were devised by composers and teachers to try to help students achieve greater fluency. One of the best such books I've ever seen, although it's a little bit on the advanced side, is the Vocalise-Étude of the French composer, Gabriel Fauré, F-A-U-R-E.
7.67: Fauré was the director of the Paris Conservatory in the 19th century and a very influential French composer, teacher of multiple generations of major French figures, including Maurice Ravel, among others. He was an amazing composer and also a gifted pedagogue. As it happens, he was in charge, at one point, of writing little entrance exams for students who wanted to get into the singing classes. He composed a series of little pieces called vocalizes, that were wordless pieces that could be sight-read by singers with the piano accompaniment. You can get hold of a book like that.
7.68: Edition Peters in London has a beautiful edition you can buy of these pieces. You can take them home, try to bash through them at the piano or try to sing the lines and expect that the results are going to be horrible because it's difficult. That's part of the point. Then, like anything, you start at 2% proficiency, and you try to get a little bit better each time. You can look at the vocalizes of Gabriel Fauré. There are many, many, many useful books for harmonic, melodic dictation, and so on. You can take them and either listen to a CD or recording online, or there'll be a bit of music notation, and you have to practice singing it or reproducing the rhythms.
7.69: That's my introductory foray into the wonderful world of ear training. You can spend years and years on that, by the way. In some respects, your ear is never definitively formed. You can always continue to improve, no matter how experienced you are as a musician. Before we move on to the next and final lecture in this series, does anybody have any questions, concerns, or complaints about the exercises we've looked at so far?
7.70: In the cases when people would spontaneously like to engage in making a song, see what they could do, how do they know when they've done a good job at it?
7.71: You've probably seen there's a comic book in French called Astérix. There's a character in there who's a pretty terrible musician who always has a harp with him. Every time he starts playing, you see all these jagged, discordant music notes coming out of the instrument. Everyone runs for cover. So that's one way: you just check the reactions of the people in the room. Unless they're especially indulgent as a group of friends, usually you can tell if your efforts are meeting with a positive perception or not.
7.72: But more seriously, how can you tell? Well, you might not be able to tell if you haven't trained your ear. You might not be able to tell the difference very easily between an interval that's been accurately reproduced, sang, and one that's completely inaccurate. I've noticed this with people.
7.73: You can listen to ordinary people whistling or humming a song, and you can see to what extent they've managed to perfect these skills. Because a lot of people, when they're whistling or singing—I've noticed this many times—they'll just randomly modulate; they can't hold the pitch. So they'll start off in C major, singing some little tune, and then by the time they're done, they're in F ♯ major because they don't remember the tonic; they don't remember where they started from. The intervals get progressively more and more out of tune, and then they get farther away from where they started.
7.74: Other people, even some completely untrained musicians, will be exactly on pitch all the way through. It's amazing. With these sorts of things, I wonder, I think it is partly physiological. I think there are individuals who have an easier time remembering and reproducing intervals and pitches accurately than others. There's a faculty called perfect pitch that some people have—"l'oreille absolue," absolute pitch, some people call it—which is the ability to recognize a note by name simply by hearing it. You can hear a pitch and then say, "Oh, that's an A flat, that's an A, that's a G," and so on.
7.75: I'm not an expert on this topic. There's a bit of literature about it now, about what exactly that is, where that skill comes from. It might be hereditary, but it appears that you can increase the likelihood of developing perfect pitch if you start as a child at an instrument. It certainly seems to help to be in a musical environment.
7.76: I've seen claims that it's possible to acquire something like absolute pitch later in life, although very often it seems to be more of a trick than an actual instance of perfect pitch, where you can memorize a reference pitch—some people get very good at doing this—they can remember a frequency somehow and then use that as a reference point to think, "What would be a perfect fourth higher than that?" Or, "What would be a fifth lower than that?" And then they can find all the notes, which is actually a very impressive skill. It's not quite the same as absolute pitch, but it's very impressive nonetheless.
7.77: But absolute pitch can also be a detriment in some respects. So remember that before the development of—well, the widespread adoption of things like tuning forks and ease of travel amongst different parts of the world, if you were living in some village in Italy and you wanted to send a piece to another orchestra or ensemble or choir in Greece or somewhere else, that other place, even if it was just 10 miles away, their tuning standard might not be the same. There was no reliable means to establish a consistent system of pitch and tuning from one town to another, let alone from one country to another.
7.78: But now there's basically a universal standard where the pitch A is equivalent 440 cycles, and that's the case basically throughout the world, with some exceptions. There are some orchestras that tune slightly higher than that—442, sometimes 443—but you can think of that as a universal standard that's being adopted.
7.79: Different musical traditions and eras, for example, if you go back into the Baroque, the instruments were not tuned to the same pitch as the instruments of today. They were tuned almost a semitone lower, sometimes more. So the pitch has tended to rise over time. The basic reference of tuning has risen somewhat.
7.80: So if you're playing early music on period instruments, on authentic instruments from the period—imagine it's a recorder sonata or a piece for harpsichord or something— then to somebody with perfect pitch, it's going to sound wildly flat because it's at least a semitone lower than it would be if it were played on a contemporary concert grand piano. So that can be disturbing to people with absolute pitch.
7.81: They also have difficulty with intervals other than the tempered sounds of the equal- tempered scale. If they have to listen to, let's say, Bulgarian wedding music, they're going to find that disturbing because the intervals are not the same. Somebody without perfect pitch might not even notice. Lecture 8: Musical Appreciation At a glance — Musical appreciation, with a recap.
8.1: So what remains to be done? Let's recapitulate. We've looked at the notated basis for music, which has allowed musicians and performers to write their musical ideas down in a fixed form and communicate them to other people in other parts of the world. We've looked at the particular language of symbols that has allowed us, through a long process of historical refinement, to fix such nebulous things as pitches to an exact standard, to come up with a concept for notating rhythm that is accurate and precise and flexible.
8.2: We've looked at the different ways that we can impart instructions to performers as to what character they have to bring out in a piece of music, the different rhythmic figures that allow us to do that. We've examined the organization of pitches into patterns called scales and keys, key signatures. We've examined phenomena such as the circle of fifths. We've also looked at some practical exercises that will allow you to work on your musicianship to whatever level you desire. That's a grand tour through the fundamentals of music theory, both in applied and in more abstract forms.
8.3: I think what remains to be done now is to try to put those different skills together. I said at the end of the last lecture, which was focused on ear training and practical exercises, that there was another level that you could try to get to of musicianship. We looked at rhythmic dictation, rhythmic clapback, melodic dictation, harmonic dictation. We looked at all the different intervals and some ways that you can try to remember them and sing them back accurately.
8.4: What you can also do is to develop your capacity to hear more than one thing at a time. This is just one of the most amazing things about music is you can have a coherent framework that allows you to integrate the horizontal and the vertical dimensions—the harmonic and the melodic—into a unified, coherent framework.
8.5: And because of our capacity, this extraordinary technology that we've refined over centuries of writing down lines with precise pitches and rhythms, we can have this beautiful thing called polyphony, which allows us to layer multiple different voices, multiple different independent rhythms and melodies into a piece of music.
8.6: And through the miracle of things like counterpoint, which codify and, to a degree, regiment these different possibilities, we can have these extraordinary musical textures that are made up of multiple different independent parts. So the next step is to learn to deal with polyphony itself, to learn to deal with that multiplicity of more than one thing happening at the same time.
8.7: I don't know of a better way to work on that skill than to work with this book. If you've seen my other courses, you'll recognize this volume. It's always on my piano, no matter where I'm traveling. I'm also going to talk about it this weekend—I'm doing a course on Bach, where this is going to be the subject of one of the lectures.
8.8: So, what this book is—Choralgesänge—a collection of over 300 four-part chorales. The chorales of Bach are short pieces drawn from his cantatas, passions, and oratorios. They consist of Lutheran hymn songs, Protestant plainsong, in other words, that Bach has taken and to which he has added three additional voices. So remember, we talked about the four different fundamental voice types? S, A, T, B: soprano, alto, tenor, and bass. Well, that conveniently gives us a four-part harmonic texture if we have those four voices singing together.
8.9: What's ingenious about these pieces—I'll get into the musical significance of them in the Bach course, but for now, we're going to stick to a more practical orientation. What's amazing about these pieces is, first of all, the hymn melodies, the plainsong that Bach started with, were in many cases quite old, sometimes 200 years old by the time he was working on them. They were from another musical era. They don't have the same characteristics as the music of Bach's day.
8.10: Remember, we were talking about—and there's a question, actually, a very perceptive question about the difference between medieval music, Renaissance music, how it tends to be less sharply directional, less teleological in its orientation than the music of the high classical style. Well, the melodies in this book, many of them, are not exactly tonal in the way we understand it now, but rather modal. They use scales that are not exactly the same as the major and minor scales.
8.11: So they exist in another musical era. But by the time Bach was working on them, the harmony of that period had moved towards a higher degree of what you might call codification. The rules had changed somewhat. The types of harmonic progressions that you would hear were not the same as they would have been 200 years ago. There was an incompatibility, in a sense, between these older melodies and the harmonic language of Bach's day. So there's a very interesting tension in these pieces between these archaic melodies and the then relatively contemporary style within which he was harmonizing them. But we'll leave that whole question aside for now.
8.12: The thing that is incredibly useful about this book is that it gives you an inexhaustible supply of four-part writing at the absolute highest level of the art. I haven't seen four- part settings from any other composer that can equal these, and there's hundreds and hundreds of them. So this is an extraordinarily useful resource for anybody who wants to improve their musicianship.
8.13: I've made this point before, but I'm going to say it again: this can enhance your musical skills more than anything else I've personally encountered, at least within this musical tradition. So what you can do is you can get the Choralgesänge— there are multiple different editions of it—you can open them up, and if you're very advanced, you can try to sight-read them at the keyboard, although that's challenging, because you have to be able to play four different independent lines at the same time. It's very hard to do.
8.14: Or what you can do is play them just a few beats at a time, maybe just one bar. Work on it really slowly, pull it apart, look at each individual voice, try to sing it, try to play it at the keyboard, and then try to play a second voice that goes along with it, and I'll explain what I mean.
8.15: I'm going to take number 188 here from this collection, which is called "Jesu, der du meine Seele." I chose this one not at random, but because it's going to be the subject of one of my Bach lectures, so that allows me conveniently to tie it together with that. So we're going to look at the first couple of bars of this four-part setting, which you can see on the screen behind you. I'm going to point out a couple of things about how it's notated and how it's written.
8.16: Because it's a chorale, the principle is that everybody singing— soprano, alto, tenor, and bass—is singing the same words. For the most part, in a texture, that is where everybody is essentially singing the same rhythms. Now, you'll see some little passing notes, some little ornamental passages in some of the voices. So the rhythms are not exactly identical, but it's written in such a manner that you can have everybody singing the same syllables on the same beats, even if some of the notes are stretched out or prolonged with additional little passing notes.
8.17: This gives us four complete independent melodic lines that together are coherent both horizontally and vertically. So they work harmonically, and they also form coherent melodic lines. So the text for the first couple of bars here is, "Herr! ich glaube, hilf mir Schwachen." We're going to isolate those two little bars. That can be roughly translated to, "Lord, I believe. Help me in my weakness."
8.18: Let's start by pulling apart the four individual lines here. Here's the soprano [plays soprano line]. These hymn melodies would have been familiar to everybody who was a churchgoer at that time. So the exercise and the essence of Bach's artistry is that he could take these very familiar melodies and elevate them to the highest level of the art form through these harmonizations. Let's look at the alto line [plays alto line]. Okay, let's hear the tenor [plays tenor line]. And the bass [plays bass line].
8.19: Four independent lines. If we put them together [plays all vocal lines together], we get that. Part of the point of this exercise is to learn to hear that not as an undifferentiated texture, a block of sound, but as four independent voices, each with their own melodic character. Let's try that again. Here's the soprano [plays soprano line]. Here's the alto [plays alto line].
8.20: Now, what you can do is you can go through this and choose any random pair of voices. You can say, "I'm just going to isolate the soprano and the alto," or "I'm just going to isolate the altos and the tenors, or just the bass and the soprano, or the bass and the alto voices, and play them together." I'm going to take just the sopranos and the altos [plays soprano and alto lines together]. Two beautiful melodic lines. Here's the bass and the tenor [plays tenor and bass lines together]. So it's one thing if you're going to do that at the piano.
8.21: It's another thing if you have to do it with your voice. An exercise you can do is to try to sing each individual line as best as you can manage. Now, you won't be able to do them literally on pitch because you don't have a two-octave voice range or a three-octave voice range, which you would need to sing something like this, but you can transpose it up or down to the most convenient octave that fits your range, and then try your best to reproduce these lines.
8.22: Here's the soprano [plays and then sings soprano line]. Now, here's the alto [plays and then sings alto line]. I'm not doing the words. I should try. I'm going to try [sings alto line, then plays soprano and alto lines together]. Now, where it gets really tricky is, you're going to try to sing one of the lines and play another line at the same time [plays soprano line while singing alto line]. That's hard because you have to do two things at the same time, and you have to have a coherent line in both.
8.23: And then what you do is you go through all the voice pairs, right? So then you try to sing the soprano; you switch them around: sing the top and play the alto. Now, I won't be able to do that because it's out of my vocal range, but maybe if I put it down an octave [sings soprano line an octave lower and plays alto line]. It gets a little bit tricky depending on the range of your voice.
8.24: This is one of the best exercises I know to develop this skill: understanding polyphony. If you sit down and do this or try to do it, you'll find that it's dizzying. It's like a form of musical gymnastics. You can keep going where you play three of the lines at the keyboard and sing one of them, or you can even play all of them at the piano and sing one of them in unison at the same time. There's all kinds of different ways you can do it.
8.25: But you could spend your life with this book and never get to the end of it. It's pretty well inexhaustible. What you will discover as you work through it, you start getting familiar with these little pieces, is that no matter how complicated the harmony gets, no matter how ingenious these four-part settings are, the individual lines are always eminently singable. They're always perfectly conceived in terms of the human voice. And not only that, they fit under the fingers incredibly well as well.
8.26: That's one of the extraordinary things about Bach. There's an abstraction to his writing, where it survives transposition from any instrument to any other instrument, pretty much intact. You can play it on anything you want. You can sing it, you can play it on a keyboard, you can have four saxophones play it, you can have a string quartet play it, you can play it on a synthesizer—it doesn't matter; it survives. It's got this extraordinary abstraction and adaptability.
8.27: You'll also notice if you spend some time with these pieces that the individual lines are extraordinarily elegant. Let's look at the bass line for this little hymn song [plays bass line]. He truly does go the extra mile because that's a way more interesting bass line than you strictly need to have for a four-part setting of a piece of plainsong. And amazingly, pretty much every line has an equivalent degree of musical interest.
8.28: So you really can learn everything from these pieces. They're extraordinary aids for composers trying to understand polyphony, harmony, voice leading, and how to set up an interesting texture, and how to set texts. And in terms of coming to grips with music theory, well, what a lot of students do—this is pretty universally taught—is to either analyze these pieces and figure out what the chords are, assign them a function, a Roman numeral function, in keeping with what we were looking at earlier, the different scale degrees: I, II, III, IV, V, VI, VII, and how they fit into the key of the piece, that's a harmonic analysis that is widely taught.
8.29: Or you can isolate a particular line from this piece—it could be just the bass, and you ignore all the other lines, or you might just take the soprano more commonly— and then you try to write the remaining three voices. In order to do that, of course, you need to understand voice leading, which is what we talked about earlier today, the different principles involved in leading a group of different voices together with a coherent texture.
8.30: Now, the other thing that these pieces allow you to do is to come to a better understanding of cadences, which we talked about earlier. Remember, we looked at the different types of cadences and how you can have a perfect cadence, an imperfect cadence or a half-cadence, and plagal cadences, and so on.
8.31: I want you to look at this phrase, and we're going to try to determine how it ends, what type of cadence? Remember that the cadence signifies the end of a phrase; it's a form of musical punctuation [plays opening phrase]. The end of that phrase is a perfect cadence. How do I know that? Well, I can look at the bass line here—if you look at the screen behind you, on the word "Schwachen," on the end of the second bar there —"hilf mir Schwachen"—you have a bass progression from D to G [plays D–G (below)]. Because this piece is in G minor, if I have that V to I progression in the bass, D to G [plays D–G (below)], that tells me this is a perfect cadence.
8.32: It's a cadence that ends on G in a piece that is in G. Let's hear that again [replays the phrase]. Hear that more slowly right at the end [plays final cadence]. There's your perfect cadence. One more time [replays final cadence].
8.33: Let's keep going [plays next phrase]. That's a half cadence. This is a cadence from I to V [plays D–G], from D to G [plays D–G]. The first cadence, remember, gives us a perfect cadence [plays V-I cadence: D to G]. And the second cadence is a half cadence [plays I-V cadence: G to D], so a less definitive feeling of close.
8.34: And then what you do is you go through the piece, you look at all these different phrase endings, and you try to determine what cadence they are. What is the quality of this close? [plays another phrase] There's another perfect cadence [plays another phrase]. These two phrases that I've just played are very similar to the opening of the piece. They're basically variants of the opening two phrases.
8.35: In the following phrases, things get a little bit different [plays next phrase]. Now, what you might have noticed is that this phrase seems to end in F, which is a little strange because we're meant to be in G minor. But this is, again, the strange characteristic of these melodies—they wander; they're not as sharply oriented towards a tonic. They're not as sharply directional as a piece that was originally written in this era would have been, the era of Bach. Remember, these melodies are much older than that.
8.36: That means that these pieces will wander sometimes from key to key and then back again. Remember, we started here [plays phrase in G minor]. Then in this phrase [plays phrase ending in F major], we end up somewhere else. That's a perfect cadence, but it's not a perfect cadence in G; it's a perfect cadence in F. Now, let's hear the next phrase [plays phrase ending in B♭ major], perfect cadence in B♭. Now we're winding back home. This is now a half-cadence in G minor [plays phrase ending in G minor]. And the final phrase [plays final phrase ending in G major]. If you've done your ear training exercises, you've noticed that the piece doesn't end in minor; it doesn't end in G minor, but in G major.
8.37: Why is that? We started like this [plays phrase in G minor], and we end with this chord [plays G major chord]. That has a term which is a Picardy third, and what a Picardy third is, or "Tierce de Picardie," is simply the habit that composers had in the Baroque, and to a degree also in the Classical eras, of ending a piece in a minor key with a major third rather than a minor third.
8.38: The reason for this, historically, is that the minor third is a slightly more dissonant interval than the major third. Especially if you were playing in those older tuning systems before equal temperament, the minor third could be quite a chaotic interval. So, in order to end the piece with a reasonably stable sensation of close, you would end with a major third rather than a minor third.
8.39: Let's try to put this piece together, and I want you to pay attention this time, not only to this four-part texture that we've been pulling apart, but also to the qualities of the cadences and the way the piece moves around. We have a perfect cadence in G, a half- cadence in G. Then the same thing repeated. Then we move to F, we move to B ♭, then we eventually move back to G. It moves around quite a lot [plays the chorale]. And thus concludes the music theory lesson. Any questions?
8.40: So first of all, thank you for breaking down the class. It was really insightful. Now that we've learned quite a bit about music theory, I'm just curious, what's your piece of advice for someone to be able to take in all the theory while still experiencing music as an experience? Or on another note of that question, for someone who hasn't really been exposed to classical music, for example, or things like that, how would you suggest that they can learn to appreciate or experience the music properly, if that makes sense?
8.41: I don't know about properly because music is an intensely personal phenomenon, and different people have completely different relationships with this art form. So it depends. It depends on what you want that relationship to be like. But it's an interesting question because when you're learning these things, it can be dizzying, and it can take you outside of the fluency that you thought you had previously, where you would sing a melody and not be thinking about it—you're not thinking analytically in terms of intervals, in terms of cadences, in terms of phrase structure. You're just reproducing it.
8.42: The way that a native English speaker might not need to preoccupy themselves with questions of syntax and word order, you're not thinking about the parts of speech when you are having a conversation with somebody. You're not going verb, object, and so on, adjective. It's the same in music. You can learn these things—you can learn the terminology, and it will certainly help, but in the act of making a piece of music or performing it, you probably aren't thinking analytically.
8.43: If you're playing a piece for somebody, all of that falls away, sinks into the background, and you're focusing on what you're communicating, what you're trying to express to the person you're playing for. So some of this can be thought of as skills that you work on that you attempt to absorb so that they become second nature, and then you don't think about them.
8.44: You can, of course, work on them continuously. I personally start every working day by playing something at the keyboard. I do that all the time. That's like a form of warming up. It's like a form of exercise. But the idea is to not have to think about it all the time, not to be reaching for the terms, not to be thinking analytically.
8.45: The exercises that we've looked at help you to become familiar with the language of music so that you can write it down, you can communicate it, and you can read it. You can understand what you're hearing. But at a certain point, it becomes instinctive, it becomes habitual, just like learning a foreign language. The exact way that that plays out, of course, is entirely individual, but it will eventually sink into the background.
8.46: I don't really know how to formulate this question, but I noticed that different people with different personality types tend to like different types of music. Let's say people who care about a lot of abstract thinking and so on, they like abstract music. People that are a bit more, let's say, living simple lives, they also usually listen to very simple music. Is that a common thing that as your personality changes or develops, or let's say as you develop as a person, you start listening to other music, the taste of music, what sounds good and what doesn't sound good changes?
8.47: Obviously, I'm not a psychologist, so I'm not going to venture into waters that are not mine. But I can make one comment about this, which is the result of just observing my own relationship with music. I'll start there.
8.48: I did take the OCEAN test once to see what my personality was like, the Big Five personality traits. You can do these tests that will give you a score on all of those different parameters. I did that test, and one of the things that it revealed was in terms of openness, I'm way off the charts, like 99.9% or something, which I suppose wasn't surprising, but it explained one thing, which is that my relationship with music is one of continuous expansion. I'm voraciously curious about the musical phenomenon. I'm constantly hearing new things.
8.49: I'll approach any genre, any historic period, any geographic region with dispassionate interest at first, which is to say I won't go at it with any a priori judgment. I won't even be thinking about whether I like it or I don't like it. I'm not interested in that question when I first start listening. I'm just thinking, "Okay, what is this? Let's give it a listen." Then you start listening. It might take three or four times to really get a sense of what it is—still not thinking about whether I like it or not. I don't care about that question very much.
8.50: What you find is that if you're extremely high in openness, you're going to be naturally curious about lots of things, and you're going to want to continuously expand into waters that you don't already know. But obviously, statistically, not everybody is on the extreme outer edge of openness.
8.51: It also makes it so that I have a very high tolerance for innovation, novelty, exploration, and experimentation in music. I'll listen to things that 99% of the population would find unlistenable, but I'm interested in lots of things, and I have to nourish that curiosity and that desire to explore. But I recognize that on that dimension, I'm not typical. That seems to be a function of personality, at least to a certain extent.
8.52: I know people who have other personality traits, but they're not particularly high in openness. For them, it can be very, very difficult and just frankly, unappealing to sit down and listen to a bunch of things they're not familiar with, even if it's only slightly outside of what they're used to. You can push them to a degree and say, "Try this, listen to this, see what you think." Sometimes they will, but it's not really in their nature.
8.53: Also, the other thing is a lot of people have a relationship with music that seems to be —I find this very interesting—seems to be predicated on nostalgia, where a piece of music will evoke a particular time in their life. It's like, "Oh, yeah, that time I was 16. This is what I was listening to then." They find it enjoyable to go and listen to that again because it helps them to maybe relive something, a pleasant memory or a part of their life that they would like to remember.
8.54: I don't really have that relationship with music exactly, partly because I'm a professional and I'm listening to so many things all the time, but that seems to be where it's at for a lot of people, where they want to stick with things that have that biographical resonance for them, things that remind them of an experience they had or a time in their life. Then you can get stuck there.
8.55: There's guys who just listen to oldies on the radio all the time for decade after decade. They just want to hear the Eagles or whatever. I understand that. It's not my experience of it, but I think it's very easy to get caught on things that work, that you enjoy, and that you know what to expect. I would never in a million years judge that because God knows life is hard, right? You don't necessarily want to torture yourself with more unfamiliar, uncomfortable experiences than you need to.
8.56: But the corollary to that, though, is that you might also be cheating yourself of the opportunity to expand into things that might really enrich your life. So I'd always try to encourage people to get into the habit of listening to things that you're not familiar with. We all know what the gaps in our culture are, the things that we know we might find interesting, but we don't take the time. I certainly do. I've got a long list of books that I'd really like to read that I haven't.
8.57: The advantage of music is that it takes a lot less time to listen to, even a very long piece of music, than it does to read, say, a 600-page novel. The time commitment is actually not that considerable, unless you want to sit down and listen to the entire Ring cycle by Wagner, which will take you a long time. But otherwise, you can get a pretty good idea of a lot of different musical styles by sampling them; you just dip into them. You listen to one movement of a piece. You don't even listen to the whole thing. Don't listen to all four movements of a Mozart symphony. Just listen to one movement. That could take you three minutes. That's a pretty low cost of entry time-wise, and it's something that you can pretty easily fit into your life.
8.58: So to sum up the question: to a degree, it's a function of personality, definitely. Some people will naturally just be voracious listeners and always wanting to hear everything. Others might have to push a little bit in order to develop that as a habit.
8.59: I'm just thinking about the construction or composition of some of these, like the four- part harmonies, specifically, because it seems like it would just turn into this maddening Rubik's Cube of three of them working in one not. Do you have a sense of what the typical process is? Do they start with the soprano line and then the bass, I guess, would create the fundamental support for it, and then the alto and tenor would fill it in? Or is it more this intuitive process of hearing it as complete harmony altogether once you've amassed a level of experience and expertise with it? Yeah, I'm curious about the process of composing itself.
8.60: We don't know exactly how Bach did it because he was in the habit of destroying his sketches. He didn't save them. There's only a few fragmentary things here and there where there's little pencil indications on some of his ink scores. But for the most part, we have very little insights into his process of composition.
8.61: But as far as how students typically learn to do this, you break it down into steps. There's no other way to do it because it's a very complex task. The first step is to isolate the top line—you don't look at Bach's four-part setting. You separate the top line out, which is the original Lutheran hymn. Then you look at it as a phrase, and you look at the cadences. You start there. You look at the ends of the phrases.
8.62: That's easy to do because if you look at this sheet music here, at this score, you'll see that every now and then, you come to the end of a phrase, and there's a little symbol above the note—as you can see here, that little hat over the G, which is called a fermata. The fermata indicates a pause or the end of a phrase. So all the four-part chorale settings of Bach make this very clear by having a fermata at the end of the phrase where the cadences are.
8.63: So in this case here [plays opening soprano line of "Jesu, der du meine Seele"], and then there's a fermata on the last note [plays G] telling you that's the end of the phrase. If you wanted to make a four-part setting, you would first observe where the cadences are, and based on the trajectory of the line and where it seems to be going harmonically, you make a decision. Am I going to end with a half-cadence, a perfect cadence, a plagal cadence, a deceptive cadence, or something else?
8.64: Often, there aren't that many possibilities. There aren't a lot of viable possibilities for interpreting this in terms of a cadence. You can try them at the keyboard, and you'll quickly see that the perfect cadence is the one that fits. So then what you do is you start by identifying the cadences. You say, "This is going to be a perfect cadence in G, and this is going to be a half-cadence in G."
8.65: You don't write a single note. You're just identifying the cadences and the tonality, the key of the piece. You take note of any modulations where you move to a different key. You observe, "Oh, here we seem to have a perfect cadence in F. We're moving towards F there. Then we seem to be moving to B♭," and so on and so forth. So you start with a little harmonic and phrase analysis of the piece.
8.66: Then, once you've determined that, you just write the bass at the cadential points. If your line is doing this [plays opening soprano line of “Jesu, der du meine Seele”], then you just write those two bass notes that allow you to affirm what the cadence is [plays D–A, G–G], and you do that throughout the piece. So then what you've got is this little fragmentary bass that only has a couple of notes at a time.
8.67: The next step is to write a complete bass line. Based on that, what you've done is you've chosen your points of orientation. You know how the phrases end, you know what the harmonic context is, you know what key you're in, you know if it's a half cadence or a perfect cadence and so on.
8.68: Then you try to write a line that works with the soprano, observing all the principles of voice leading that we looked at earlier. So you avoid forbidden parallels, you avoid crossing voices, you try to make it so that you're mostly moving by step with some leaps to make the line interesting as necessary, but mostly in conjunct motion, and so on and so forth.
8.69: Once you've got a complete bass line that you're satisfied with, then you can start to think about the inner voices. You might begin by only harmonizing the cadences and then filling in the rest of the lines. You start by understanding the structure, the function, the harmonic function, and the phrase structure. If you don't understand that, you won't be able to write a note. You have to have a sense of what key you're in and so on.
8.70: Then, once you have a sense of that, you start dealing with, as you said, the whole Rubik's Cube of fitting the voices together. At first, it's extraordinarily difficult because at any given juncture, there are 30 possibilities. But what you learn, just as in chess or indeed with Rubik's cubes—my daughter's really into those. I learned that there's actually a method, by the way, for solving them. There are competitions where people can solve a Rubik's Cube in 10 seconds. It's completely mind-boggling.
8.71: Anyway, what you have to figure out is that any move you make has consequences downstream of that note. If you set up a chord in a particular way, then it locks you into the next set of possibilities. So if you choose something that doesn't work, then even if that chord is by itself coherent, it's going to lead you into something where you get completely jammed up, and it doesn't work. You have to think multiple moves ahead.
8.72: Yeah, it's a complex task, but thousands of music students learn to do it. It's hard, but it's possible. One of the things that studying music has taught me is that there's a very big difference between extremely difficult and impossible. Extremely difficult is doable.
8.73: You said earlier that you're very high in openness. I also took the test, and I'm also very high in openness—I think it's like 96 or something. I was wondering if you have some artists or types of music that you've really enjoyed a lot that are really outside the box.
8.74: Oh, yeah, sure. Definitely. When I was first starting to study music, the stranger and the more out there, the better, as far as I was concerned. It was all kinds of things. I got very interested, particularly, in French and German avant-garde music of the 1950s. There were a bunch of composers from that era that this post-war generation, born in the 1920s, that I really gravitated towards.
8.75: There was an era, historically, that is completely singular in the history of music, which is the immediate post-war. There was this sense among the young artists at that time that civilization had narrowly escaped a complete cataclysm; it had very nearly just completely fallen to the ground. They were trying to come to grips with this.
8.76: One of the things that occurred to them was, to paraphrase Theodor Adorno, it's impossible after Auschwitz to write poetry in a 19th-century style. Once these things have blown up in the world, you don't see the world in the same way. A lot of the younger composers, born in the 1920s, who experienced the war firsthand and experienced the aftermath of it in all the big European capitals, were faced with this problem: Do you return to the aesthetics of the late 19th century?—which for them was a world that was gone; you can't go back there again. Or do you move forward with something else? And if you move forward, then what is that something else?
8.77: They developed these approaches that were marked by a technological utopianism, let's say, this belief in the possibilities of the future, the possibility that you could build maybe a new and better society out of the rubble of the old. For most of human cultural history, the pace of change was extremely slow—you wouldn't have really noticed much difference from one generation to the next, culturally and musically speaking. Things would be largely stagnant for centuries at a time, where if there was any change in the technical fabric of music, it would happen so slowly that you wouldn't really notice it over your lifetime.
8.78: It starts to speed up dramatically in the 20th century, and it produced all of these amazing things—where this had never happened before—where suddenly there's electronic music. And suddenly you can experiment with entirely new forms, entirely new types of harmony. You can produce microtones on instruments. You can do all kinds of crazy things. There's this excitement in the air about all of that, and also, along with it, this desire to turn away from a catastrophe into something else. So there is an extraordinary creative ferment in the air.
8.79: I was very interested in the music of that period, the composers such as Karlheinz Stockhausen, who is quite well known in Germany and internationally as well. The Beatles were huge fans of his work. In France, a figure like Pierre Boulez, B-O-U-L-E-Z, was another musician that I was very interested in. As far as pop music went, anything that was exploding with creative potential, where everything was new, stimulating, and unexpected, that's what I gravitated towards. So there's my answer.
8.80: Why isn't the grace note just written like a regular note with a link to the next one?
8.81: Because it's not played the same way. There's a couple of distinctions—some of the distinctions are functional or technical in nature. The grace note allows you to put an accent on a dissonant tone, for example, and immediately resolve it. This has to do with the grammar of music and the rules for resolving dissonances.
8.82: But you could start a piece like this [plays ornamental B ♭–D leading to A, G], where the upper note that I started on is an accented passing tone or an accented dissonance [plays ornamental B♭–D leading to A, G], and it's resolved on a weak beat. And in the Baroque here, you might have written that as a grace note, so it was not to have the dissonant tone appear to fall right on the beat. So there's a technical reason for that.
8.83: But also in terms of performance, it's not the same thing. A grace note or a string of grace notes implies a rhythmic flexibility that can be very difficult to obtain if you write it with a precise rhythmic value.
8.84: The third part of it is that in Baroque music, the ornaments were not always written in the score. They were often, in fact, not given, and it was expected as a part of the performance practice of the day that the performer would embellish this skeletal melodic line with ornaments, and the performer would know how to do that because they would have absorbed this whole repertoire of ornamental figures. So there are historical, technical, and aesthetic reasons for the use of grace notes.
